20023-the-letters-of-queen-victoria-vol-:
Queen Victoria came to the throne in 1837, and her letters from 1837 to 1843 fill the first volume of her published letters. The book pairs those letters with background on her family and the House of Brunswick. Her father came from that old German house, which also ruled Hanover.

Readers see a young queen in her first years of rule, writing in her own words. The opening pages trace her birth and family ties before the letters begin. For anyone who wants the start of the Victorian age from the queen herself, the volume gives a direct, personal record.
20920-morale-a-story-of-the-war-of-1941-:
An Area Officer loathes his quiet coast watch in Morale, Murray Leinster's tale of the war of 1941-43. He longs for the west, where strange fighting flares each day. Guarding calm shores for the sake of civilian morale galls his young, keen spirit.

Leinster, a master of pulp science fiction, wrote this as a future-war tale. Odd weapons and new tactics haunt its imagined conflict's edges. Morale itself, the faith of plain folk, stands as a weapon in play. The story shows how writers between the world wars dreamed the next war, half right and half wildly wrong.
a-lover-s-complaint-pg1543: A young woman's anguished confession fills this edition of Shakespeare's enigmatic narrative poem: seduced by a charming, faithless youth, she weeps over her ruin yet admits she would yield again. Forty-seven dense stanzas of regret and desire. Beautiful, puzzling, and very human.
arxiv-2510-00143:
Eugene Yang and three colleagues at the Johns Hopkins Human Language Technology Center wrote this 2025 report on the TREC 2024 NeuCLIR track. NeuCLIR tests search systems that find news and technical documents across languages. The team entered every task, combining several ranking and translation methods. Their report records what worked, what failed, and why.

Their pipeline paired a fast retriever with rerankers based on mT5 and GPT-4 models. Variants learned from translated data or from examples a language model generated. GPT-4 reranking generally beat the mT5 reranker, which beat plain neural search overall. Longer passages, cut into 450-token chunks, gave a clear boost while halving the index. For report writing, systems that packed in the most checked facts scored best with the judges.
arxiv-2510-00443:
Lin Lin wrote this 2025 survey paper on the mathematics of quantum signal processing, a core quantum algorithm technique. The method encodes a polynomial as a product of simple two-by-two matrices set by phase factors. It underlies quantum singular value transformation, used for simulating Hamiltonians and solving linear systems. Lin reviews what is now known about computing those phase factors reliably.

Recent progress generalizes the method beyond polynomials to wider function classes. Other advances pin down the true computational cost of finding phase factors. Numerical stability, long a practical worry, gets a careful treatment in the survey. Solutions lean on a surprising mix of nonlinear Fourier analysis and fast polynomial arithmetic. Structured matrix elimination also plays a key role in the newest algorithms. The article, written for a major mathematics congress, maps the field for newcomers and specialists alike.
arxiv-2510-00543:
Zeyu Chen and five colleagues published this 2025 paper on training medical language models across hospitals that cannot share patient data. Privacy law forbids pooling records, yet each hospital's data skews differently. Their approach fine-tunes models federatively, using low-rank adapters that are cheap to exchange. Local adapters train on site, then merge into a global update round by round.

A blockchain identity scheme keeps track of which model belongs to which institution. Experiments used deliberately lopsided medical text datasets to stress the method. Federated tuning improved generalization across clients compared with isolated training. Crucially, the weakest client gained the most, narrowing the fairness gap. Convergence stayed stable despite the extreme heterogeneity of the data. The authors present federated low-rank tuning as a practical template for multi-center medical AI. Knowledge flows between institutions while raw records never leave home.
arxiv-2510-00643:
Gruntkowska at KAUST and Gaponov bring error feedback to the Muon family of optimizers in this 2025 arXiv paper on distributed deep learning. New optimizers such as Muon, Scion, and Gluon exploit each network layer's geometry through linear minimization over non-Euclidean norm balls. They train large models well on one machine, but no principled distributed version existed, and communication costs in clusters stayed unaddressed. Earlier distributed attempts were heuristic, without convergence guarantees.

Their algorithm, EF21-Muon, compresses communication in both directions and repairs compression errors with an error feedback memory. It handles stochastic gradients and momentum, and it reduces to the original optimizers when compression is switched off. The theory covers non-Euclidean smoothness and matches the best known Euclidean rates. NanoGPT experiments showed up to seven times lower communication cost with no loss of accuracy.
arxiv-2510-00843:
Noda computes partition functions for two-dimensional Coulomb gases with circular singularities in this 2025 arXiv paper on random matrix theory. The model places repelling points in the plane under a radial potential, like eigenvalues of random normal matrices. A weight function with a root singularity and a jump on a circle inside the droplet makes the partition function encode counting statistics. Precise asymptotics for such setups were partly conjectural.

Noda establishes full large-n asymptotic expansions for the moment generating function of a certain random polynomial built from the points' moduli. The expansion is written in parabolic cylinder functions, which confirms a conjecture of Byun and Charlier. The result gives the first free energy expansion for Coulomb gases with general circular root- and jump-type singularities. Even the previously studied zero-jump case gains new formulas. The tools include the Euler-Maclaurin summation formula applied with care.
arxiv-2510-01143:
Dong and seven co-authors, spanning Meta, Carnegie Mellon University, and Yale, propose Bridge in this 2025 arXiv paper on language model inference. Services sample many responses to one prompt and pick or combine the best, yet each sample is generated blind to the others. That independence wastes information, since an insight in one rollout could rescue another. Bridge rethinks batched hidden states as a holistic tensor, so parallel generations can exchange information while decoding.

The addition is cheap, adding a few percent of parameters to the host model. In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, Bridge raised relative accuracy gains by up to fifty percent and made correct answers more consistent. Trained once, it scales to any generation width and beats independent sampling. It composes with post-generation aggregation method, such as best-of-N selection. The authors frame interdependence as an axis for inference scaling.
arxiv-2510-02043:
Karnoor and Choudhury estimate full-body pose from sparse wearable sensors without user-specific training in this 2025 paper. Pose tracking from a few on-body sensors fails to generalize because location readings scale with each user's body size. Conditional diffusion models learned that dependency and stumbled on new users. The authors reformulate the task as an inverse problem instead.

Their method, InPose, conditions a pretrained diffusion model on rotational measurements alone. A likelihood term built from the measured locations then guides the generative sampling. The output is the pose sequence that best explains the sparse signals for any body. Zero-shot generalization follows because rotations carry less body-size bias than positions. Applications range from rehabilitation and sports coaching to home virtual reality. The design separates what the prior knows about human motion from what the sensors actually measured. That separation is what lets one model serve unseen users.
arxiv-2510-02143:
Su and seven co-authors test whether authors can spot their own best work in this 2025 science-of-science paper. Peer review must find high-potential papers in a flood of submissions, a task growing harder in fast fields like AI. The authors asked researchers at a leading AI conference to rank their own submissions by quality. In total, over thirteen hundred researchers ranked more than twenty-five hundred papers.

Tracked for over a year, self-rankings proved remarkably prophetic. Papers authors ranked highest earned twice as many citations as their lowest-ranked ones. Self-rankings were sharpest at spotting future hits with very high citation counts. They also beat peer review scores at predicting citation outcomes. Game-theoretic reasoning explains why: authors hold private knowledge of their work's depth and promise. The authors suggest conferences could mine self-rankings as a cheap signal.
arxiv-2510-02243:
Nguyen, Tran, Nguyen, and Pham package retrieval-augmented question answering into a builder's framework in this 2025 paper. RAG systems answer questions by fetching documents into a language model's context. Assembling a good one still means hand-wiring data preparation, fine-tuning, and evaluation. AccurateRAG supplies the whole pipeline as one framework.

Tools cover raw dataset processing and fine-tuning data generation. Embedding and language model fine-tuning sit beside output evaluation in the same workflow. Developers can build and test a complete RAG application locally. Experiments report the framework beating previous strong baselines on benchmark datasets. The authors claim new state-of-the-art question-answering performance from systems built with it. Industrial backing from Qualcomm AI Research signals deployment intent. The contribution is engineering consolidation: fewer bespoke scripts between an idea and a measured QA product. Accuracy work shifts from plumbing to the parts that matter.
arxiv-2510-02343:
Buck-Kaeffer and co-authors release BluePrint, a dataset for training social media personas. Their 2025 paper addresses a missing standard in agent research. Language models can simulate online crowds at scale. Such studies would be hard or unethical with real people. Yet no shared data existed for tuning realistic agents. The team built SIMPACT, a toolkit for capturing behavior with privacy care. It frames user modeling as next action prediction. Public Bluesky posts about politics supplied the raw material. Anonymized users were clustered into behavioral personas.

Models were scored at cluster and population levels. Fine-tuned models matched persona writing styles well. They struggled to copy broader behavior patterns, though. Action diversity and community habits proved hard to fake. Text realism alone does not make a believable crowd. The dataset gives the field a common measuring stick.
arxiv-2510-02843:
Wach presents the first H.E.S.S. analysis of a famous supernova remnant. The remnant is IC 443, the wreck of a star that exploded long ago. It sits about fifteen hundred parsecs away. Its shock wave is plowing into a dense molecular cloud. That crash makes it a prime site for cosmic-ray acceleration. The H.E.S.S. telescopes in Namibia recorded its very-high-energy gamma rays.

The data came from just over eleven hours of viewing in 2004 and 2005. The signal was modest but clear enough to map. Its shape and spectrum matched earlier results from Fermi-LAT, MAGIC, and VERITAS. A joint look across wavelengths favors a hadronic source. In that picture, fast protons strike the cloud gas. Their collisions spawn the gamma rays through pion decay. The study adds an independent check on a key cosmic-ray laboratory.
arxiv-2510-02943:
Westling Dolling, Henry, and Ahlkrona steady the math of ice sheet models. Floating ice shelves are often modeled with the Shallow Shelf Approximation. Big steps make the ice thickness swing and crash the run. Their fix is the Thickness Stabilization Scheme, or TSS. It slips an extra thickness equation into the driving stress term. The term then acts as if it were treated implicitly.

Tests covered calm and high-shear shelf setups. Without TSS, high-shear runs broke past five-year steps. With TSS, steps of fifty to one hundred years stayed sound. Errors in thickness and speed stayed under one percent there. Even a ten-thousand-year step held stable, though accuracy faded. Longer steps free computing power for finer grids instead. The trick should help the coupled climate models as well. Long forecasts of Antarctica and Greenland stand to gain most.
arxiv-2510-03143:
Khodamoradi, Mansouri, and Zilles map the difficulty of clustering when the data is nearly stable. Clustering groups points under objectives like k-Means and k-Median. Stable instances barely change when costs are nudged. The authors use a broader notion called almost stable. It sits near a classic resilience idea from Balcan and Liang. A penalty variant lets each point opt out of clustering for a price.

Some almost stable cases fall to polynomial-time algorithms. Other cases resist every exact method for a long time. Super-polynomial lower bounds back that hardness claim. The bounds rest on the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a standard belief. Small doubling dimension shapes much of the analysis. One question stays open at the end. No one knows if near-optimal approximations exist for almost stable cases. Their closeness must hold in cost and in structure alike.
arxiv-2510-03243:
Tao and co-authors schedule language model requests by guessing answer length from the prompt itself. First-come serving lets one long job block many short ones. Shortest-job-first would fix that, but lengths are unknown ahead. Their scheduler, PARS, learns to rank prompts pairwise instead. A margin ranking loss trains the length predictor. Scheduling then approximates shortest-first with little overhead. The system plugs directly into the vLLM serving stack.

Experiments spanned several models and real inference datasets. Average and tail latency both improved over classic policies. Existing learning-based schedulers also fell behind PARS. Reasoning workloads, with long hidden chains, benefited too. Predictors even transferred across different model families. A ranker trained on one model scheduled another's traffic well. That portability lowers the cost of adopting the scheme. The code and datasets are slated for open release. Interactive services feel latency wins most directly.
arxiv-2510-03443:
Chems-Eddin, Feryouch, and Tamoussit wrote a 2025 arXiv note on the Krull dimension of rings of integer valued polynomials. Such polynomials have fraction coefficients yet return whole values on a chosen set. Their rings sit between polynomial rings and rational ones. Krull dimension counts the longest chain of prime ideals and measures a ring's size in a sense. The note computes that dimension for choices of base domain and test set.

The authors treat a wider ring where polynomial entries come from a larger domain than the values must land in. Results vary with the class of the base ring, echoing surprises for polynomial rings. For nice rings the dimension grows by one, but exotic rings can break that pattern. The note gives ring theorists a map of when the answer holds. It extends work on a topic that began with Ostrowski and Pólya over a century ago.
arxiv-2510-03643:
Carter and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper training a reinforcement learning controller for deep brain stimulation using only brain signals that doctors can measure in patients. Stimulation eases Parkinson's symptoms, and learning controllers can adjust its frequency and amplitude. Earlier controllers leaned on biomarkers available only in brain on chip simulations, not in living patients. This team trained a TD3 agent on a model of the basal ganglia, feeding it in vivo measurable activity. 

The controller suppressed biomarkers tied to Parkinson's severity more strongly than clinical stimulation patterns. It did so while relying only on information an implant could sense. That measurability is the paper's central advance, since a controller is useless if its inputs cannot exist in a patient. Personalized agents become plausible once the inputs are realistic. Battery life should benefit, because stimulation fires when needed rather than constantly. The work moves stimulation closer to clinical trials.
arxiv-2510-03843:
Nguyen and colleagues at Google wrote this 2025 arXiv paper about Smart Paste, a tool that fixes pasted code automatically. Inside Google, code is pasted about four times more often than it is typed. Pasted code usually needs edits, from renaming variables to matching local style rules. The paper describes how the team built and scaled it across a huge codebase.

Smart Paste suggests the needed edits right inside the code editor, and developers can accept or ignore each suggestion. Since launch, developers have accepted 45 percent of its suggestions. Accepted edits now account for over one percent of all code written there. Each accepted suggestion saves developers about 22 keystrokes on average. The authors share lessons on data collection, model serving, and user interface design. Their account is a practical guide for shipping AI help inside real developer tools.
arxiv-2510-03943:
Samanta and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on moving data inside future supercomputers with light instead of copper wires. High-performance machines now move so much data that electrical links waste energy and lose signal quality. Stacking chips in three dimensions helps, but copper connections keep the same basic limits. The authors propose a stacked platform that sends fast data optically between layers.

Their design uses through-silicon optical vias to carry high-speed signals vertically through the stack. Electrical links remain in place for power delivery and short, low-latency hops. Benchmarks project the optical platform beating leading electrical designs on bandwidth per area. The team also reports progress on the physical vias and on a flexible die bonding method. They outline a path toward very low energy per bit for high-speed links. Such interconnects could decide how large and efficient future AI computing systems can become.
arxiv-2510-04143:
Kitsios and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper showing that code clone detectors falter on functionality they never saw in training. Semantic clone detection asks whether two snippets do the same thing, whatever their wording. Neural detectors score near perfectly on standard benchmarks, but those benchmarks test clones of familiar functionalities. Real developers also hunt clones of new functionality, and the authors identify three practical tasks with exactly that shape.

Re-evaluating six state-of-the-art models on unseen functionality, they found sharp F1 drops for specialized models, averaging about a third and reaching nearly half. Generative language models matched the specialists without task training and generalized far better, losing only a few points. The team then added contrastive learning: a contrastive classifier for the specialists and contrastive in-context learning for the language models. Both changes recovered much of the lost performance on unseen functionality.
arxiv-2510-04443:
Seth Bernstein and four coauthors wrote this 2025 review paper on the harms of generative AI in computing education. Much early research praised the benefits of AI help for students who learn to code. Reports of harm were scattered and had never been gathered in one place. The team ran a systematic review across three large research databases. Their search covered work from 2022 to 2025.

The search found more than sixteen hundred papers, and strict screening kept 224 of them. Four reviewers read each paper and coded the harms it reported. The harms fell into groups such as cheating risks, weaker thinking skills, and misplaced trust in AI output. The map showed which harms get studied often and which are barely touched. It also showed which student groups are rarely studied at all. The authors call for stronger evidence and wider study populations.
arxiv-2510-04543:
Elias Dubbeldam and three coauthors at the University of Amsterdam wrote this 2025 position paper on deep learning for table data. Neural methods still trail classic tree models on rows and columns, despite years of work. One camp draws graphs between features to capture how features interact. Those graph methods, the authors argue, train only for prediction scores. They never check whether the learned graph matches the true feature links.

The team tested that claim on synthetic data with known ground truth graphs. Existing graph methods failed to recover the true interactions in those tests. Forcing the true structure into a model improved its prediction scores as well. So the neglected target turns out to help the favored one. The authors call for structure aware training and for scoring interaction recovery as a standard metric. Trust and explanation both depend on getting the links right, they argue.
arxiv-2510-04643:
Xiangyu Li and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a team of AI agents that invests like a fund firm. Language model agents can analyze markets, but they differ from human firms in one way. Human pros rehearse trades in simulation before risking money, and they build views of trends. The team built QuantAgents, a system of four agents that meet and argue like a firm. One runs simulated trading, one watches risk, one reads news, and one manages.

Meetings cover market analysis, strategy design, and risk alerts, in a cycle. Agents earn feedback from two sources: real market results and the accuracy of their simulated forecasts. That second signal rewards foresight, not lucky outcomes. Across their tests, the framework led on the metrics they tracked. The headline result was a return near three hundred percent across three years. The authors present the structure as the source of the edge.
arxiv-2510-04743:
Luis Alfredo Ixquiac Méndez and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a detector that sees single electrons with fine detail. Electron microscopes need sensors that catch each electron and place it precisely. Direct detectors at low energies place events no finer than their pixel size, tens of microns across. The team built a detector around a cerium doped crystal that flashes when an electron lands. A camera reads flashes and locates each event.

At an electron energy of seventeen kiloelectronvolts, the device resolved detail under one micron across. It flagged single electrons with efficiency and purity both above eight in ten. At thirty kiloelectronvolts the score rose to about ninety six in a hundred. The detector also supported diffraction studies with very short sample distances. Those distances approach how far electrons travel in air before scattering. That hints at electron diffraction done at normal air pressure, without vacuum chambers.
arxiv-2510-05743:
Holme and Tsvetkova trace seventy-five years of artificial agents in social science. From the first programmable computers, researchers simulated societies to understand them. Each technology wave, from big data to language models, reshaped the questions asked. Their 2025 review follows that entwined history to today's agentic AI.

Early simulation studies struggled to convince a world that barely knew computers. Social systems science then rose, followed by intelligent game-theoretic agents. Big data brought an epistemic upheaval to the behavioral sciences. Now generative AI agents can play almost any role inside an experiment. Hand-run stochastic simulations from 1951 already show the method predating the hardware. The authors stress a two-way flow of ideas throughout. Success was long judged by machines behaving indistinguishably from humans. AI shaped social science while social science shaped AI's goals. That mirror motive still drives today's language-model experiments.
arxiv-2510-05943:
Tan and colleagues build Earl, a system for scaling agentic reinforcement learning. Agentic RL trains language models through multi-turn interaction and tool use. Context lengths explode during training, inflating memory until jobs crash. Their 2025 system attacks the memory and data-movement bottlenecks directly.

A parallelism selector adapts model and training parallelism across RL stages. It reacts dynamically to sequence length and system load. A data dispatcher exchanges intermediate batches in a layout-aware, decentralized way. Together they raise throughput and reduce long-context out-of-memory failures. Stable large-scale training proceeds without hard context limits or length penalties. A seventy-billion-parameter example shows batches outgrowing single GPU memory entirely. Hard caps on context, the usual workaround, restrict model potential. Intermediate tensors, the second bottleneck, stop dominating cross-device traffic. Systems design, not algorithms, is the contribution claimed here.
arxiv-2510-06443:
Shragai and four co-authors show phonons carry an intrinsic thermal Hall effect in a famous spin liquid candidate in a 2025 condensed matter paper. The thermal Hall effect appears in many magnetic insulators, but its origin stays controversial. Proposed carriers include magnons, phonons, and fractionalized spin excitations. In alpha-RuCl3, a quantized version was attributed to Majorana edge modes.

The team measured the acoustic Faraday effect ultrasonically. The measurements show its phonons possess Hall viscosity. This non-dissipative viscosity rotates phonon polarizations and deflects heat currents sideways. The resulting phonon effect is intrinsic, arising from phonon Berry curvature. It accounts for a significant fraction of the measured thermal Hall signal. The material's thermal Hall effect is therefore phononic and intrinsic. The acoustic Faraday technique emerges as a general probe for exotic states.
arxiv-2510-06743:
Maria Levchenko, a scholar in the digital humanities, builds a fair way to test AI reading of old documents. Her 2025 paper evaluates language models used for optical character recognition on historical texts. Standard accuracy scores miss period-specific errors that matter to historians. A model can also cheat if the test texts leaked into its training data.

Her framework adds two new measures for eighteenth-century Russian books printed in Civil font. One scores how well archaic characters are preserved. The other counts archaic characters inserted from the wrong century. She tested twelve multimodal models against traditional OCR tools. Gemini and Qwen models beat the traditional tools overall. Yet they showed a quirk she calls over-historicization, adding old letters from incorrect periods. Extra post-correction steps made results worse, not better. Her protocols also control contamination and test output stability over repeated runs.
arxiv-2510-07043:
Tian Qin leads a team benchmarking how well AI agents plan trips under constraints. Their 2025 paper introduces COMPASS, a multi-turn test for tool-using travel planners. Agents must respect hard limits like budgets and dates. They must also optimize soft preferences, such as scenic stops or short drives.

The benchmark builds a travel database for twenty national parks. It covers transport, lodging, and ticketing, with tools mirroring booking sites. A user simulator lets agents negotiate across several turns. Frontier models were put through the scenarios. Two gaps stood out. Agents reliably produced acceptable plans but rarely optimal ones. Performance also collapsed when trips combined flights, hotels, and permits together. Reasoning models beat non-reasoning ones on the same tasks. The open Qwen3-32B reached near twenty percent optimality, rivaling some closed systems. GPT-5 led the field. The gaps name exactly where travel agents still fail.
arxiv-2510-07243:
Enguehard and a large team present LeMAJ, a framework for grading legal answers given by language models. Their 2025 paper notes that legal analysis is long, nuanced, and hard to score. Reference answers are costly to produce for every question. Generic judging methods vary wildly in this domain. LeMAJ instead mimics how lawyers read. It breaks each answer into small, self-contained legal data points, then grades each point for correctness and relevance.

The method needs no reference answer, which suits real legal work. On the team's own data and on the open LegalBench set, LeMAJ beat several baseline judges. Its scores tracked human expert judgments more closely than rivals did. It also raised agreement among the human annotators themselves. The team released their legal data points for part of LegalBench. Finer-grained judging could make automated legal tools safer to evaluate.
arxiv-2510-07343:
Zhang, Brekelmans, and Ver Steeg introduce Local MAP Sampling, a framework that sharpens how diffusion models solve inverse problems. Their 2025 paper covers tasks like removing blur or filling missing image parts. Diffusion Posterior Sampling aims to cover the whole range of plausible originals. In practice, users usually want the single most accurate reconstruction. Optimization-style solvers often win there but lacked a clear probabilistic story. LMAPS solves a small best-estimate problem at each step along the diffusion path, stitching local answers into a global one.

The framework supplies a principled covariance shortcut and a steadier objective. Across restoration and scientific tasks, the method set new best quality marks. Gains of at least two decibels appeared on motion deblurring, JPEG repair, and quantization tasks. Inverse scattering benchmarks improved by well over one decibel too. The unified view explains why such solvers work so well.
arxiv-2510-07443:
Haine and co-authors build a condensed version of a scheme's homotopy type, a shape that encodes its loops and symmetries. Their 2025 paper refines two classical objects at once: the etale homotopy type and the proetale fundamental group. Condensed mathematics, which mixes topology with algebra, supplies the language. The first half proves the new object behaves well under integral maps and fits into the expected fiber sequences. A description through Galois categories, recently developed by some of the same authors, powers many arguments. Explicit computations include rings of continuous functions, grounding the abstraction in familiar terrain.

The second half delivers a surprise. The fundamental group of the complex affine line, expected to be tame, comes out nontrivial in this theory. A standard completion recovers the known proetale group, reconciling the two.
arxiv-2510-07543:
Douglas, Kenyon, Ovenhouse, Panitch, and Tata build a quantum version of the dimer model, a statistical mechanics staple. Dimers are domino-like objects that tile a graph, and counting their arrangements is a classic combinatorics problem. The 2025 paper imports machinery from quantum topology developed by Reshetikhin and Turaev, the same tradition that produced the Jones polynomial for knots. Applying it to knotted bipartite ribbon graphs in three-dimensional space yields a polynomial invariant unchanged by deformation.

As a concrete application, the authors compute the expected number of loops in the double dimer model on planar bipartite graphs, a quantity tied to height functions and critical phenomena. Companion code computes the paper's quantities for small examples. The construction bridges two mature fields that rarely talk: knot invariants and exactly solvable lattice models.
arxiv-2510-07643:
Asiryan wrote this 2025 number theory paper on the cuboid polynomial, a degree-eight polynomial tied to the search for a perfect cuboid. A perfect cuboid would be a box whose edges, face diagonals, and space diagonal are all whole numbers. None has ever been found. The polynomial studied here encodes part of that problem through two coprime integer parameters. Asiryan asks whether it can factor into smaller integer polynomials.

He proves that it cannot, so the polynomial is irreducible over the integers. The proof rules out each possible splitting pattern in turn. A four-plus-four split forces an equation that has no integer solutions. A two-plus-six split fails through an exact divisor test and a discriminant barrier. Every remaining pattern regroups into one of those dead ends. The result tightens the algebraic picture around a famous open problem, though the cuboid question stays open.
arxiv-2510-07843:
Park, Chae, and Heath wrote this 2025 article on speeding up virtualized radio access networks with SIMD hardware features. Mobile networks are moving from fixed boxes toward open, software-run designs. Running baseband processing on ordinary servers must still meet real-time and energy targets. SIMD instructions process many data values in a single step. The authors examine how well that parallelism fits the heaviest radio workloads.

Key physical-layer jobs such as channel estimation, MIMO detection, and error correction map naturally onto SIMD lanes. The article gives design guidelines drawn from that fit. Prototype results show clear throughput and energy gains over conventional CPU-only processing. The approach keeps the flexibility and easy integration that made virtualization attractive. Open problems remain in balancing workloads and handling mixed hardware. The authors frame SIMD as an enabling tool for flexible, efficient networks on the road to 6G.
arxiv-2510-08243:
S. Azam develops new structure tools for a class of Lie algebras in a 2025 arXiv paper in pure mathematics. Extended affine Lie algebras generalize the affine algebras used in algebra and physics. Their global structure is hard to grasp directly, so smaller local pieces matter a great deal. Local affine subalgebras, sitting inside the big algebra, help reveal how the whole is built.

Azam builds a localization theory, a formal way to pass from the whole algebra to local parts. The goal is to construct local substructures that carry real meaning, especially affine ones. As a natural side result, the work defines filtration for these algebras. A filtration is a chain of nested pieces that grades the algebra step by step. The study is driven by modular questions about integral forms of these algebras, the author notes.
arxiv-2510-08343:
Anne Müller, Mohd Kashif, and Nico Döttling build a translator from Haskell programs to encrypted circuits in a 2025 arXiv paper. Fully homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on data it cannot read. Only basic operations work on such ciphertexts, so programs must become Boolean or arithmetic circuits. Writing circuits by hand is tedious compared with normal coding.

Their transpiler converts Haskell, a high-level functional language, into Boolean circuits fit for encrypted runs. A second contribution runs the circuit gates in parallel, layer by layer, automatically. They test the tool on private information retrieval and on the AES encryption standard. Automated parallel runs beat some hand-tuned parallel versions of AES under encryption. With sixteen threads the AES evaluation took twenty-eight seconds. With one hundred threads it dropped to eight seconds.
arxiv-2510-08443:
Øyvind Auestad, Geir-Arne Fuglstad, and Annika Lang design a numerical method for noisy heat flow on surfaces in a 2025 arXiv paper. They study parabolic stochastic equations, where diffusion spreads a quantity while random noise keeps disturbing it. The noise follows Whittle-Matérn fields, whose roughness is set by powers of an elliptic operator. Computing on curved surfaces needs finite element methods adapted to that geometry.

Their fully discrete scheme approximates both the solution and the noise with surface finite elements. Matching the noise discretization to its covariance structure is the key design choice. They derive strong and pathwise convergence rates, describing how errors shrink as the mesh refines. Numerical experiments verify the predicted rates in practice. The method targets applications like membranes and thin films, where surface geometry and random forcing both matter.
arxiv-2510-08543:
Nikhil Reddy Varimalla and co-authors benchmark how well video language models understand cultural norms in a 2025 arXiv paper. Models deployed worldwide must grasp social situations through local cultural lenses. Their benchmark, VideoNorms, holds over one thousand video and norm pairs from United States and Chinese cultures. Annotations draw on speech act theory and mark adherence, violations, and supporting evidence.

A human-AI pipeline built the data: a teacher model proposed annotations, and trained human experts validated and corrected them. Benchmarking open-weight video models revealed consistent trends across systems. Models did worse on norm violations than on adherence, and worse on Chinese culture than United States culture. They also struggled to cite non-verbal evidence and to name the exact norm behind a speech act. Unlike humans, models performed worse in formal, non-humorous contexts.
arxiv-2510-08643:
Yong Yu and co-authors describe the digitization of astronomical glass plates at Shanghai Astronomical Observatory in a 2025 arXiv paper. Old photographic plates hold a century of sky positions that modern astrometry can still mine. Commercial scanners failed their tests: poor positioning repeatability, uneven illumination, and high distortion. Micrometer-level accuracy demanded a purpose-built digitizer instead.

SHAO's first dedicated digitizer, built from 2013 to 2017 with a Japanese partner, used line scanning in strips. Assembling the strips yielded complete plate images, and the machine digitized thirty thousand Chinese astronomical plates. Shanghai's government then authorized the lab to serve surveying, medicine, and biology as well. A new generation, developed from 2019 to 2024, rides on air-bearing guide rails for smoother motion. It adds a high-precision sCMOS camera, a vibration-isolated foundation, and an electro-pneumatic plate holder.
arxiv-2510-08743:
Cox and a large team of astronomers present a catalog of galaxies from the CEERS survey in this 2025 arXiv paper. The survey used the James Webb Space Telescope to image a patch of sky called the Extended Groth Strip. The catalog gives brightness measures, estimated distances, and physical traits for more than eighty thousand galaxies. Older Hubble images of the same field add detail at shorter wavelengths.

The team measured galaxy light with detection software run in two modes, one tuned for bright objects and one for faint ones. They estimated distances by fitting model spectra to the observed colors, and checked those estimates against galaxies with known distances. The distance errors stayed small, though they grew for fainter and more distant galaxies. Three separate fitting codes produced the masses and star formation rates, and the full set ships in a public data release.
arxiv-2510-08843:
Goldberg, Poss, and Shtern offer a new way to describe uncertainty when planning under the unknown, in this 2025 arXiv paper on robust optimization. Planners often guard a decision against a whole set of possible values for shaky inputs. Classic sets treat each input separately, missing the fact that linked quantities move together. The smooth uncertainty set instead caps how far apart each pair of inputs can drift. Experts can set those caps from physics, or from known correlations.

The team then shows how to solve the guarded problems efficiently. Special structures allow compact rewrites, a column generation method builds the answer piece by piece, and the worst-case subproblem becomes a cheapest-flow puzzle on a network. In experiments drawn from published problems, their model's decisions matched a leading curved-set model in quality but arrived far faster. Their solver also beat standard methods on both time and memory use.
arxiv-2510-09243:
Gonella and co-authors build the first large dataset for teaching AI to write emergency warning messages, in this 2025 arXiv paper. During floods, attacks, and other crises, clear warnings save lives, yet language research on emergencies has mostly classified messages rather than generating them. CrisiText contains over four hundred thousand warning messages spanning almost eighteen thousand crisis situations across thirteen scenario types. The team built it from existing crisis descriptions, extended into chains of unfolding events.

Each event is paired with a warning written under expert guidelines, keeping terminology correct and advice factual. Every message also ships with three weaker variants, so researchers can study quality differences. The authors benchmarked supervised fine-tuning, preference alignment, and zero-shot and few-shot prompting. They also tested performance on unfamiliar scenario types and whether an automatic post-editor improves drafts.
arxiv-2510-09343:
Jinyuan Liu and six co-authors work on thermal infrared image enhancement in a 2025 arXiv paper. Infrared cameras sense heat rather than light, and their images often suffer noise, weak contrast, and blur at the same time. Older methods fix one flaw at a time, while all-in-one methods built for normal photos transfer poorly because heat imaging works differently.

The team proposes a network called PPFN, which uses prompt pairs drawn from the thermal imaging process itself. For each kind of damage, the matching prompts guide the network's features, so one model can adapt to single or mixed damage. A selective training scheme then teaches it harder mixed cases step by step. The authors also built a high-quality benchmark across many scenes. Their method improved results by almost nine percent on complex damage while keeping key structures sharp.
arxiv-2510-09443:
Raffaele Cristodaro, Benjamin Kraner, and Claudio Tessone examine what sanctions did to a privacy tool in a 2025 arXiv paper. Tornado Cash is a smart contract protocol that hides the link between deposits and withdrawals on a blockchain. In August 2022, the United States Treasury sanctioned it, giving researchers a rare natural experiment on decentralised finance.

Drawing on transaction data from Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, and Polygon, the authors document a sharp and lasting drop after the sanctions. Transaction volume, user diversity, and overall use of the protocol all fell and stayed low. They then track the partial lifting and final removal of the sanctions by the Office of Foreign Assets Control in March 2025. Activity recovered only partly, and the rebound stayed limited. The case shows how strongly regulation can bite, and also how hard full enforcement is in decentralised systems.
arxiv-2510-09843:
Ana-Maria Boldeanu and Mircea Neagu build a geometry around a classic ecology model in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Lotka-Volterra system describes species competing for a shared resource, the textbook equations of population dynamics. The authors ask what geometric structure those equations carry when viewed through the Lagrange-Hamilton formalism of mechanics.

Working with the least squares variational method, they develop the shapes the system produces. It is phrased in terms of nonlinear connections, d-torsions, and a Lagrangian Yang-Mills electromagnetic-like energy, borrowing the language of gauge theory for a biological system. From that viewpoint they then discuss the Jacobi stability of the competing-species dynamics. Jacobi stability concerns whether nearby paths converge or diverge. The paper contributes a worked example of how far the machinery of theoretical physics can be carried into models of living systems.
arxiv-2510-10043:
Krajewski and Włodek Kluźniak model accretion onto naked singularities in this 2025 arXiv paper in astrophysics. Almost every galactic core holds a supermassive compact object, presumed to be a Kerr black hole. The Event Horizon Telescope has finally let astronomers test that picture for our Galaxy and for M87 at scales near the gravitational radius.

A naked singularity is the rival possibility: a singularity not hidden behind an event horizon. The authors study how gas accreting onto such an object would look and behave. Comparing those predictions with black hole predictions gives observers a way to tell the two apart. The work sharpens what telescope data must show to rule the exotic option out.
arxiv-2510-10143:
Faust and F. Sottile attack the Spectral Edges Conjecture in this 2025 arXiv paper in spectral graph theory. The conjecture concerns discrete periodic operators, which model waves on repeating structures. It says the extrema of the dispersion relation, the curve linking wave frequency to momentum, occur in a single band, standing isolated and non-degenerate.

The authors present two infinite families of periodic graphs that satisfy the conjecture. Each verified family strengthens belief in the general claim and tests the tools used to study it. Corners of the graphs play a key role in their approach. The result supports the broader program of understanding how periodic structure shapes the spectra that govern waves in crystals and engineered materials.
arxiv-2510-10343:
Rensi, Pietro Rossi, and Marco Bianchetti learn the exact SABR model in this 2025 arXiv paper on financial mathematics. The SABR model is a standard tool for interest rate volatility. In practice it relies on an analytic approximation whose accuracy fails for high volatility, long maturities, and far out-of-the-money options, even admitting arbitrage.

Machine learning methods have tried to replace the approximation, but often simplify the SABR dynamics or skip systematic validation. The authors train a model against the full dynamics across the whole range of market conditions. An exact, fast SABR pricer would remove a known source of mispricing in rates markets, where tiny volatility errors move large sums.
arxiv-2510-10443:
Li, Yacheng Kang, and Ren-Xin Xu study heat-driven deformations in magnetized neutron stars in this 2025 arXiv letter in astrophysics. Fast-spinning neutron stars are prime targets for searches for steady gravitational waves. A star squeezed into a slight oval shape radiates such waves, and present detectors are listening for them.

The authors give the first study of thermal deformations in magnetized, super-Eddington neutron stars with column accretion, where matter funnels onto the magnetic poles. Strong fields guide heat unevenly through the crust, and the resulting hot and cold patches deform the star. Their estimates feed straight into detectability, since they set how strong the wave signal can be. The work links accretion physics with gravitational-wave astronomy.
arxiv-2510-10643:
Áron Holló and four co-authors extend a classic quantum simulation technique to systems that lose or gain energy, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Chebyshev expansion method computes how quantum states evolve in time, and it is well established for Hermitian systems with a bounded spectrum. Real open systems, though, are described by non-Hermitian matrices. The team shows the method remains valid across the entire complex plane, so it suits arbitrary non-Hermitian matrices too.

They find that the errors seen outside the usual spectral bounds come from numerical rounding, not from any fundamental limit. By choosing the spectral radius and time step carefully, these errors can be suppressed effectively. They derive an analytic upper bound for the rounding error, giving simulators a practical rule for picking time steps. As a demonstration, they compute how wave packets evolve in the Hatano-Nelson model, a standard non-Hermitian test case.
arxiv-2510-10943:
Thi-Nhung Nguyen and seven co-authors measure how bias spreads when language models talk to each other, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Single models are known to stereotype social groups. Multi agent systems, where several models collaborate, add new dynamics that were largely unexplored. The team proposes an evaluation framework with three agent level metrics tracking how bias emerges, propagates, and amplifies during interaction. They test systems across three bias benchmarks, varying the underlying models, group configurations, communication styles, and adversarial settings.

The results are stark. Communication triggered up to 70 percent new bias emergence, spread bias across more than 80 percent of agents, and amplified stereotypes more than threefold in their experiments. Denser and more competitive communication generally made bias worse. The systems also proved highly vulnerable to simple bias injection attacks, and existing defenses gave only limited protection.
arxiv-2510-11043:
Yuemeng Xu and sixteen co-authors describe Gryphon, the gateway system ByteDance built for petabit scale cloud traffic, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Traditional gateways based only on switching chips hit hard limits: small on chip tables and little flexibility. Pure software gateways cannot sustain terabit line rates. Gryphon integrates data processing units directly into the chip's forwarding path. This hybrid expands table scale by up to a thousandfold while sustaining 1.6 terabits per second at only about eight microseconds of added average latency.

A hierarchical co offloading scheme runs the data plane, keeping over 99.9 percent of traffic on the fast path with software fallback for complex operations. In the control plane, an abstraction layer called P4Bridge decouples hardware specifics from policy configuration. Gryphon has run in production for over a year on hundreds of nodes across multiple availability zones.
arxiv-2510-11343:
Drones must broadcast a Remote ID with their position and identity, but the standard does not specify how receivers can trust that the broadcast is genuine. Jason Veara, Manav Jain, Kyle Moy, and Aanjhan Ranganathan design an authentication layer for them in this 2025 arXiv security paper. Spoofing, relay, and replay attacks against unauthenticated Remote ID could undermine surveillance and future drone-to-drone coordination.

Their system TBRD builds on the TESLA broadcast authentication protocol and on trusted execution environments in mobile devices, adding a verification mechanism scoped to each mission. The design stays compatible with standards and with the limited computing power of aircraft. Evaluation used a standards-compatible proof of concept plus a simulated four-drone swarm mission under adversarial conditions. TBRD cut authentication overhead by half compared with digital signatures and reduced computation time a hundredfold, arguing it can scale within current Remote ID infrastructure.
arxiv-2510-11443:
Jacobi elliptic functions extend the sine and cosine to problems whose period depends on amplitude. Hajime Sato and co-authors extend that classic theory in this 2025 arXiv analysis paper. Their new functions and integrals carry three parameters instead of one, tied to equations involving the p-Laplacian.

The authors construct Wallis-type integral formulae for the new functions, named after the classic product formulas for pi. For the new integrals they derive a Legendre-type relation, equivalent to Elliott's identity for Gaussian hypergeometric series. They also prove nontrivial inequalities about the binomial expansions of these functions. When the parameters take classic values, the usual theory comes back.
arxiv-2510-12143:
Harsh Kasyap and four co-authors poison federated learning through its conscience. Federated systems train across many clients without moving data, which invites poisoning. Bias also spreads innocently through skewed local data. Their 2025 arXiv paper weaponizes that channel on purpose: a fairness-constrained tuning attack.

The malicious client trains its model to increase a fairness loss, scored by tuning against metrics like demographic parity and equalized odds, while keeping global accuracy intact. Bias that preserves accuracy is sneaky and hard to spot, since dashboards watch accuracy, not equity. Tested against leading Byzantine-robust and fairness-aware aggregation schemes across data sets and settings, the attack raised bias by up to ninety percent. Most sobering, one malicious client sufficed. Defenses tuned for accuracy sabotage, the study shows, can wave through an attacker whose payload is discrimination itself. Fairness checks must become a security wall, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2510-12543:
Benjert, Lakis, Lengler, and Ravi pin down the diameter of a random graph model designed to mimic real world networks, in a 2025 arXiv computer science paper. Geometric inhomogeneous random graphs place vertices in space with varying importance, copying properties seen in real networks. Their diameter, the longest shortest path between two vertices, governs the runtime of many protocols.

The authors prove the diameter of the threshold version of the model grows proportionally to the logarithm of the number of vertices. The result was previously known only in one dimension, where the proof leaned heavily on that setting. Their proof combines a Peierls type argument with a new renormalization scheme, and replaces topological connectivity arguments with cleaner recent machinery. A simple construction gives the matching lower bound. Because runtimes on these graphs track runtimes on real networks in practice, the theorem informs expectations for real algorithms.
arxiv-2510-12843:
Tiwari and Chauhan propose a new neuron model for spiking neural networks in this 2025 arXiv paper. These networks communicate with brief electrical-style spikes and suit energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware, chips modeled on the brain, but they forget earlier tasks when learning new ones in sequence. The core tension is stability versus plasticity, keeping old knowledge while absorbing new signals.

Their model, Local Timescale Gating, gives each neuron two parallel traces, one fast and one slow, plus a learned gate that adjusts how much each trace counts locally. A variance-tracking rule, inspired by biological homeostasis, keeps firing activity steady. On a hard temporal classification benchmark the model reached clearly higher final accuracy than a recent continual learning baseline, and it needs no external replay memory. The design also maps onto Intel's Loihi chip features.
arxiv-2510-12943:
Borah, Jin, and Mihalcea study how curiosity varies across cultures, and whether language models mirror that variation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Curiosity drives human questioning, but its style and topics differ by society. Using Yahoo! Answers data from many countries, the authors built CUEST, a framework measuring human-model alignment in curiosity through language style and topic preference, grounded in social science ideas.

Across open and closed models, they found that language models flatten cross-cultural diversity, expressing curiosity in ways that align more closely with Western countries. Fine-tuning strategies designed to induce curiosity narrowed the human-model alignment gap by up to half. The authors also show that matching a culture's curiosity patterns improves a model's adaptability there, which they argue matters for future natural language research.
arxiv-2510-13143:
Niimi studies how example choice and chance interact in language model ensembles in this 2025 arXiv paper. One-shot predictions, where a model sees a single example before answering, are very sensitive to which example is picked and how diverse ensemble members' outputs are. Niimi varies both factors: how representative the example is, and the sampling temperature that sets output diversity.

Two one-shot strategies were compared. One used centroid-based representative examples chosen to sit at the center of a class. The other used randomly sampled examples. Both ran across settings. The representative strategy with higher temperature clearly beat random selection on both classification and regression style scores. It even exceeded five-shot prompting, where the model sees five examples, by wide margins on both measures. Niimi concludes that representative selection plus controlled diversity is the practical recipe for effective one-shot ensembles.
arxiv-2510-13343:
Takayama and Fujita propose a multi-agent learning model that pays attention to the order in which agents act. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds on the Multi-Agent Transformer, a recent model that treats agent decisions as a sequence. Such models improved results, yet they never explicitly weighed which agent should move first. The work extends an earlier short conference paper.

Their model, AOAD-MAT, adds a subtask that predicts which agent should act next. This prediction is folded into the training loss, so the system learns both good actions and a good acting order. The design keeps a Transformer-based actor-critic structure, which judges actions while a policy network chooses them. Tests on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge and Multi-Agent MuJoCo benchmarks show AOAD-MAT beating the original MAT and other baselines. The gains support the value of learning action order directly.
arxiv-2510-13543:
Cohen builds a fuzzing framework that hunts prompt injection flaws inside AI-powered web browsers. His 2025 arXiv paper targets agentic browsers, which follow instructions and act with the user's privileges. Hidden instructions on a webpage can trick such an agent into unwanted actions. Testing for these flaws inside a real browser gives full context and observability.

The fuzzer generates malicious page content from templates or by mutating attacks with a language model. Immediate feedback on whether the agent obeyed a hidden instruction steers later attempts. The system detected weaknesses with zero false positives in his tests. All tested browsers blocked simple attacks, yet failures grew as mutations sharpened. By the tenth iteration, even the best tools failed in 58 to 74 percent of cases, and page summarization features proved riskiest in his runs. Stronger generator models found first successes much faster.
arxiv-2510-13643:
Khan and Krawczyk probe two weak spots of a DINOv2-based anomaly detector: attacks and uncalibrated scores. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds on AnomalyDINO, a training-free detector that compares deep features by nearest neighbours. Such few-shot detectors now inspect products with only a handful of normal examples. Their safety under attack, and the meaning of their confidence, were barely examined.

To attack the system in a white-box way, the authors attach a small linear head to frozen features just for crafting perturbations. Standard gradient attacks then degrade every score they track on two benchmark datasets. Tiny, invisible tweaks can flip neighbour relations and force confident errors. Raw anomaly scores also prove uncalibrated, so confidence and correctness drift apart. A simple Platt scaling fix turns scores into usable probabilities. Calibrated outputs flag attacked inputs through higher uncertainty, a practical defence baseline.
arxiv-2510-13843:
Chou, Qin, and Li turn electronic health records into text-like chains so a language model can learn patient profiles. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces SerialBEHRT, a base model for clinical data. Health records are tabular and event-based, clashing with how language models read step by step. That clash hides long-range patterns across a patient's many visits.

SerialBEHRT extends the SciBERT language model with extra training on structured record chains. This ordering lines clinical events up in time, letting the model learn time and context links. The result is a richer profile of each patient's history. Testing targets forecasting which antibiotics will work, a concrete problem in hospital drug use. SerialBEHRT beat leading record representation methods in their benchmarks. Its edge was also steadier across settings than rivals managed. The authors credit the time-ordering trick as the key design choice.
arxiv-2510-14143:
Alexandr Kalinin and co-authors introduce cubic, an open-source Python library that speeds up image analysis with graphics processors, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Modern microscopy produces ever-larger two- and three-dimensional data sets, but bioimage tools often lack proper interfaces, GPU support, or broad 3D capabilities, and they integrate poorly with compute-heavy workflows.

Cubic augments the widely used SciPy and scikit-image interfaces with GPU-accelerated options drawn from the CuPy and RAPIDS cuCIM libraries. Its interface is device-agnostic. Operations run on the GPU when the data already live there and on the CPU otherwise. Workflows from preprocessing through segmentation and feature extraction speed up with no rewrite. The team tested cubic by benchmarking operations and by rebuilding published deconvolution and segmentation pipelines, achieving large speedups while keeping fidelity, which they present as a foundation for scalable, reproducible bioimage analysis.
arxiv-2510-14243:
Caolu Xu and co-authors introduce spatial computing communications, a framework for running multi-user virtual reality across distributed edge-computing networks without lag or energy waste, in this 2025 arXiv paper. VR is demanding: many users share a virtual space while their positions and the base stations serving them keep changing, and every millisecond of delay breaks presence.

The framework models physical space, meaning users and base stations, and virtual space jointly, using a description of user dynamics and resource needs. Deploying resources becomes a multi-objective optimization balancing latency against energy across edge servers. Their solver, MO-CMPO, blends supervised learning with preference-guided reinforcement learning fine-tuning on a sparse graph neural network to generate Pareto-optimal tradeoffs. In simulations using cellular base station data, the method achieved better tradeoff quality and lower decision latency than baselines, giving practical deployment rules for edge-supported VR.
arxiv-2510-14543:
Jiang, Wang, and Chen, in a 2025 arXiv paper, tackle few-shot learning across images and text. Here a model must sort new examples after seeing only a few labeled ones. Models that link vision and language start with a rough alignment between the two. Fine-tuning methods then adjust it slightly. The authors note that all such methods adjust in a single step. That is too weak when image and text features are heavily tangled.

Their method, Flow Matching Alignment, learns a velocity field instead. That is a rule that moves features gradually, so alignment improves over many small steps. A fixed pairing plan keeps categories matched during training. Added noise eases the shortage of training examples, and a solver that stops early saves time while helping accuracy. Across several benchmarks and model backbones, the method beat one-step approaches. The largest gains came on the hardest datasets.
arxiv-2510-14743:
Puskás and a large team of co-authors ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether galaxy mergers in the early universe lit a fire under star formation and black hole growth. Mergers are credited with both at later times, but evidence at high redshift is thin. Using JADES survey data, the team assembled a mass-complete sample of 2,095 young galaxies and identified major merger pairs probabilistically.

They built a control sample of non-merging galaxies matched in redshift, mass, isolation, and environment. Pairs closer than about twenty kiloparsecs showed a modest boost in specific star formation rate, about twelve percent above the controls, fading by fifty kiloparsecs. Averaged histories split pairs into two families: systems still approaching, with rising star formation, and systems past closest pass, which peaked earlier. Surprisingly, pairs showed no significant excess of active galactic nuclei, so encounters alone do not seem to switch black holes on.
arxiv-2510-14843:
Zahr and Liva analyze, in a 2025 arXiv paper, error-correcting codes designed to work at any rate while staying close to the theoretical limit. MacKay-Neal codes are a flexible family whose rate can be adapted, and spatial coupling, linking many small code blocks into a chain, is known to push decoding thresholds toward capacity. The authors combine the two: the inner code is a protograph-based spatially coupled low-density parity-check code.

Using density evolution, the standard tool for tracking decoding messages over iterations, they compute the ensembles' asymptotic thresholds. A specially defined parallel channel model makes the analysis tractable. The thresholds land within 0.15 decibels of capacity for the binary-input white Gaussian noise channel, across the full rate range from zero to one. One code family can thus serve slow, ultra-reliable links and fast ones almost equally well.
arxiv-2510-14943:
Yang and co-authors simplify how a language model can grade its reasoning, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Training with verifiable rewards teaches models to solve problems, but at test time no verifier is present, so they learn to self-verify. Earlier approaches made the model generate a solution, then a separate verification, using two prompt templates. The routine is slow.

The authors prove a shortcut. The true reward of a solution equals a score readable from one number. That number is the model's next-token log-probability for a chosen token at the solution's last token, adjusted by a constant and the KL coefficient. Their algorithm, LaSeR, adds a loss term aligning this last-token score with the verifier's reward, jointly improving reasoning and self-grading. At use time the score costs one extra token of inference. Experiments show better reasoning and stronger inference-time scaling from the self-reward.
arxiv-2510-15043:
Dufresne-Piché and Nadarajah generalize, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a family of high-order simulation schemes prized for running stably on unstructured grids. Energy stable flux reconstruction methods form a family of linearly stable variants, and each can be rewritten as a filtered discontinuous Galerkin scheme. That filtered viewpoint is the lever the authors use to widen the family.

They introduce Sobolev Stable discontinuous Galerkin schemes, a conservative, linearly stable generalization built through the filter framework, and review how generalizations relate to it. Von Neumann analysis compares the schemes with the extended variant. The two families behave differently in dispersion and dissipation, yet both raise the time step, the CFL limit, by a similar amount, with similar spectral accuracy. The edge goes to the new schemes: the parameter range over which they enlarge the time-stepping limit is larger, giving practitioners more room to tune.
arxiv-2510-15143:
Victor Gitton and Renato Renner settle an eight-year-old conjecture about quantum correlations in a small network, in this 2025 arXiv paper. When three parties share quantum systems from three separate sources, their measurement results can show non-classical patterns that no classical setup can reproduce. The triangle network is the simplest case with this feature, but its math is non-convex and hard, so general proof methods have been missing.

One test case is the Elegant Joint Measurement distribution, a tidy, highly symmetric pattern that quantum systems can produce in the triangle network and that many suspected no classical system could match. Gitton and Renner now prove that suspicion correct. They combined inflation, a causal inference technique, with symmetry reductions and a large-scale optimization algorithm to keep the computation feasible. Their computer-assisted proof runs in exact arithmetic, giving a firm certificate rather than a numerical hint.
arxiv-2510-15343:
Raghvender and six colleagues simulate a family of tellurite glasses at the atomic level to explain their prized optical behavior. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies glasses built from tellurium oxide mixed with thallium oxide and titanium oxide. Such glasses are strong nonlinear optical materials, useful for switching and amplifying light, but their performance depends on atomic structure that is hard to see directly.

Using first-principles molecular dynamics, the team built large models of the glasses and checked them against measured x-ray data. Adding thallium oxide broke the tellurium-oxygen network apart, lowering coordination and creating loose oxygen atoms. Adding titanium oxide did the opposite, stitching the network back together with small titanium-bearing rings. Their computed vibration spectra matched measured trends as the mix changed. A small share of titanium oxide kept the tellurite network's strong optical nonlinearity while restoring its connectivity, a useful recipe for glass designers.
arxiv-2510-16043:
Jordan Stone, Youssef Saleh, Darryl Wright, and Jess Riedel survey physics experts on whether our vacuum could decay and whether technology could trigger that decay. Vacuum decay would replace the present vacuum with a lower-energy one, and the new region would spread near light speed, rewriting physical law everywhere it reached. The stakes make expert judgement worth recording carefully.

Twenty experts answered what the authors believe is the first structured survey on both questions. Average replies put the chance that our vacuum is metastable below half, and the chance that arbitrarily advanced technology could induce decay, if decay is possible at all, lower still. Disagreement was wide on both points. Participants said progress hinges on theories beyond the standard model, and even believers in decay expected artificial induction to challenge a civilisation with galactic resources.
arxiv-2510-16243:
Lanke Fu and four co-authors attack a stellarator design trap: optimizing the plasma first and the coils second can yield beautiful physics wrapped in impossible magnets. Their remedy folds a fast coil model directly into the plasma optimization, a quasi-single-stage approach.

The proxy rests on QUADCOIL, a differentiable coil optimization code that scores realistic metrics like forces and permanent-magnet layouts at speeds earlier tools could not match. In one study the method redesigns the MUSE stellarator's permanent magnets with twenty-nine percent fewer magnets than the previous solution. In another, coils for the ARIES-CS concept cut both peak and average electromagnetic forces by twenty-seven percent. Designers can now balance plasma quality against coil cost inside one loop.
arxiv-2510-16443:
In a paired 2025 report, Dimitris Stefanopoulos and Andreas Voskou share their win in a defence contest. The task was to train a model that stays right on clean data and on attacked data. Attacks came from a shuffle trick that swaps values to break patterns. The event was part of the same ECML-PKDD 2025 physics challenge as their attack win.

First, the pair made 15 million fake training samples with that same shuffle trick. Then they trained a model with a shared-weight block plus a fusion tail. It scored 80 percent on mixed clean and attacked data. That beat the next team by two points and took first place.
arxiv-2510-16543:
Lasha Berezhiani, Gia Dvali, and Otari Sakhelashvili work out a time result in quantum gravity in 2025. Quantum gravity seeks one frame for gravity and quantum rules. They use a strict method, called BRST, that keeps the maths gauge-clean. A gauge is a free choice in how fields are drawn. Their aim is to state how the total energy driver acts in that frame.

They derive an exact identity for that driver in the bulk of space. Up to an edge term, it is a paired product of two BRST parts. That form shows time flow acts as a re-timing on true degrees of freedom. Yet they show this does not make time flow trivial. Backgrounds, bulk links, and scatter results still shift in real ways.
arxiv-2510-16643:
Aaron Ray leads five co-authors in a 2025 study on robots that grasp words about place. A 3D scene graph maps a room as objects linked by spatial ties. Language models can reason over such maps, but full maps swamp their text window. Their fix stores the graph in a graph database, not in the prompt. The model then pulls just the parts it needs per task.

A query tongue called Cypher is the model's tool for those pulls. Tests cover task steps and questions about scenes. Cypher pulls beat both full-window dumps and code-writing pulls by a lot. Wins hold for small local models and big cloud ones. Token use for scene facts drops sharply at the same time.
arxiv-2510-17043:
Md Ahmed Al Muzaddid and William J. Beksi improve person matching across cameras in a 2025 paper. Person re-identification links images of the same person across views. Systems describe each person with a feature summary. One summary per identity class acts as its representative.

Earlier work mostly used the plain average of a class's summaries. A few studies tried other representatives only during retrieval. The authors show those choices give weaker matching results. Their method picks generalized representatives beyond simple class averages. The number of representatives per class can be tuned per application. Applied over several existing embeddings, the method improved results substantially. Better representatives, they argue, are an overlooked lever in re-identification.
arxiv-2510-17143:
Shantnav Agarwal, Javier Alonso-Mora, and Sihao Sun teach drone teams to haul loads with no central boss in this 2025 paper. Loads hang from cables below two or more drones in flight. Past methods need one central planner or steady radio links. The team drops both needs so each drone plans on its own.

Each drone learns by copying a central planner that sees the full scene. Smooth path nets keep moves tied to true motion laws. Each drone can train in under two hours on a plain laptop. Tests in sim and real flights match central plans on hard paths. The work suits teams that fly where links are weak or lost.
arxiv-2510-17743:
Alexandr Grebennikov and Matthew Kwan solve a grid puzzle about points and lines. How many points can sit in a square grid with few on any line? Each straight line may hold at most k points, where k is fixed. Earlier work settled the question only for much larger k values.

For large constant k, the pair proves the best count is exactly k times n. Here n is the side length of the square grid. Their proof builds on recent work by three other researchers. It also borrows ideas from Jain and Pham. The same approach gives new bounds for higher-dimensional versions.
arxiv-2510-18043:
Joong Ho Choi, with seven co-authors, shrinks the prompts and files that agent workflows feed to language models. Long chained prompts and rich data streams make such work slow and costly. CompactPrompt cuts low-value tokens from prompts and groups linked phrases so meaning survives the trim.

Attached documents are compressed in parallel, with repeated patterns shortened and numeric columns quantized. On finance question benchmarks, total token use fell by up to about three fifths, while answer quality dipped only slightly for the strong models tested. Teams running agents at scale get a pipeline that lowers bills without gutting results.
arxiv-2510-18143:
Huan Song, with eight co-authors, grows training data for small language models by studying how they fail. Small models are cheap and fast but trail big ones on hard, specialized tasks. Fine-tuning helps, yet preparing data by hand is slow. Their PaDA-Agent reads validation results to find failure patterns first.

Augmentation plans are then drafted to shrink the generalization gap directly, not just to fix single wrong answers. Experiments beat strong model-based augmentation baselines on the tasks tried. Teams deploying small models get an evaluation-driven loop that turns weak spots into fresh, targeted practice data.
arxiv-2510-18343:
Emily L Hunt, with Tristan Cantat-Gaudin and five co-authors, measures completeness of a star cluster census in 2025. Open clusters are loose groups of stars born together, useful tracers of Milky Way structure. Nobody knew how many clusters the Gaia DR3 census missed, or why.

The team simulated clusters and ran over eighty thousand injection-and-retrieval tests against the census method. A simple logistic model, fitted to those tests, predicts detectability from star count, parallax error, and data density. Parallax error means uncertainty in a star's measured distance. The model proved highly accurate and revealed surprises, like faster-moving clusters being easier to detect.
arxiv-2510-18743:
Kasun Wijewardhana and his five co-authors propose feeding a new kind of antenna system wirelessly. Pinching-antenna systems run signals through waveguides and pinch the guide at chosen points to radiate, creating clear line-of-sight links that fight the heavy losses of millimeter-wave and terahertz signals. But wired feeding ties installation to spots near the base station, leaving distant users poorly served.

Their wireless-fed version powers the waveguides without cables, extending coverage beyond the base station's neighborhood at lower cost. Indoor and outdoor scenarios in the article show advantages over the wired design. Numerical results add that the wireless-fed systems deliver higher data rates than conventional fixed antennas. The authors close with research directions needed to bring the concept into next-generation networks.
arxiv-2510-18943:
Reinaldo Francener, Victor P Goncalves, and Gabriel Rabelo-Soares study the muon trident process. They look at far-forward detectors at the Large Hadron Collider. In this process, a muon hits an ion. It then makes a pair of charged leptons.

The team works out cross sections for two routes of the process. They also predict event rates for muon and tungsten hits. The rates suggest the process can be seen at FASER. Tau pairs from muon hits may show up there for the first time. Bound states from quantum electrodynamics may show up too.
arxiv-2510-19043:
Jiaxing Ma and three co-authors show that measurement back-action creates linked thermal noise across many vibration modes in modern mechanical sensors. Sensors now resolve the basic thermal noise floor over a wide band, not just near resonance, which speeds data taking and reveals brief signals once hidden.

Stronger measurement, though, pushes back on the device. The authors find that this back-action correlates noise from modes far apart in frequency, so measured spectra depart from standard single-mode and independent multimode predictions. Sensor designers must account for that coupling to read broadband data correctly.
arxiv-2510-19443:
Adithya Nandakumar, Ricarda S Beckmann, and Vid Irsic explore how bursts of accretion change the long-term spin of massive black holes when superradiance is also at work. Superradiance lets an axion cloud drain spin from a rapidly rotating black hole, while infalling gas adds spin back, and real feeding arrives in uneven episodes rather than a steady stream.

Simulations show the contest between angular momentum gained from accretion and lost to the axion cloud decides the outcome. Boosts that arrive before the main spin-down phase matter most, because they can delay or reshape that drop. The results refine predictions linking black hole spins to ultralight particles.
arxiv-2510-19643:
Konstantin Hess and three co-authors tackle a statistical problem in estimating how treatments affect different patients over time.
