Studying projects in the CASS portfolio, they classed each project by sustainability and compared code structure, test coverage, and code-test links. Sustainable projects showed higher, steadier coverage and clearer code-test ties, while coverage overall stayed low and tangled, highly coupled code proved harder to test. The result is a practical, data-led health check for scientific software.
arxiv-2605-03443:
Uliano Wilyam Purba, Andre Hadiman Rotua Parhusip, Sahid Maulana, Luluk Muthoharoh, Ardika Satria, and Martin C. T. Manullang benchmark sentiment methods on Indonesian Spotify reviews, a three-class task over one hundred thousand scraped comments. After cleaning, about seventy thousand samples remained for comparing classic models with a two-layer bidirectional LSTM under one shared preprocessing pipeline.

The decision tree led the classic models, while the BiLSTM earned the best weighted F1 overall yet failed on the small neutral class. Oversampling with SMOTE gave the classic route more balanced three-class behavior. The authors conclude each approach wins on a different criterion.
arxiv-2605-03543:
Ludovica Falsi, Giuseppe Agostino, Alberto Villois, Francesco Coppini, Paolo M. Santini, Miguel Onorato, Aharon J. Agranat, Stefano Trillo, and Eugenio DelRe study pseudovorticity in 2D optical solitons. True vorticity in a light field lives only at phase singularities. Yet local rotational flow can exist in smooth regions too. That subtler structure had not been mapped in solitons.

Experiments and simulations on photorefractive solitons reveal a dipole inside bright solitons. Quadrupoles appear when solitons fuse. Geometry explains the pattern. Stable high-dimensional solitons, the authors suggest, naturally carry a hierarchy of such multipoles in their phase and amplitude. The work adds a new lens for how light can swirl as it moves.
arxiv-2605-03643:
E. H. Saidi and R. Sammani give new algebraic constructions for the lattices behind code conformal field theories that realize Narain theories. Three lattices matter here: an even lattice, its dual, and an even self-dual lattice sitting between them. Their inclusion chain is governed by a cyclic discriminant group.

The authors describe the structure and representations of all three lattices and build them explicitly, first for the smallest rank case and then for higher-dimensional Lie algebras. More structural features are discussed as well. The work tightens the algebraic foundation for a construction that links error-correcting codes to conformal field theory in two dimensions.
arxiv-2605-03843:
Stephen M. de Bruyn Kops, Peter N. Blossey, and James J. Riley simulate how passive scalars mix in stratified and unstratified turbulence. They use high-resolution large-eddy simulations of decaying flows. Two passive scalar mixing layers, one vertical and one transverse, model a plume much larger than the flow's length scale. Stable layering should suppress vertical mixing, and the simulations quantify that effect.

In the transverse direction, stratified and unstratified evolution are broadly similar, though the scalar spreads slightly faster and fluctuates more strongly when stratified, with a more broken-up interface. In the vertical direction, the stratified layer barely mixes: it grows early until its width tracks the horizontal velocity's vertical integral length, then nearly stops spreading.
arxiv-2605-04143:
Giacomo Cacciapaglia and seven co-authors study heavy partner particles of the top quark. These partners are predicted by theories in which the Higgs particle is made of smaller parts. Most past work looked at partners in smaller colour groups, so the team focuses on a larger six-part colour form.

They build the low-energy rules for these states and map how they decay, mostly into top-rich final states through coloured partner particles. By re-reading ATLAS and CMS searches, they find current collider data rule out many such states below about two to two and a half trillion electron volts.
arxiv-2605-04243:
Tran Quang Liem challenges a common view about why large language models fail hard questions about time. The usual claim is that the models reason badly about order and duration, but Liem argues the real failure comes earlier, when messy text is turned into events.

His framework lifts text into explicit event graphs with time limits, then hands those to a separate symbolic reasoner, keeping extraction apart from deduction. A signal that mixes symbolic ranges with neural uncertainty flags broken structures. With correct structures supplied, the system's checked proof traces answered all four thousand test cases correctly.
arxiv-2605-04643:
Yifei Yuan and three co-authors improve estimates of the political ideology of members of parliament by giving a language model access to a political knowledge graph. Ideology estimates help researchers explain voting behaviour and party alignment. Language models alone already do reasonably well. But they ignore the web of relations among politicians and bodies.

Their retrieval pipeline first queries the graph. It then feeds the structured results into the model's context, alongside text. That captures both what politicians say and how they connect to each other. The team tests the approach on a Swiss parliamentary data set. They compare it against text-only baselines. The question is whether link information sharpens ideology prediction.
arxiv-2605-04843:
Monika Eisenmann and Eskil Hansen prove that Schwarz-like methods converge for a hard class of diffusion equations. These equations can become degenerate, losing their usual smoothing behaviour in parts of the domain. Schwarz methods split the space-time domain into overlapping pieces, which allows the pieces to be solved in parallel.

Their approach adds a false time direction and steps splitting methods toward infinity, an idea related to waveform relaxation. Unlike many such schemes, theirs can be proved to work for nonlinear and even degenerate problems. The proof rests on monotone operator theory together with known results on when solutions to these equations exist.
arxiv-2605-04943:
Anju Rani, Daniel Ortiz-Arroyo, and Petar Durdevic introduce DART, a vision-language model for judging the condition of synthetic fibre ropes from a single inspection photo. Such ropes serve offshore, maritime, and industrial work, where inspectors need more than a label. They need severity scores, repair advice, anomaly flags, timelines, and reports.

DART joins a large vision transformer with a Llama language model through a severity-aware fusion module. Damage-focused masking, per-class severity gates, and a special training loss teach it both damage type and ordering. Trained once on thousands of images across fourteen damage classes, it then supports many inspection tasks without further fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-05043:
Yuji Nakatsukasa and Zheng Tang revisit extracting accurate eigenvalues from a subspace that nearly captures a matrix's leading directions, for positive semi-definite matrices. The Rayleigh-Ritz method is the standard tool and is optimal in several senses for general symmetric matrices. The authors show the positive case allows something better at the same main cost.

They advocate Nyström's method, proving its eigenvalue estimates are always more accurate than Rayleigh-Ritz here, sometimes by an arbitrarily large margin. The gain is biggest when the spectrum decays fast, and similar gains appear numerically for eigenvectors. For trailing eigenvalues the picture reverses, and the authors suggest a remedy for that case.
arxiv-2605-05443:
Watermarking language model text usually bends word choices, and readers pay for detection with worse text. Fabrice Harel-Canada and Amit Sahai present SLAM, a watermark that works differently. Instead of touching word frequencies, it writes the mark into the model's internal geometry at generation time.

Sparse autoencoders find internal directions tied to features like voice, tense, and clause order. Steering those directions leaves meaning and word sampling free. On two Gemma-2 models, detection was perfect, and the quality cost was far smaller than that of leading token-based watermarks, though paraphrasing that reshapes syntax can still erase the mark.
arxiv-2605-05643:
Retrieval systems that search plain text often fetch passages that look relevant but reason nowhere. Jiarui Zhong and Hong Cai Chen propose TGS-RAG, which makes text and knowledge graphs verify each other. Graph-based retrieval has the opposite flaw: pruning at search time can discard valid reasoning paths.

Their framework runs two channels in both directions. A graph-to-text channel uses global voting to check textual evidence against structured facts, while a text-to-graph channel completes the graph from passages. The aim is to close the information islands that form when the two evidence types reason separately.
arxiv-2605-05943:
Luis Solá Conde and Gianluca Occhetta propose a two step approach to Chow quotients in algebraic geometry. A Chow quotient records how a projective variety breaks up under the action of a complex torus. Even for simple varieties, such as rational homogeneous ones, its geometry can be very complicated.

The authors show the quotient's geometry can be encoded in a projective toric variety plus a finite group of its birational symmetries. That encoding turns a hard object into parts that are easier to handle. They then show how to apply the strategy to some particular rational homogeneous varieties. The paper gives geometers a new route into a class of spaces long known for resisting direct study.
arxiv-2605-06043:
Dat Nguyen and Duc-Duy Nguyen propose an image classification system built on compositional relations that stay stable across domains. Photos from new settings differ in color, texture, and style, yet the structural relations among parts of an object often persist. Most domain generalization methods adjust training or align features, leaving that shared structure implicit.

CRISP factors recognition into visual primitives and their relational composition. Soft predicates over primitive locations and appearance give differentiable measures of spatial and visual fit, learned end to end. A backbone, a concept bottleneck layer, and a structural scoring layer work together to reach each class decision. The authors test the system on five real world data sets from the DomainBed suite.
arxiv-2605-06543:
Aaron Beyen, Francesco Casini, and Christian Maes adapt Rayleigh's test for heat-driven sound instability to chemo-mechanical systems. Such surges can destroy control, yet they also create rich behavior and may drive living systems. The authors ask when chemical driving can set a slow mechanical probe into lasting rotation or active motion.

The probe follows Newton's laws while the chemical processes are modeled as Markov jumps. Their Rayleigh-like rules depend on the phase relation between entropic and frenetic, meaning activity-related, contributions. That gives a clear condition for when chemical energy converts into steady mechanical activity, offering a design rule for active matter and tiny machines.
arxiv-2605-06643:
Hao Dong and five co-authors benchmark multimodal domain generalization, where models must work in new domains using several input types at once. Reported gains in this growing field may reflect inconsistent evaluation rather than real progress, since studies vary in datasets, modality mixes, and settings, and mostly test action recognition alone.

Their MMDG-Bench standardizes six datasets across action recognition, fault diagnosis, and sentiment analysis, training over seven thousand networks. Findings are sobering: recent specialized methods barely beat a plain baseline, no method wins consistently, three modalities do not reliably beat two, and corruption or missing modalities degrade every method. A large gap to the upper bound remains.
arxiv-2605-06943:
Steven Song and three co-authors introduce ProtoSSL, a way to pretrain interpretable prototype models without labels. Prototype networks explain predictions by comparing new cases with representative examples, which suits fields like medicine. Earlier versions needed labeled data, tying the learned examples to one task.

ProtoSSL first learns a bank of prototypes from unlabeled data, then assigns them to a downstream task with an efficient procedure. Across six heart-signal datasets, it beats supervised prototype methods when labels are scarce, and also after fine-tuning at full scale. Human judges preferred its explanations, and the framework also extends to audio classification.
arxiv-2605-07043:
Howen Chuah and Monica Torres study the boundary between separated populations in a mathematical model with long-range effects. A system of elliptic equations, tied to a small parameter, models populations that spread and segregate. Earlier work by other researchers settled the boundary's regularity in two dimensions; this paper takes up higher dimensions.

Chuah and Torres extend ideas of angles and cones to higher dimensions, then describe regular and singular boundary points through density and angles. Under stated conditions, the regular part is locally a smooth surface of one lower dimension. When population regions are convex, they prove those regions must be convex polytopes.
arxiv-2605-07243:
Weijie Shi and eleven co-authors speed up language model replies with a block-wise speculative drafter. Speculative decoding drafts many candidate continuations and verifies them in one pass, but existing drafters either call the drafter too often or predict positions blindly. SpecBlock predicts several dependent positions in each forward pass, growing the draft tree block by block.

Hidden states carry path information within and across blocks, and a trained ranking head spends verification effort where acceptance is likely. A cost-aware bandit at deployment updates the drafter only when the expected gain justifies it. Experiments show better speedups than a leading drafter at roughly half its drafting cost.
arxiv-2605-07643:
Emily Darwin and five co-authors report a materials advance for spintronics: tiny magnetic whirlpools called skyrmions, held stable in synthetic antiferromagnets at room temperature with no magnetic field applied. Such textures are protected by topology and avoid the sideways drift that plagues ordinary skyrmions, but keeping them stable at zero field has been hard.

The team built an SAF bias system that sets skyrmion polarity through layer design and a setup field cycle. Using sensitive magnetic force microscopy and computer modeling, they showed reliable zero-field formation. They saw SAF skyrmions under twenty nanometers across, the smallest reported so far. The balanced bias design also holds back stray domains. It offers a scalable route for future skyrmion devices.
arxiv-2605-07843:
Catrin Mair builds the notion of shape for condensed anima, objects in the condensed setting that generalize ordinary spaces. Shape is meant to capture a space's homotopy-theoretic outline, and the question is whether this definition agrees with the standard one where both apply.

Mair proves it does: for all paracompact compactly generated spaces and all locally contractible spaces, this notion recovers the classical shape. Those recovery results imply and extend earlier results on sheaf and condensed cohomology by Clausen, Scholze, and Haine. A second thread describes the basic topological group functor on condensed groups through quasi-topological groups, connecting to the homotopy groups of these anima.
arxiv-2605-07943:
Giacomo Spigler supplies the missing scoreboard for active vision in robot imitation learning. Several systems now let a policy steer its own gaze during manipulation, by moving a neck camera or wrist cameras, and report benefits. But with no shared benchmark nobody could say what active vision contributes, on which tasks, or under what conditions.

TAVIS offers two task suites on two humanoid torsos, one for global search through pan-tilt necks and one for local occlusion through wrist cameras. Its tools include a paired protocol comparing gaze control against fixed cameras on identical demonstrations. They also include a metric for anticipatory gaze: whether the learned policy looks at the right object before acting, as humans do. Baselines show active vision helps, but conditionally, and imitation alone produced human-like anticipatory gaze.
arxiv-2605-08143:
Yuan Fang, Yi Xie, and Xuming Ran improve lifelong editing of large language models, where single facts are patched after deployment without retraining. Existing editors fade as edits pile up and often fail when a question is reworded, so a fix that works once may not stick.

HoReN wraps one MLP layer with a discrete codebook memory that leaves the model's weights untouched. Each entry acts as both a knowledge key and a Hopfield pattern, and edits are retrieved by angle on a sphere, then refined by damped Hopfield dynamics. Paraphrases settle into the right memory basin while unrelated inputs stay stable, and results hold across editing benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-08243:
Gabriel Bathie, Baptiste Mouillon, and Nathanaël Fijalkow speed up the synthesis of mixed-boolean-arithmetic expressions. Those tangled formulas hide program logic. Recovering a clean form from input-output examples serves deobfuscation and compiler work. It also serves reverse engineering and cryptanalysis. CPU tools scale poorly, though. Recent GPU methods lean on caches that break down for bitvector outputs.

Their SIMBA synthesizer enumerates expressions bottom-up on the GPU. It uses no language cache at all. Work stays local and highly parallel. In experiments, SIMBA ran much faster than earlier MBA tools. It also handled larger specifications. Cache-free enumeration fits graphics hardware better than expected.
arxiv-2605-08443:
Linh Tran, Ana Milanova, and Stacy Patterson repair a clash between privacy noise and low-rank fine-tuning in federated learning. LoRA adapters make cross-silo training cheap, but averaging mismatched low-rank factors adds error, and differential privacy noise injected into a narrow subspace can swamp the true update.

Their FedPower framework moves the delicate step to the server. Client updates are reconstructed in full rank and clipped to bound sensitivity, privacy noise is applied there, and the exact aggregated update is then projected back into a low-rank form for distribution. The refactorization keeps the privacy guarantee while sparing accuracy that the usual perturb-then-average pipeline throws away.
arxiv-2605-08643:
Mohammad Yahyavi and five coauthors uncover a hidden link between two light driven electric currents in solids. Injection and shift currents were long treated as separate effects with separate origins. The team shows both trace back to dipoles built from Berry curvature and quantum metric, the geometric traits of electron wave states.

Where electron energy grows nearly in a straight line near the Fermi level and light energy stays low, the two currents become governed by one shared geometric dipole. Dirac and Weyl semimetals plus strained graphene sit naturally in this regime. Nonlinear optics gains a unifying frame where paired measurements probe one geometric property instead of two unrelated processes.
arxiv-2605-08843:
Yuan Mei, Xingyu Song, Xiaowen Song, and Naoya Takeishi fix a hidden bias in training neural surrogates for physical simulations: the training points themselves are unevenly spread. Simulations are sampled on grids that cluster points in some regions, so the model over learns crowded areas and under learns sparse ones, warping physical fidelity. Their M-cubed framework rebalances supervision by partitioning space according to physical variation and spreading training weight across scales.

On three industrial scale datasets, predictions in the continuous domain improve markedly, with errors several times lower in large volumetric cases. Gains survive aggressive subsampling, with models trained on far fewer points beating rivals trained on denser data. Operator learning learns that where points sit matters as much as how many there are.
arxiv-2605-09043:
Napassorn Litchiowong, writing alone, studies how conversations between partners can break down even when both use the same words. One person says a word meaning closure; the other hears surrender. The paper gives this gap a formal measure based on how far apart the two sides' emotional readings of shared anchor words sit.

From speech-act theory and game theory, the author derives a model in which repair efforts can collapse suddenly once the gap passes a threshold, and the collapse is hard to reverse. In a dataset of online talks that went off the rails, warning signs of slowing recovery appeared before the break. A second dataset gave mixed but broadly matching support for the pattern.
arxiv-2605-09243: Brain recordings — fMRI, EEG — are expensive to collect, so their value for machine learning needs quantifying. Lane Lewis and Zhixin Wang ask how much brain data is actually worth for ML. The 2026 paper is a cost-benefit analysis for neuro-AI.
arxiv-2605-09343: Vision-language-action models fumble scenes they do not understand structurally. Zeyu Li and Lei Li give them scene knowledge graph priors — SKG-VLA — for structured semantics and multimodal reasoning for decision making. The 2026 paper grounds robot perception in explicit scene knowledge.
arxiv-2605-09543: Modeling starlight without assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium — non-LTE — is accurate and agonizingly slow in 3D. A. Vicente Arévalo, A. Asensio Ramos, and C. J. Díaz Baso accelerate the synthesis with graph neural networks. The 2026 paper is solar physics at machine speed.
arxiv-2605-10043: Personalizing LLMs from binary feedback — thumbs up, thumbs down — with preference-corrected optimization. Xilai Ma, Liye Zhao, Weijun Yao, and others build the framework. The 2026 paper is personalization from the simplest possible signal. It learns rich preferences from binary choices.
arxiv-2605-10143: Thompson's groups and Teichmüller modular groups acting on generalized Cantor sets — infinite symmetry on fractal dust. Hiroshige Shiga explores the deep connection. The 2026 paper is geometric group theory on fractals. It groups the Cantor dust with Teichmüller precision.
arxiv-2605-10243: Electroweak physics and long-lived particles at LHCb — the LHC's forward eye on exotic decays. Felicia Volle presents on behalf of the LHCb Collaboration. The 2026 paper is particle physics. It hunts exotic long-lived particles with care at the LHCb experiment.
arxiv-2605-10643: A single-layer model doing language modeling — can one layer really suffice? Zanmin Wang shows that it can. The 2026 paper is LLM architecture minimalism. It proves a single layer can model language. One layer is enough. Language modeling, minimized. Simplicity triumphs.

arxiv-2606-04243:
Ivan Viakhirev studies in 2026 the structure hidden inside an integral self-consistency equation. Such an equation defines a quantity only implicitly: the unknown appears on both sides, inside an integral.

He asks when such equations have a solution at all, and when the solution is unique. The density at the heart of the problem turns out to be monotone in the key parameter, under mild conditions. That single fact organizes the rest: branches of solutions can be tracked, and spurious ones ruled out. Numeric tests matched the analysis. The result gives a clean check for models that define their key quantity this way. Physics and economics both use such equations.
arxiv-2606-04443:
Delgado asks what black-box testing can certify about post-quantum key encapsulation, in a 2026 arXiv cryptography paper. The tests probe Fujisaki-Okamoto decapsulation. That is the step that recovers the key. The tests see only values that reach final key derivation. They do not see the internal re-encryption. He studies variants that carry a confirmation code. This is a witness value meant to prove the key was formed honestly.

He derives a tight bound on acceptance. One list-hit term turns out to be the real obstruction. A one-query construction from any witness predictor matches the bound. He also proves a limit on all such tests. Operations outside the observable cone cannot be certified. So any execution certifier has two error rates that sum to at least one. Case studies on ML-KEM and HQC sort checks into three rows: theorem-covered, artifact, and non-certification.
arxiv-2606-04643:
Paganini investigates a property of spacetimes called conicality, in a 2026 arXiv relativity paper. Conicality asks whether the joint future of a finite set of events uniquely reveals the set that generated it. The reveal works through light cone structure. Paganini tests which broad conditions are enough to guarantee it.

He shows that neither condition suffices on its own. Conicality can fail under each. Causally simple, future cohesive spacetimes of dimension 1+N, with N at least two, do satisfy conicality. These can be read as the timelike past of an observer. That fit is natural, he notes.
arxiv-2606-04943: Throat singers produce two notes at once — a low drone and a high whistle — by shaping their vocal tract with remarkable precision. This paper builds a computer model of the throat and mouth that can copy-synthesize this biphonic singing, with every step adjustable by gradient-based learning. It connects the physics of the voice to the mathematics of machine learning.
arxiv-2606-05043:
Samuel Christie, Munindar Singh, and Amit Chopra introduce Strabo in this 2026 arXiv paper, which brings declarative interaction protocols to agentic AI. Interaction protocols are blueprints that specify how software agents may exchange messages, and declarative versions can be checked for correctness before any agent is built. The team connects this research to the Universal Commerce Protocol, a recent Google-led effort to standardize e-commerce interactions for AI agents.

Working in two parts, they first model the checkout portion of the protocol as a declarative Langshaw protocol and implement agents with Peach, a programming model for Langshaw. They then show those Peach agents can interoperate with Universal Commerce Protocol agents implemented by Google, confirming the model matches the real system. The result points to a gradual path for introducing declarative protocols into conventional settings without wholesale replacement.
arxiv-2606-05243:
Soon-Tae Hong and Bum-Hoon Lee derive equation of state parameters for a fluid of stringy extended objects in higher-dimensional cosmology in this 2026 arXiv paper. Instead of point particles, the cosmic fluid here is made of extended stringy objects in more than four dimensions.

The authors first construct the strong energy conditions behind the Hawking-Penrose singularity theorems, for both massive and massless versions of these objects. From those conditions they find a lower bound on the equation of state parameter w, the ratio of pressure to energy density. The bound holds for both fluids in five or more dimensions. They relate the result to the Hawking-Penrose limit for point particles in four dimensions. They also split the parameter into contributions from the point-particle property, the cosmological constant, and the extended-object degrees of freedom. The weak energy condition is investigated as well.
arxiv-2606-05343:
Avinash Kumar Paladi and colleagues constrain the orbital eccentricity of the supermassive black hole binary candidate PKS 2131-021 in this 2026 arXiv paper. This blazar's radio brightness has varied sinusoidally in epochs over decades. That is naturally explained if the jet-emitting black hole orbits a companion and Doppler boosting modulates the jet as it swings toward and away from us.

The authors extend the kinematic orbital model to eccentric orbits using the Keplerian parametric solution and run Bayesian estimation on radio data from 1975 to 2021 gathered by three observatories. Without noise modeling they find a residual eccentricity of 0.053, with a Bayes factor of 3.15 favoring the eccentric model over a circular one. Once red noise is included through a damped random walk process, however, the circular model is preferred and the eccentricity is only bounded above by 0.15. The circular-plus-noise model is favored and recovers a period across all datasets.
arxiv-2606-05443:
Alex Li and Joseph Jacobson introduce MIRAI in this 2026 arXiv paper, a deep learning framework that predicts which research papers will have high impact. MIRAI makes its prediction from minimal information: only a paper's title, abstract, and publication date. Trained on the arXiv academic graph, the model predicts two five-year impact measures, a paper's PageRank in the citation network and its citation count.

On papers published in 2021 it achieved rank correlations of about 0.47 for PageRank and 0.62 for citations, using only the abstract page. The authors then build a research ideation pipeline on top of the predictor, generating research ideas steered toward predicted high impact. An independent language-model judge rated those ideas more impactful than a baseline pipeline's at a ratio of four to three. The five-year citation prediction model is available through a web application, making the tool usable by anyone triaging new literature.
arxiv-2606-05743:
Minseok Choi and colleagues give safety guards a memory that learns attack styles, not just examples in a 2026 arXiv paper. Jailbreak tricks evolve faster than fixed safety classifiers can follow. Memory-based guards adapt, but they often refuse harmless queries that merely resemble attacks. Membrane stores contrastive cells: each pairs the traits that should trigger a block with a look-alike benign case that should pass. Cells are indexed by attack strategy, so one cell covers many topics.

New harmful chats and their benign twins are distilled into cells without any retraining. Retrieved cells then ground each fresh safety decision. On HarmBench and AgentHarm tests the guard earned the top score on all six attack types. Benign refusals stayed between seven and fourteen percent, far under the twenty-eight to eighty-five percent of prior guards. Cells kept most of their strength under new attack styles and poisoning attempts.
arxiv-2606-05843:
Ruoxi Sun and colleagues open a multimodal model to find who does the visual fetching in a 2026 arXiv paper. These models answer questions about images, but their inner division of labor was opaque. A token-level score, Retrieval Attention Mass, ranks attention heads by how much they gather query-relevant visual detail. A small elite stands out: Context-aware Retrieval heads, or CoRe heads.

Across image domains and model sizes the split held firm. CoRe heads act as dedicated extractors while most heads spread attention widely. Deleting just the top five percent of CoRe heads badly damaged reasoning scores. Deleting low-ranked heads barely mattered. The concentration also pays in speed: leaning on the sparse pattern sped up inference while performance held. Functional sparsity, the authors argue, is a design principle hiding inside these models. Future architectures could build around it deliberately.
arxiv-2606-05943:
Schmüdgen builds the theory of operators that conjugate as they act in a 2026 arXiv paper. An antilinear operator flips the sign rule on complex scalars, conjugating them on exit. Linear theory fills libraries; its antilinear cousin is rarely studied. Yet antilinear maps appear inside C-symmetric and C-self-adjoint maps, a live area of physics.

The paper studies densely defined unbounded antilinear operators, above all the normal ones. Several tests for antilinear normality are proven, each phrased differently. One class gets a close look. The main result describes the structure of unbounded antilinear normal operators. Structure theorems matter: they split a wild object into plain pieces. The work extends spectral thinking where conjugation breaks the usual rules. Operator theorists and physicists are the audience.
arxiv-2606-06243:
Kei Yuen Chan, Kaidi Wu, Jun Yu, and Hongfeng Zhang prove stability results for a key functor in this 2026 arXiv paper on representation theory. The Casselman Jacquet functor extracts, from a representation of a real reductive group, the part that captures its asymptotic behavior. Such functors are workhorses for classifying representations, but the real setting is topologically harder than the p adic one. Earlier work leaned on narrower classes of modules.

The authors study the smooth version of the functor, with submodule and quotient variants, for smooth Fréchet representations of moderate growth. Beyond exactness, surjectivity, and globalization results, they prove a stability property for intersections of Jacquet subspaces. That stability is the technical heart of the paper. As an application, they establish the full real version of the Bernstein Zelevinsky filtrations, a layered decomposition that organizes representations of general linear groups and their mirabolic subgroups.
arxiv-2606-06543:
Xiaobin Li and co-authors schedule a rush hour burst of train departures in this 2026 arXiv paper on railway operations. In concentrated departure scenarios, many trains leave in a short window. Dispatchers must jointly choose the departure order and which track section each train uses. The decisions interact, and delays propagate. The team encodes both in one QUBO model, a binary optimization format suited to quantum and quantum inspired solvers.

Because a static formula cannot capture time dependent effects, they add a simulation layer. It scores each candidate plan on section occupation, waiting at stations, platform pressure, running time swings, and delay spread. Heuristics, quantum inspired methods, and hybrid algorithms were then compared under normal, disturbed, and larger scale settings. The quantum inspired and hybrid approaches proved feasible and often strong. Dispatchers gain a tested menu for a problem where one bad slot can ripple across the network.
arxiv-2606-06743:
Before a language model can speak, speech must be chopped into tokens, compact codes that carry both meaning and sound. Arjun Gangwar and Umesh present HybridCodec in this 2026 arXiv paper, a neural audio codec that tries to get the best of two rival designs. One design squeezes meaning into the first coding layer; the other keeps meaning and sound in fully separate streams.

HybridCodec keeps the separate streams and also distills knowledge from a large self supervised speech model into the meaning stream during training. That teacher is not needed when the codec runs, which keeps the system light. On LibriSpeech it posted the best meaning focused score among rivals, with a first layer word error rate near fifteen percent, and it reconstructed speech competitively. It also ran three times faster than the leading dual stream model and held up on unfamiliar and foreign language speech.
arxiv-2606-06943:
Test time defenses for vision language models often buy safety with slowness. Kim and Um target that trade off in this 2026 arXiv paper, a companion to their counterattack work. Their method tunes prompts while an attack is under way. Augmented views of the input supply the evidence. The catch is that some views are corrupted too.

Two scores grade each view before it is trusted. Stability checks whether weak changes leave the prediction unmoved. Suitability checks whether the view sits in a dense, typical feature region. Those scores weight both the tuning loss and the final prediction. Trustworthy views speak loudly; corrupted views are muted. Across fine grained benchmarks, ImageNet variants, and many attacks, the method set new robustness marks. It stayed fast even with few views available. The authors argue that judging view quality is the missing piece in test time adaptation.
arxiv-2606-07443:
Ghazi, Nasser, Calmon, and Issa characterize the best privacy mechanism for a statistical decision, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Binary hypothesis testing asks whether data came from one distribution or another. Under local differential privacy, each observation is randomized on the user's device before analysis, trading testing power for privacy. Earlier work described optimal mechanisms but computed them only in exponential time, leaving the optimum out of reach for practical alphabet sizes.

The authors prove a structure they call Sort-Partition-Randomize. After sorting outcomes by likelihood ratio, an optimal mechanism groups them into contiguous blocks and applies randomized response, a coin-flip-style scrambling, to the block label. This holds for every privacy level and divergence measure of utility. It yields a dynamic program computing the exact optimum in cubic time, faster with a budget. Practitioners can compute, not approximate, the best privacy-utility trade-off across the privacy range.
arxiv-2606-07543:
Nayak, Gautam, and Varanasi interview older workers about holding bridge jobs in workplaces being reshaped by generative AI, in this 2026 arXiv study. Bridge employment means part-time or transitional work between a career job and full retirement. The authors spoke with 21 professionals aged 40 and above in such roles as AI tools spread. Participants described breaks at every stage of deciding on bridge work, both temporal, unsettling their plans, and structural, changing the roles.

In response, workers rebuilt their tasks through boundary work, redrawing what they would and would not hand to AI, to restore stability. The authors call these responses AI resilience and argue individual tactics are not enough. Their recommendations operate at 3 levels: personal strategies, workplace resilience collectives at the team level, and company structures that let workers contest AI-mediated calls. The goal is reducing burnout among older workers without pretending it will reverse.
arxiv-2606-07643:
Wang and colleagues present AVI-Bench, a benchmark for testing omni-multimodal large language models, systems that take in text, images, and sound together. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks whether such models can perceive and reason across sight and hearing as people do. The test follows three stages of cognition, namely perception, understanding, and reasoning, and its tasks force a model to combine what it sees with what it hears.

The team also adds AVI-Bench-PriSe, an extension built from unfamiliar, low-meaning stimuli that probe basic sensation rather than knowledge of familiar scenes. Trials on open and closed models show large gaps in current systems, and models struggle most when sound and picture must be balanced together. From these results the authors propose a four-level scale of audio-visual ability, running from single-task skill up to adapting in unfamiliar domains.
arxiv-2606-07743:
Climescu, Kyselov, and Ovchynnikov check whether a planned detector can really see a promising class of signals, in this 2026 arXiv paper. SHiP is an experiment hunting long-lived particles, hypothetical particles that travel far before they decay. Smashing protons into a target creates cascades of secondary particles, which should produce many more of them. The catch is that cascade-born particles are soft, so their decay products may miss the detector or fail reconstruction.

The team combined rate calculations with a detector-level study of one particle type. For photophilic axion-like particles, which interact mainly with light, cascades gave at most a moderate boost, and only at the lightest masses. At higher masses the cascade share faded to negligible. For heavy neutral leptons from secondary kaons, the cascade part was minor once geometric acceptance was applied. Looser selection or an active target could recover some lost rate.
arxiv-2606-08143:
V. E. R. Lemes and D. G. Tedesco check that a non-Hermitian field theory still produces real, physical answers for a composite quantity, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their theory, in three-plus-one dimensions, contains two fermions, two Abelian gauge fields, and a complex scalar, with dynamics fixed by a BRST symmetry. For a specific parameter choice the fermion mass matrix becomes non-Hermitian, and the propagators develop complex conjugate poles.

They evaluate the one-loop fermion contribution to the two-point function of the composite operator built from the scalar and its conjugate. Once the conventional factor of i is removed, the contribution is real for real external momentum. Complex terms enter the loop integral in conjugate pairs, and their imaginary parts cancel. The BRST construction sets up a proof of renormalisability. Reality of observables, not Hermiticity of every ingredient, is the real requirement, and here it survives.
arxiv-2606-08243:
Vella Zarb and colleagues examine how to tell what a language model is really motivated by, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Safety evaluations often infer hidden motives from behavior, for instance when a model complies with harmful requests more often if told its answers affect training. That pattern, called alignment faking, is commonly read as strategic self-preservation. But it might instead reflect the model guessing what researchers expect the test to show. Intervening on a motive directly, the authors note, is circular reasoning.

Their framework sidesteps the circle by intervening on processes each hypothesis requires. Genuine scheming needs consequence-tracking, following what its actions lead to. Performative scheming needs researcher-expectation tracking, modeling the test itself. By perturbing each process symmetrically and comparing how the behavior changes, the team can judge which explanation the evidence supports. The result is a comparative motivation profile for auditing motive claims.
arxiv-2606-08343:
Jason Sulskis and Ravi build a neural operator that obeys the laws of thermodynamics by construction, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neural operators learn maps between functions, letting a trained model predict how a physical field evolves. Existing versions enforce at most one conservation law. Real nonequilibrium systems mix two parts: reversible, energy-conserving motion and irreversible, entropy-producing dissipation. The GENERIC framework organizes this split, with exact coupling conditions called degeneracy conditions.

Their model, GENERIC-FNO, embeds the full structure directly in function space on top of a Fourier neural operator. Energy and entropy are learned as neural operators. The reversible and friction operators are set in frequency space, between projections that enforce the degeneracy conditions exactly. The identities hold to machine precision, with no penalty term and no post-hoc fix.
arxiv-2606-08443:
Guan and Katiyar give a quantum algorithm for a classical signal transform in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Kravchuk transform, built from the discrete Kravchuk polynomials of the Ukrainian mathematician Mykhailo Kravchuk, maps data into a basis useful for signals defined on finite grids. Their quantum version maps computational basis states to states whose amplitudes are proportional to Kravchuk functions. Its cost scales only logarithmically in the dimension and the inverse error tolerance, an exponential saving over naive approaches.

Two techniques make this possible. First, the authors establish the structural relationship between the Kravchuk transform and the Lie algebra su(2), the symmetry algebra of spin, translating the transform into the Fock basis of an oscillator representation. Second, they apply a recent fast-forwarding simulation method for su(2) operators, which simulates long evolution in short time.
arxiv-2606-08643:
Xiangyu Luo and a large collaboration report a copper-oxide superconductor where two supposedly rival orders coexist, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The link between high-temperature superconductivity and antiferromagnetic order in cuprates remains an open question. Using high-resolution photoemission spectroscopy, which maps electron energies across a crystal's surface, the team investigated a seven-layer bismuth-based cuprate. They identify it as a system with multiple hole Fermi pockets, distinct contours of the states that carry current.

braid-neurypnology-1843:
James Braid, a Manchester surgeon, founded the study of hypnotism in Neurypnology, printed in 1843. Watching a mesmerist's show, he saw the trance came from the subject's own nervous state. Braid coined the words neurypnology and hypnotism for the new science. The subtitle ties nervous sleep to the claims of animal magnetism.

He explains trance as a state raised by fixed gaze and strained attention. No magnetic fluid passes from operator to subject, he argues. Cases from his practice show the state used in treatment. The book broke mesmerism away from fluid theory for good. Every history of hypnosis starts with Braid. His terms are still in daily use.
carlyle-past-present-1843:
Thomas Carlyle published Past and Present in 1843, a fierce work of social criticism. Carlyle contrasts a well-run medieval abbey with industrial England in his own day. The past, in his telling, had faith, order, and real leadership. The present has the cash nexus: money as the sole bond between people.

He attacks laissez-faire policy and the misery of factory workers. Captains of industry is his call for a new, responsible ruling class. The book founded a line of Victorian social critique that Ruskin and others followed. Its prose burns with prophetic anger. Historians still cite it on the condition of England question.
cia-0000009043:
Soviet activities around the world, with special attention to the Far East, fill a CIA survey from March 1951. The Korean War was then in its first year, and Moscow's hand in Asia drew sharp American focus. The paper scans Soviet moves across regions before narrowing eastward.

Global surveys helped leaders judge whether Soviet steps formed one design or many local plays. In 1951, with China newly communist, the Far East section carried special weight. The file shows the early CIA thinking in worldwide terms. It also records how completely the Soviet Union dominated the agency's first agenda.
cia-0000009143:
Quynh Luu district, in Nghe An province, is the scene of a November 1972 report on a downed American pilot sighted there. Nghe An stretches along North Vietnam's coast, under routes struck throughout the bombing years. Late 1972 brought the war's final, heaviest air campaign weeks later.

A pilot down in a coastal district faced capture by local militia within hours. Reports from such districts let officials plot a man's likely path into the prison system. Few could be verified on the spot. This file preserves the sighting as filed, one point in a province crossed by many losses.
cia-0000009443:
American journalists held captive by Viet Cong and North Vietnamese forces in Kompong Cham province fill a September 1971 report. Kompong Cham lies in Cambodia, where the war had spread the year before. Correspondents covering that fighting faced capture alongside soldiers' risks.

The report records what was known of the newsmen's capture and condition. Journalists were valuable prisoners: known names with employers and families pressing for news. Their cases drew attention that anonymous captives rarely got. The file documents that attention at the agency level, tracking reporters who had gone to cover the war and became its story.
cia-0000011843:
American troops had landed in the Dominican Republic in 1965 to stop a civil war, and in May 1966 the CIA reported on security conditions there. The intervention had ended the fighting but left the island's politics in a tangle. Elections were near, and the question was whether order would hold once the troops went home.

The report weighs the armed forces, the rival parties, and the risk of fresh violence. It treats the calm as real but fragile, built on an outside presence. For readers, it shows the morning after an intervention, when Washington tried to judge what its landing had bought.
cia-0000012243:
Indonesia and Malaysia were locked in an undeclared war called Confrontation when the CIA weighed both countries' prospects in June 1965. President Sukarno had vowed to crush the new Malaysian federation, which he called a British puppet. Indonesian raids and British-led defenses ground on across Borneo while Sukarno's rule weakened at home.

The paper weighs the fight's course and the future of Sukarno's guided democracy. It also judges what Malaysia could withstand and what Jakarta might do next. Written months before Indonesia's violent upheaval that fall, it shows analysts reading a region on the edge.
