The path method then draws avoidance routes toward the destination. Tests in two busy scenarios showed safer, smoother sailing. The authors offer the approach as a step toward smarter bridge decision support.
plos-pone-0350043:
Machines that caption sounds learn from human-written descriptions, and Laura Hekanaho and colleagues compared those descriptions in English and Finnish. Their 2026 PLOS One study is among the first to inspect this training data as language, including descriptions written by blind and sighted Finns.

The Finnish collections varied far more than the English one, which the authors trace partly to English writers working in a second language. A close reading of one hundred fifty descriptions showed what people choose to mention about a soundscape and what they leave out. The findings matter for accessibility tools, since captions trained on thin descriptions will describe the world thinly.
plos-pone-0350343:
Yoann Zafiriou and co-authors tested whether resilience protects anaesthesia staff during a simulated crisis in 2026. The specialty carries high burnout, and resilience is often promoted as a shield, but its link to the body's stress response was untested.

Thirty-four anaesthetists, trainees, and nurse anaesthetists completed a resilience scale, then faced a high fidelity child airway emergency simulation. Heart rhythm measures and self rated stress were tracked. Resilience scores sat in a mid range, yet neither body nor mind stress responses tied significantly to them. The result questions easy claims that resilient staff simply stay calm under fire.
plos-pone-0350643:
Jorge Maurino and co-authors studied procrastination among clinicians who manage spinal muscular atrophy in Spain in 2026. Delaying hard decisions is a known failure of self control, worsened by stressful clinical work, and the team linked it to burnout and regret.

Thirty-seven professionals from a national registry completed standard scales for delay, regret, attitudes to evidence, and burnout. About a third showed moderate to high procrastination. Modelling explored whether burnout feeds delay through regret over past choices. Even a small study matters here: if delay is common in rare disease care, systems, not just willpower, need redesign.
plos-pone-0350743:
Ivan Nirmalaraj, Nicholas Sookhan, and J. Scott MacIvor test a new way to measure how worn a bumble bee's wings are, in this 2026 study from a Toronto-area national park. Wings fray with flight, so wear hints at a bee's age and foraging effort, but existing scoring is coarse and subjective. The team photographed the forewings of more than two hundred sixty worker bees from three species and measured edge complexity using fractal geometry.

Fractal scores tracked human visual wear grades more closely than a simpler perimeter-to-area measure, and unlike that measure they were not distorted by body size. Undamaged wings also differed between species, giving each a baseline. The authors propose fractal dimension as a sensitive, objective tool for judging bee condition in field studies, useful for tracking colony stress and pollinator health.
plos-pone-0350943:
Maria Clara Ferreira, Frederico Kremer, and Vanessa Galli built a software tool that guesses which circular RNAs, a loop-shaped class of RNA, help plants weather cold and drought. Loops are hard to study one by one, so prediction narrows the field. Their tool reads the RNA's letter sequence, chops it into short fragments, and turns those fragments into numbers using a technique borrowed from language software, then classifies with a random forest.

Trained on rice and maize loop RNAs with known stress links, the tool sorted independent test sets well enough to serve as a screening instrument. Breeders hunting stress-resilient crops face thousands of candidate molecules; a ranked shortlist from sequence alone saves seasons of bench work. The authors offer the tool as an open starting point for a corner of plant biology that lacked one.
plos-pone-0351143:
Adults and children may not value the same rewards. Money means a lot to adults. Its pull on children is less clear. Sebastijan Veselic and colleagues compared fifty-one adults with thirty-nine children. The children were aged seven to twelve. Three tasks tested value, effort, and attention control. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Adults responded more strongly to money-like rewards. Children reacted about equally to both reward kinds. Food and treats counted as primary rewards here. Tokens and money counted as secondary rewards. The gap suggests learned rewards gain power with age. The authors add a caution. The two reward types were not perfectly matched. Age studies must weigh what a prize means to each group.
plos-pone-0351243:
Christoph Steup and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One genomic study of bowel cancer that has spread to the liver and been treated with antibody drugs targeting the EGFR pathway. Such treatment can shrink initially inoperable tumors enough for surgery, but resistant cell clones may grow meanwhile. The team sequenced tumor samples from thirty patients, taken before and after treatment, and compared them with public cancer genome datasets.

Samples taken after treatment carried resistance-linked mutations more often, spread thinly across many genes rather than concentrated in a few. Neither the total mutation count nor the well-known RAS status predicted whether tumors became operable. Reassuringly, even where resistance mutations appeared in subclones, they did not block successful removal of the liver tumors. The authors question how much routine profiling adds in this setting.
plos-pone-0351543:
Many insects stop eating as adults, living only to mate, and their guts fill with air instead of food. Hollister W Herhold and colleagues scanned such insects with micro CT imaging to measure that hidden air, in this 2026 PLOS One study spanning several insect orders.

The inflated gut was known from mayflies and one other group; scans now show it in stoneflies, webspinners, dobsonflies, moths, and true flies too. Species that had lost adult feeding carried strikingly more gut air, a link statistics confirmed strongly. Why the air helps is unsettled: buoyancy, display, or flight balance are candidates the authors weigh for future tests.
plos-pone-0351643:
Ju Zhao and colleagues sharpened satellite estimates of soil moisture over China's Wujiang River Basin, a rugged karst landscape where fields and rock fracture the ground. A NASA satellite reads moisture coarsely, and one model for all seasons fits none of them well there. The team trained separate seasonal models, mixing satellite drought indicators with terrain data, and compared five learning algorithms.

The seasonal CatBoost models beat single-model baselines, doing best in spring and autumn. Reading the model's reasoning showed its logic shifting with the year: winter estimates leaned on terrain, summer ones on heat and water signals. That rotation matches how moisture actually behaves in the basin. Better seasonal soil moisture maps feed drought warnings and water planning in mountain country where ground sensors are sparse.
plos-pone-0351943:
Edita Garskaite and seven colleagues turn eggshell waste into fire-resistant wood. Their 2026 study closes a loop: shells that bakeries discard become mineral protection for timber. First, water-insoluble proteins were extracted from shell membranes and fragments by boiling with denaturing agents. The mineral shell was converted into a calcium solution. Pine sapwood then soaked in two baths, phosphate first, calcium second. Inside the wood, the two met and grew a bone-like mineral, carbonated hydroxyapatite, in place.

Microscopy showed modest saturation: the wood's channels stayed mostly open. Element maps, though, showed calcium and phosphorus spread evenly throughout. Diffraction confirmed the mineral's identity and its carbonate substitution. Fire behaviour was measured with two calorimeter instruments. Timber construction is booming as a low-carbon choice, but wood burns. A waste-derived mineral grown inside the fibres, rather than coated on top, could protect buildings while giving eggshells a second industrial life.
plos-pone-0352143:
Zhiqiao Cheng, Ping Li, and Jingsheng Pan ground steel slag asphalt under accelerated wear to learn how its skid resistance ages, and how much slag a road crew should use. Steel slag, a steelmaking waste, grips tires well but roads must stay grippy for years at real temperatures. The lab program crossed three slag contents with three temperatures and measured two standard grip indicators as abrasion cycles piled up.

Both grip measures fell steadily as wear accumulated, and heat sped the decline sharply, a warning for hot-climate highways. The two indicators moved together closely, so either can track the other in monitoring. With wear curves in hand, engineers can set slag doses by climate zone instead of habit, and schedule resurfacing before a polished road turns treacherous in the rain.
plos-pone-0352243:
Xiaorong Bai and five colleagues run a brisk walking trial for overweight older women in China. Their 2026 study is a cluster-randomised trial with fifty-four women aged sixty to sixty-nine. Half walked briskly three times a week for twelve weeks. Sessions ran from thirty-five to sixty minutes. The other half kept their usual routines. Fitness, balance, and life satisfaction were measured at the start and the end.

Walking delivered broad gains. Heart and lung fitness, flexibility, strength, and endurance all improved significantly. Balance got better too, a serious benefit at this age. Life satisfaction rose with the physical gains. Body composition, though, did not shift in twelve weeks. Between-group differences reached significance clearly only on the chair stand test of endurance, while effect sizes grew across measures. The prescription is refreshingly plain: regular brisk walking, no equipment, measurably rebuilds fitness and mood in older women.
plos-pone-0352443:
Elizabeth A McHuron, a single author, published this 2026 study estimating how much energy nursing costs marine mammal mothers each day. Direct measurements are missing for most species, blocking models of how disturbance affects populations. McHuron gathered published milk intake rates and milk energy values from marine mammals and their land relatives, tracking how both change across the nursing period.

Milk intake per body weight fell over time in all groups, fastest in bears and kin, slowest in seals. Whales and dolphins drank heavily early, then dropped fast. The patterns give modelers grounded estimates for species never measured.
plos-pone-0352643:
Mary Bitta and seven colleagues report a large trial of bringing mental health care into ordinary clinics in rural Kilifi County, Kenya, published in 2026. Specialists are almost absent in such regions. The team therefore trained non-specialist primary care workers using the World Health Organization's intervention guide. They then rolled the program out across more than one hundred public facilities in a randomized stepped sequence, with refresher supervision each quarter.

Detection rose sharply once facilities crossed over. Monthly diagnosis rates for epilepsy roughly doubled, while depression, dementia, and substance misuse diagnoses climbed from near zero, all statistically robust after adjustment. Psychosis and suicidality showed raw gains that did not survive adjustment. Health worker stigma fell and patient outcomes improved. The authors call the scale-up feasible and effective, while asking for tests in other settings before general claims.
plos-pone-0353143:
Li and colleagues combined several data layers to find drivers of irregular heartbeat caused by a cancer drug in a 2026 study. The drug, widely used against cancer, can trigger atrial fibrillation, a serious rhythm problem. The team started with drug safety reports, then layered gene, protein network, and immune data.

Candidate targets emerged where drug targets, disease genes, and changed genes overlapped. Hub genes were checked in independent data sets, and docking tests probed direct binding. Naming the mediators could lead to heart-protecting companions for the cancer drug, so patients gain the cancer benefit with less rhythm risk.
plos-pone-0353343:
Altınalan and colleagues combined gene studies of a benign inner-ear tumor in a 2026 analysis. The tumor grows on balance and hearing nerves and often causes gradual hearing loss. Pooling four public data sets let the team find gene changes too faint in any single study.

Thousands of genes differed between tumor and normal tissue, even under strict cutoffs. Changed genes clustered around tissue scaffolding, hearing and nerve signaling, immune activity, and cell growth. Some changed genes already have known drugs that act on them. The map offers fresh leads for biomarkers and drug ideas for a tumor that today is handled mainly by watching or surgery.
plos-pone-0353743:
Chen and colleagues, in a 2026 study, profile the chemistry of backfat in Ningxiang pigs, a prized local breed in China, as the animals fatten. Backfat chemistry shapes pork quality, yet the fattening months, from about six months to a year old, were poorly charted. Samples at four ages were scanned for small molecules and matched against carcass traits.

More than one hundred fifty compounds shifted significantly with age, including fats tied to appetite control and fat burning. Plant-derived and vitamin-like compounds built up over time, which the authors read as the fat quietly recording diet and environment. Some man-made chemicals from feed or surroundings also accumulated, a possible flag for pork safety. One network of compounds tracked carcass traits strongly, with an obscure plant alkaloid at its center. The team offers these molecules as candidate markers for breeding and quality checks.
plos-pone-0353843:
Patryk Ziobro led a team of seven authors on this 2026 mouse study of exercise wheels and social behavior. Female mice raised with a running wheel in the home cage from weaning were tested as adults meeting unfamiliar females, and compared with mice given a simple paper hut.

Wheel-raised females spent less time investigating newcomers and called less during meetings, and two weeks without the wheel did not undo it. Surprisingly, even a locked, immobile wheel produced the same effect, so the object itself, not running, changed social motivation. Ziobro warns mouse study designs to account for cage furniture.
plos-pone-0353943:
Michael Bazaco and colleagues track in 2026 how foodborne outbreaks in the United States changed over two decades, sorted by food type and germ. Four priority germs and seventeen food groups were followed with a Bayesian trend model that handles rare events and hard attribution. Prevention teams need such trends to see which foods are emerging as risks.

Listeria outbreaks tied to dairy rose while those tied to meat and poultry fell. A gut germ's outbreaks tied to dairy and poultry also rose, while a toxin producing gut germ tied to meat fell. Salmonella outbreaks tied to eggs fell as well. The method itself is offered as a reusable trend tool.
plos-pone-0354143:
Kim and Kim, in a 2026 computer study, mine the genomes of African swine fever virus for pieces that could serve in vaccines. The virus kills pigs in huge numbers across Africa, Europe, and Asia, and its strains differ a lot by region, which frustrates one-size vaccine design. The team looked for protein fragments that are common within one country's strains.

Genomes were chopped into short overlapping pieces of four lengths, and pieces enriched in each country with enough genomes were kept. Italy yielded the most pieces, while Russia's pattern differed oddly. The kept pieces were screened as candidate targets for three arms of the immune system, and many were predicted to provoke a response. They came from shell proteins, copying machinery, and large gene families. The resulting library is meant to help design vaccines tuned to each region's virus, and tests of diagnostics as well.
plos-pone-0354243:
Moohebat and Khormaei, in a 2026 study, reframe insomnia as a problem of disconnection rather than loud symptoms. Poor sleep is usually explained by an over-aroused mind. These authors asked instead whether the web of a person's psychological traits hangs together less tightly when sleep is poor. They surveyed about four hundred Iranian university students, roughly split between good and poor sleepers.

Each student's answers on twenty-seven mental traits were turned into a network, with traits as nodes and links as their ties. Poor sleepers' networks were sparser, with more isolated traits and traits that were harder to predict from their neighbors. Overall network strength, however, did not differ. In good sleepers, thinking-related traits sat closer to the center of the web. The authors suggest insomnia may mark a mind whose parts talk to each other less, a shift in how care might be aimed.
plos-pone-0354343:
Yiwei Ge and Jingkun Bi used machine learning to find what predicts whether American teenagers meet muscle-strengthening guidelines. Strength exercise is a core part of youth health advice, yet its drivers are less mapped than aerobic activity's. Their 2026 study drew on a national youth risk survey of about twenty thousand high school students.

About three in five students met the guideline of strengthening on at least three days weekly. The model sorted students well. Overall physical activity level was the top predictor, followed by sex and fruit intake. Explanation plots showed how each factor bends the prediction. Ge and Bi say explainable models can help schools target the habits that travel with strength training.
plos-pone-0354743:
Guolong Zhang, Qian Dan, and Yutian Zhang published this 2026 communications paper on drones kept aloft by laser power. A laser-fed unmanned aircraft can serve ground users, but someone must decide its flight path, its transmission power, and which user it serves at each moment, fairly. Their goal was to lift the weakest user's data rate as high as possible.

The joint problem resists direct solution, so they split it into three smaller problems and solved them in turn with approximation methods. Simulations showed the algorithm settling quickly and steadily on its answer.
plos-pone-0355043:
Di Zhao and three colleagues compare the mitochondrial genomes of gliding and climbing squirrels to see whether their different ways of moving left marks on their DNA, in this 2026 study. The team newly sequenced the full mitochondrial genome of one rare flying squirrel species and lined it up against published genomes from both flying and tree squirrels. Basic organization, gene order, and composition proved highly conserved across the family.

Beneath that stability, four energy-related genes evolved faster in the flying squirrel lineage, and codon usage bias ran stronger there too. These are signs that natural selection pulled the two lineages differently, plausibly matching their energy demands. The reconstructed family tree settled into four subfamilies with strong support and placed flying and tree squirrels as sister groups. The authors offer the genome as a foundation for future work on squirrel evolution.
plos-pone-0355343:
Lixian Mou and fellow doctors test a new scan for finding thyroid cancer that has returned or spread after treatment. Doctors usually track a blood marker for this cancer, but that marker can mislead in both directions. Their scan uses a tracer that sticks to a protein common on cancer-supporting tissue, and they compared scan results against the blood marker in patients checked over about three years.

The scan judged cases more accurately than the blood marker in patients whose hormone levels were held low, and it was flawless in a smaller group tested under stimulation. It also found spread in several patients whose blood marker read negative, mostly in neck lymph nodes. Mou and colleagues say the scan can catch disease the standard marker misses.
plos-pone-0355543:
Nina Wanča, Jakub Jehlička, and Anna Hála studied a new children's exhibition that opened at the National Museum in Prague in 2023. The display was built for children aged five to ten and mixes hands-on stations with more traditional presentation. Rather than lecturing, it asks young visitors to explore and figure things out for themselves.

Over two and a half months the researchers watched hundreds of interactions involving more than two thousand visitors. Older children engaged more deeply, but they made up less than a quarter of the child visitors; most were younger than the intended audience. Many of those younger children seemed to struggle with the exhibition's open-ended design. The authors suggest ways to better match the content to the children who actually come.
plos-pone-0355743:
Bounmy Keohavong and co-authors feed in 2026 four alternative poultry ingredients to specially fed roosters to see how processing changes their value. The ingredients included distillery grains and meals from coconut, palm kernel, and jatropha. Birds received each feed as loose mash or as pellets, and in a second test mash received an enzyme that breaks down a tough plant fibre.

Pelleting raised how much dry matter and nitrogen birds kept and raised usable energy for all ingredients. Adding the enzyme also helped, most for the coconut and palm meals rich in that fibre. Both steps could let feed makers use fibrous byproducts more fully.
plos-pone-0355843:
Getahun Tamiru Yirsaw and co-authors reviewed outcomes for newborn babies treated for meningitis in public hospitals in Harar, Ethiopia. Newborn meningitis kills and disables many infants in low-income settings, yet local outcome data were scarce. Their 2026 study extracted records for about five hundred admitted newborns across four years.

One third of the babies had a poor treatment outcome. Risk climbed with assisted vaginal delivery and with laboratory-confirmed spinal fluid infection. Very high white cell counts in spinal fluid also tracked with poor outcomes. Yirsaw and colleagues argue earlier recognition and closer watch on these flagged babies could improve survival in similar hospitals.
plos-pone-0355943:
Ali Sait Özer and three co-authors address a power problem in wind energy systems in their 2026 engineering paper. Wind-driven generators that excite themselves can produce rough, uneven voltage, especially when the loads attached to them are unbalanced or draw current unevenly. A device called a DSTATCOM is meant to smooth that output, but it only works well when it can estimate the load current accurately.

The authors propose a new control method built around an improved phase-locked loop, a circuit that tracks the timing of the electrical signal. Their design filters messy load currents more cleanly, so the compensator can keep the source current balanced and smooth. Tests using real-time hardware simulation, including changing wind speeds and noisy measurements, showed the controller held up well.
plos-pone-0356143:
Fengliang Chen, writing alone, builds a trust-centered influence model in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on public health communication. Health messages spread through repeated peer and institutional contact, yet many computer diffusion models treat trust weakly. Privacy shocks can also abruptly reshape who seems credible.

The framework treats trust as a bounded, directed, and spreading state on a time-stamped network linking users, physicians, and shock events. A temporal graph model learns influence pathways, and an optimizer assigns interventions under a budget. In controlled simulations matched to the model's own assumptions, it beat comparison methods and lifted simulated intentions more than simple heuristics. Real-world testing, the author stresses, is still required.
plos-pone-0357043:
Shambal Kassahun Ferrede, Mulatu Werkina Eticha, and Habtamu Molla Ayele review births delivered with forceps or vacuum help at a university hospital in northwest Ethiopia, counting harm to newborns. Assisted vaginal delivery can save lives when done well, yet local evidence on baby outcomes was thin. Charts covered about three hundred such births across two years, and the team modeled which maternal and delivery traits tracked with adverse newborn results.

The results section tallies how common adverse outcomes were in this group and which factors stayed linked after adjustment, forming the study's core evidence. Ferrede and colleagues argue that knowing the local rate and its drivers helps the hospital train staff and choose instruments more safely, rather than importing assumptions from distant settings.
plos-pone-0357443:
Odey Bsharat and co-authors compare essential oils from a Mediterranean thyme relative gathered at two Palestinian sites, Hebron and Bethlehem. The herb is prized for oils rich in thymol and carvacrol, two compounds with germ-fighting reputations. Oils were drawn from fresh and dried leaves by steam, checked for makeup, and tested against oxidation, bacteria, and crop-damaging fungi.

Site changed the oil's character clearly: Hebron oil leaned rich in thymol, while Bethlehem oil leaned rich in carvacrol. All oils fought oxidation modestly and blocked bacteria across a useful range, with the strongest antifungal effects against the crop fungi tested. Bsharat and colleagues say origin and drying must be stated when such oils are sold or studied, since both shift performance.
plos-pone-0358043:
Yuye Wu and five colleagues search bladder cancer data for a tissue pattern that keeps immune cells out of tumors, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Checkpoint drugs free the immune system to attack, but only some patients benefit. Working across several public datasets, including spatial samples that preserve where cells sit, the team tracked a combined signature. It joins support cells, a growth signal called TGF-beta, and blood vessel lining. Those are three ingredients of a barrier around tumors.

The barrier direction reappeared in every section of an independent spatial cohort, a clean replication. Tumors scoring highest on it leaned toward not responding to a checkpoint drug, though after full adjustment the evidence stayed suggestive rather than conclusive. The authors are candid about the limits, including that some pattern assignments tracked sample sections. Their contribution is a testable barrier score and a map of which cohorts support it.
plos-pone-0358243:
Kerong Wang led a team of eight authors testing bedside ultrasound after cardiac arrest, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When a stopped heart restarts, called ROSC, families face an agonizing question: will the person wake up? Early signs of brain outcome are hard to read, yet they shape care decisions within hours.

Wang's team tested whether a quick ultrasound at the bedside can help judge neurological outcome early. A fast, noninvasive check would be valuable in crowded emergency settings. Honest early information helps doctors plan intensive care and helps families prepare. The study does not promise certainty, but any reliable early signal in this setting carries real weight for everyone involved.
plos-pone-0358343: Johnson and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on one of the hardest talks in medicine: delivering bad news in an emergency room. As a scoping review, it maps what studies say about how that talk is delivered. Emergency rooms are loud, fast, and public, which makes a gentle talk harder. A clear map can point to training that helps staff and families.
plos-pone-0358543:
Tendai N R Gwanzura leads a team of seven tracking COVID-19 deaths among Floridians living with HIV across the vaccine divide, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The cohort is vast, over one hundred twenty-two thousand people, followed from March 2020 through 2021. The authors compared the period before vaccines became available with the months after, asking whether the survival gaps between racial, ethnic, and neighborhood groups narrowed once shots existed.

Overall mortality actually rose in the vaccine period, driven by the Delta surge. Beneath that average, the gaps moved differently. Black patients carried about double the mortality hazard of white patients before vaccines, and a still elevated gap after. Hispanic patients' excess hazard, equally stark before, essentially vanished in the vaccine period. Living in a highly vulnerable neighborhood raised risk specifically once vaccines existed. Availability alone, the authors conclude, did not deliver equity.
plos-pone-0358643:
Nusrat Jahan and three colleagues build a decision support system that explains its own predictions and suggests what to change, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Managers like the accuracy of deep learning but distrust answers they cannot inspect. The framework combines a predictor with feature attribution, which shows what drove each call, and counterfactual reasoning, which finds the smallest changes that would flip an outcome.

They tested it on employee attrition and customer churn data, separately and combined. Accuracy reached roughly ninety-one percent for attrition and eighty-seven percent for churn, with well calibrated confidence scores. The explanations scored high on fidelity checks, and the suggested actions cost less than those from comparison methods. For a manager, that means not just a warning that someone may leave, but a plausible, affordable lever to pull first.
plos-pone-0358943:
Rania F Zaarour and six colleagues report laboratory findings on waterpipe smoke and lung cells in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. Hookah smoking is widespread worldwide, yet its effects on the airway lining are still being mapped. The team exposed healthy human bronchial cells, grown in the lab, to condensed waterpipe smoke and watched how the cells coped.

Stronger doses lowered cell survival, but a weak dose mainly triggered autophagy, the cell's internal recycling system, rather than killing the cells outright. Blocking that recycling pushed more cells into death, which suggests it acts as a defense under smoke stress. The exposed cells also showed damaged DNA and raised inflammatory signals. The findings add cellular detail to concerns about waterpipe smoke, while hinting that cell survival pathways shape the harm.
plos-pone-0359643:
Barry Chioza and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on brain research methods. It presents an optimised method for fluorescence-activated nuclei sorting, a technique that separates cell nuclei using glowing tags. The sorting prepares cortical cell types, the cells of the brain's outer layer, for epigenomic analysis.

Epigenomics studies chemical marks that control genes without changing DNA itself. Sorting clean nuclei by cell type first makes those marks readable cell group by cell group, instead of a blur of the whole cortex. Neuroscientists mapping how brain cells differ beneath identical DNA are the audience for a sharper sorting method.
pmc-10436543:
Glaviano, Foo, Lam, and co-authors review a key cell pathway known as PI3K, AKT, and mTOR, often shortened to PAM. Healthy cells use this chain of signals to stay alive, grow, and divide at the right times. Signals from growth factors feed into the chain under tight control.

When control breaks down, the same pathway can help cancers grow and spread. The review explains how the chain works step by step, then surveys drugs built to block parts of it. Readers gain a clear map of a major cancer target and of the promise and limits of drugs aimed at it.
pmc-13194743:
Feng Zhu leads a 2026 engineering paper on making tiny hemispherical resonator gyroscopes, devices that sense rotation for precision navigation. Their quality factor, a measure of how cleanly the shell vibrates, and its frequency splitting decide performance. Standard coating lays a continuous metal film on the shell, which adds damping and drags quality down.

The team used patterned coating instead, depositing titanium and platinum films only in designed patches on the curved shell through three-dimensional masks. Coated devices lost little quality, reaching a quality factor above eight million, with even performance around the shell and tiny frequency splitting. Cutting film coverage reduces friction damping, the authors show, and a model links pattern to uniformity.
pmc-13197443:
Ceren Demir and colleagues ran a 2026 trial of home posture exercise for fibromyalgia, a long-term pain condition. Guidelines pair the drug duloxetine with exercise for this condition. The team tested whether a home posture program adds benefit beyond the drug alone.

Fifty-one patients split into an exercise group and a control group, both on the drug. The exercise group trained at home three times a week for four weeks. Both groups improved in pain, mood, sleep, and quality of life. The exercise group gained more in sleep quality, physical quality of life, and trunk bending range. Pain and mood gains did not differ. The trial was short, with no later follow-up.
pmc-13200443:
Azza M El-Derby and colleagues review cancer-killing viruses for liver cancer in a 2026 article. Oncolytic viruses infect and burst cancer cells while sparing normal ones. Results in solid tumors still lag hopes, and liver cancer's dense, immune-suppressed setting is among the toughest.

The review covers natural and engineered viruses in lab and clinical work on liver tumors. Barriers include thick scar-like tissue, fast liver immune clearance, and uneven tumor traits. Fixes under study include stroma-targeting designs, viruses tuned to low-oxygen zones, and lab-grown tumor models to test delivery. Engineering now arms viruses to wake anti-tumor immunity. The authors map how these strands could yield stronger next-generation viruses.
pmc-13202443:
Stronger, water-resistant paper made from farm and mining waste is the aim of a 2026 study led by Oumaima Bendalahcen. The research article treats date palm fibers to enrich their cellulose, reinforces the sheets with phosphate waste rock, and coats them with a bio-based terpene phenolic resin.

The mineral additive, rich in calcium and magnesium oxides, bonded with fiber sugars to strengthen cohesion inside the sheet. After resin coating and heat pressing, the paper shed water far better and showed large gains in stiffness and tensile strength over the untreated material. Ductility also improved, and the authors present the recipe as a route to high-performance paper that valorizes two waste streams.
pmc-13203043:
Prescribing guidelines aim to trim opioid use, and a 2026 systematic review by Jihoon Lim measures whether they actually do. The review and meta-analysis gathers studies of opioid prescribing guidelines for adults, focusing on chronic noncancer pain, and pools their effects on use prevalence, dosage, and treatment duration.

From 190 records found in four databases, seventy-one studies entered the meta-analysis. After guidelines took effect, opioid dose per person and prescription duration fell year by year among chronic pain patients in the pooled estimates. Declines also appeared in the general population and in cancer and acute pain groups, showing effects spilling beyond the intended audience.
pmc-13209143:
A thyroid failure so severe it squeezed the heart is reported in a 2026 case authored by James Nelson Okema from northern Uganda. The article presents a 65-year-old woman with five months of worsening breathlessness, swelling, and slow pulse, arriving with chest pain and signs of cardiac tamponade from fluid around the heart.

Ultrasound confirmed a large effusion collapsing the right ventricle, and urgent drainage removed over half a liter of straw-colored fluid. Fluid tests argued against tuberculosis, the usual suspect in that region, while blood tests revealed severe autoimmune hypothyroidism driving the picture. Gentle thyroid hormone replacement followed drainage, her circulation recovered at once, and later scans showed the fluid gone.
pmc-13210143:
A two-faced enzyme in a tropical parasite appears impossible to delete, and a 2026 study headed by Juliana Martins Ribeiro works around that barrier in Leishmania infantum. Using CRISPR editing, the team tried to knock out an atypical phosphatase-kinase that tunes stress signaling, then studied parasites with lowered or raised expression instead.

Full deletion failed repeatedly, even with a spare copy supplied first, suggesting the gene is essential for the parasite's free-living stage. Halving expression stretched the parasites' shape, disturbed their cell cycle, and made them far more sensitive to oxidative attack inside host cells. Overexpression instead hardened them against antimony drugs, linking the enzyme to treatment resistance.
pmc-13210243:
Island mothers' DNA carries the timetable of early human settlement, and a 2026 genetics study by Anjana Welikala sequences it at full resolution in Sri Lanka. The research article analyzes 139 complete mitochondrial genomes from Sinhalese, Sri Lankan Tamil, and Vedda people, merged with 247 published genomes worldwide.

Four settlement phases emerged from the family trees reconstructed in the analysis. The earliest phase aligns with the first entry of modern humans into South Asia, backing the southern coastal dispersal route out of Africa for the region. West Eurasian lineages arrived later by way of India, and every studied population shows a marked shrinkage in effective size across its history.
pmc-13211943:
Chatbot safety filters work unevenly across languages, and a 2026 vulnerability analysis led by Saubhagya Joshi measures the gap with disguised harmful prompts. The study attacks a health-oriented language model in English, Spanish, and transliterated Hindi, using emoji and letter-permutation ciphers across self-harm, violence, and drug abuse categories.

One thousand prompts per language became six thousand model interactions for human coders to judge. Hindi prompts broke through most often under both disguise styles, with Spanish and English resisting better in the comparisons. Violence-related prompts succeeded more than the other harm types overall, and the authors urge stronger multilingual moderation before such tools guide health decisions.
pmc-13231943:
Nicolas Niessen and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry finding about boron compounds called NHC-boranes, where NHC is a ring-shaped carbon molecule that steadies the boron centre. They were heating a charged boron compound while trying to build a stronger acid catalyst.

Instead of the planned product, the heated compound pulled a fluorine-rich group off its own counter-ion, forming new chiral boranes, meaning versions that are mirror images of each other. The products showed an unusual cis and trans arrangement around a newly formed plane. The authors note the charged form is a very strong Lewis acid, a kind of electron-pair acceptor, and may prove useful as a catalyst.
pmc-13242143:
Okubo's team at Kanagawa Cancer Center warn thyroid pathologists against overreading a negative gene panel. Hotspot assays catch common mutations but can miss RET and NTRK fusions entirely. Reports should state the assay's scope and any residual suspicion explicitly. Pan-TRK staining may triage cases but never rules fusions out. When suspicion persists and management hinges on it, RNA fusion testing should follow. The aim is killing false reassurance, not mandating more tests.
pmc-13246043:
Chan and co-authors describe a puzzling physical sign in this 2026 ACG Case Reports Journal article. Jaundice, the yellowing caused by excess bilirubin in the blood, normally colors the whole body evenly. Their patient, a young man, turned yellow unevenly: days after fluid was drained from the right side of his abdomen, the yellowing and swelling both favored his left side.

Earlier reports blamed a channel between the abdomen and the skin left by the drainage procedure, but the authors argue that cannot be the whole story here. They present the case as an extremely rare, poorly documented phenomenon whose cause is likely several factors combined, and offer the details to help others recognize it.
pmc-13247843:
Wu and a large international team compare clinical diagnoses with brain pathology and genetics across parkinsonian disorders. Their 2026 cross-sectional study draws on 3,353 brain donors who had movement-disorder diagnoses or were healthy controls. Conditions covered include Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, and corticobasal syndrome.

Autopsy often told a different story from the clinic. Among people diagnosed with Parkinson disease, 3.1 percent actually had supranuclear palsy pathology, while 7.1 percent of clinical supranuclear palsy cases showed Lewy body disease instead. Nearly 17 percent of clinical multiple system atrophy cases had Lewy body pathology, and corticobasal syndrome most often reflected supranuclear palsy or Alzheimer pathology. The authors also examined how variants in genes such as GBA1 and LRRK2 tracked with these pathological patterns.
pmc-13248743:
Shah and colleagues describe a rare surgical emergency in this 2026 Cureus case report. A sixty-one-year-old woman arrived after a fall with low blood pressure, confusion, and a hugely swollen abdomen. Scans showed a massive cystic pelvic tumor pressing on a major vein and pushing her bowel aside, with signs of spread elsewhere.

Surgeons drained about six liters of fluid and removed her uterus and ovaries to relieve the pressure. Her recovery was stormy, with kidney injury, clots in both legs, and a bowel infection. Biopsy later confirmed a high-grade ovarian-type cancer. Too frail for drug treatment, she moved to comfort care and later died.
pmc-13248943:
Sun and co-authors report a dangerous bile tract infection in a 2026 surgical case. Their patient, a seventy-year-old man with diabetes and weak kidneys, arrived with abdominal pain. Scans found gallstones blocking his bile duct, an inflamed gallbladder, and a large abscess inside the abdomen, all driven by a highly virulent Klebsiella pneumoniae strain.

Doctors first drained the duct and removed the stones through an endoscope, then took out the gallbladder and drained the abscess. Cultures confirmed the aggressive bacterium. Bleeding from a stress ulcer and clotting problems followed, but the man recovered well. The authors stress early imaging, fast source control, and team care in such high-risk infections.
pmc-13249643:
Abel Ruiz-Giralt and colleagues propose an updated method for archaeology in this 2026 paper. Their toolkit, called Anthropic Activity Markers, reads chemical and biological traces left in old soil layers to work out what people once did at a site.

The update argues that soil chemistry values should be treated as parts of a whole, not as stand-alone numbers, since raw values can create false patterns. Using an older study of herding communities as a test case, the authors show the new maths gives firmer results. They say markers should be read as ratios mapped across space, giving a stronger base for claims about past behaviour.
pmc-13253843:
Annalena Ulsperger and colleagues test what makes science writing seem credible in a 2026 study. Readers often judge a text by its author rather than its facts. Across three experiments, with about 200 people in each, the team varied the author's stated gender and kind of expertise.

In the first test, texts said to be by high-expertise authors were rated more credible, with no gender effect. A second test found no effects at all. In the third, academic expertise raised credibility while personal expertise, meaning lived experience, did not. The authors urge care in how expertise is presented to readers.
pmc-13255743:
David Wilson and colleagues argue about emergency medicine training length in a 2026 letter to the editor. The letter responds to a study of board exam pass rates for the American qualifying exam in emergency medicine. Debate in the field centers on whether all residencies should move from three years to four.

The authors say pass rates differ little between three- and four-year programs. What seems to matter more is program age and maturity: seasoned faculty, refined curricula, and stable support. They warn that forcing longer training targets the wrong problem, and urge stronger standards and help for newer programs instead.
pmc-13258643:
Dong Yu and colleagues teach computers to rewrite enzyme genes so bacteria produce more usable protein. When foreign proteins are made in Escherichia coli, they often clump instead of dissolving. Simply picking the most common codons, the usual fix, ignores how codons sit together. Their 2026 framework learns better patterns.

One model learned codon habits from the bacterium's own genome, while a partner model ranked rewrites by predicted soluble output. Two industrial enzymes were rebuilt and tested, one starch-processing and one starch-cutting. Soluble yields jumped several-fold, and in the best case more than tenfold. The winning strategy avoids certain codon choices rather than chasing favorites.
pmc-13259243:
Emrullah Dar and colleagues built a monitoring framework that watches bridges with a handful of roving sensors. Sparse networks and shifting weather make real damage hard to spot in vibration data. Their 2026 system carries sensitive accelerometers from spot to spot on a bridge pier being strengthened.

Wavelet analysis and autoregressive models extract damage clues, then a block-wise compression step fuses the sensors' streams cleanly. After concrete jacketing, median vibration intensity dropped by about two-fifths. Statistical distance checks confirmed the change was structural, not ambient noise, at high confidence. The authors pitch the setup as cheap, reliable retrofit verification.
pmc-13260043:
Alexandra Gianaris leads a 2026 study of bacterial communities living on and in leaf-cutter ants of the genus Atta. These ants farm fungi for food and carry diverse bacteria, but the reasons for that diversity are unclear. The team sequenced a bacterial marker gene from whole worker ants. They compared four dominant Atta species and, within one species, ants kept in the laboratory, ants treated with pesticide, and the ants' fungal garden partner.

Bacterial communities differed significantly among the four Atta species. They also differed between laboratory conditions, pesticide treatment, and the fungal garden of the most studied species. Surprisingly, bacteria of laboratory-kept ants were not significantly different from those of pesticide-treated ants. The authors say that finding should prompt a rethink of standard research methods for these ants, since lab keeping alone seems to reshape their microbes.
pmc-13262543:
Hirotaka Nishijima and colleagues redraw a classic exercise test so three ways of spotting the anaerobic threshold share one axis. Trainers and doctors read that threshold, where breathing chemistry shifts, from gas exchange plots. The standard V-slope plot uses different axes than its two companion methods, complicating comparison.

Their trick converts each breath's data into a single gap value, plotted against time like the other methods. The threshold then appears as the first upward bend from a flat line. One hundred twenty-seven volunteers and patients were scored blindly by all four methods. The paper compares how repeatably each technique lands on the same point.
pmc-13262943:
Bailey Lubash and colleagues use zebrafish to learn why a ribosome-making gene misshapes the face. Variants in Pol III subunits cause human craniofacial differences, though the machinery works in every cell. Their 2026 study examines fish missing the polr3a subunit.

Mutant fish grew stunted facial cartilage and bone from neural crest cells. Surprisingly, those precursor cells multiplied and survived normally early on; death spread through the head only later. Transfer RNA output and ribosome production sagged in step. A tumor suppressor gene switched on, but blocking it alone could not rescue the face. Extra, still-hidden factors must support the growing skull.
pmc-13263243:
Mohsen Khosravi and co-authors systematically review what drives use of decision support systems in health care in a 2026 journal article. These computer systems supply guidance at the point of decisions, but uptake varies widely. Following standard review methods, they searched four databases for studies from 2000 to 2024 and assessed quality with a standard checklist.

Eighty-six studies were included, all judged high quality with low bias risk. Thematic analysis produced 11 themes and 47 sub-themes, covering system design, user traits, personalization, trust, quality, and ethical and legal issues. How much each factor mattered differed across studies. The gap was especially marked between developed and developing countries, the authors note.
pmc-13263943:
Asuman Koparir and co-authors publish a 2026 correction notice for their article on chromatinopathies, a family of disorders where faulty chromatin, the packaging of DNA, causes overlapping developmental conditions. The original paper reported new gene variants and their DNA methylation signatures, chemical marks that help identify each disorder.

The correction fixes a single entry in Table 1. For patient P62, with a variant in the gene SMARCB1, a splice-site change was printed with the wrong number. It appeared as c.336–2 A > G and should read c.363–2 A > G. The notice shows both the incorrect and correct values for the record. No other content of the article changes.
pmc-13264443:
Rodrigue Namèkinsba Doamba and colleagues report a 2026 case of a large benign growth in the small bowel that caused heavy bleeding. The growth was a Brunner's gland hamartoma, a rare lump in the duodenum, the first part of the small bowel. Such lumps are usually small and quiet.

Their patient was a 56-year-old woman who vomited blood and passed dark stools. Scans showed the bowel had folded in on itself around a mass. Surgery found a stalked tumor seven centimetres wide, and surgeons removed it. Lab tests confirmed the benign growth, fully cut out. She left hospital on day four, and no return was seen after four years. The authors say surgery fits when scope removal cannot work.
pmc-13264543:
Sarah C Haight led a 2026 study from Pakistan on how breastfeeding and depression around birth affect each other. Feeding may guard against low mood after birth, while low mood can make feeding harder. The team used long-term data from the Bachpan study to test both directions.

The study covered 1,014 mothers at five points from pregnancy to one year after birth. Any breastfeeding was common, but only 8.7 percent fed with breast milk alone at six months. Depression touched one in four mothers late in pregnancy. Mothers with depression were less likely to breastfeed at all. Breastfeeding linked to a lower risk of later depression, though that result was not firm. The authors call the link two-way and complex.
pmc-13264943:
Wan Hua Sim and a large team wrote a 2026 protocol for a trial supporting families of children who lose skills they once had, a change called developmental regression. Families need fast recognition, practical care skills, and support for their own well-being. The trial tests an online program, Family Focus, built with parents, clinicians, and researchers.

Fifty-six families will be split by chance into two groups. One gets the online program alone, and the other gets the program plus online parent coaching. The main outcome is parent stress right after the program. Other measures cover parent mood, health habits, family empowerment, family quality of life, and child health. Checks run at the start, after the program, and a year later. The team will also study uptake and what helps or blocks delivery.
pmc-13267543:
Habib Bellamlih and colleagues present a 2026 case report about flank pain that was not kidney stone pain. Their patient was a 32-year-old woman with repeated attacks of left lower back pain over fifteen days. The pain felt like renal colic, the cramping pain of a kidney stone, and she had passed a stone on the other side before.

Scans instead showed a lumbar hernia of the Grynfeltt type, where tissue pushes through a weak spot in the back wall of the belly. Such hernias make up under 2 percent of belly hernias and are easy to miss. The authors stress that this rare hernia belongs in the thinking for lasting or odd flank pain, and that CT scanning settles the question early.
pmc-13269143:
Martine Hoogendoorn and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 building a scoring method for thinking problems in schizophrenia. Patients report trouble with memory, speaking, planning, and attention on a survey called PRECIS. The team turned selected survey answers into health values that the wider public places on each state.

Four survey items were chosen after expert talks and data checks. Members of the United Kingdom public then rated health states in choice tasks and time trade-off interviews. The best state scored 0.992, near full health, and the worst scored 0.292. Worse trouble in every area lowered the score. The method lets cost studies count thinking problems more fairly.
pmc-13269443:
Mathilde G E Verdam and co-authors published a review in 2026 on response shift in patient-reported health surveys. Response shift means patients change how they judge their own health over time, which can distort measured change. The review asked how often this effect alters study conclusions.

The team examined 173 studies holding 943 survey results. About half the studies checked for an impact from response shift. Where impact was reported, evidence of it appeared in 69 percent of studies and 41 percent of results. Effects on statistical strength were common, while effects on actual care decisions were rare, at 8 percent of studies. The authors urge more work on decision impact.
pmc-13269543:
Eszter Mercédesz Müller and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 checking four cosmetic survey scales in Hungarian women around minor facial treatments such as Botox and fillers. The scales cover views on aging, distress about appearance, and early effects of treatment. Women who had finished treatment and women planning it both took part.

The survey included 210 treated women and 147 planning treatment. Most scales showed a ceiling effect, with many top scores. The distress scale matched strongly with self-esteem and fear of negative judgment measures. Two scales each formed one clean theme, while one split into three. Treated women scored higher on aging and distress scales and felt younger than planners, by 5.0 years against 2.8 years.
pmc-13269843:
Yuting Zou and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 32-year-old man with skin thickening and shortness of breath. Ultrasound of his neck and back showed thickened skin, and biopsies confirmed scleredema, a rare disease that hardens the skin for unknown reasons. Heart tests were done at the same time.

The heart showed widespread injury to the left chamber muscle and worsening heart failure, diagnosed as cardiomyopathy tied to the skin disease. Such heart involvement was previously seen mostly in older patients and remains poorly understood. No specific treatment strategy exists for it. The authors present the young patient's case to draw clinical attention to this uncommon pairing and its risks.
pmc-13270243:
Emre Yücel and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on hospital use and readmissions among patients treated with a modern antibiotic pair, ceftolozane/tazobactam, for hard-to-treat infections. The multinational study gathered real-world records for 617 adult inpatients in seven countries who got at least 48 hours of the drug.

Overall 30-day readmission was 10.2 percent, and infection-related readmission was 4.9 percent. Median hospital stay was 42 days, with six days after starting the drug. Intensive care patients, 298 of them, readmitted at only 3.4 percent but stayed a median of 59 days. Patients with cystic fibrosis readmitted at 10.9 percent. The authors stress the figures describe patterns and cannot prove cause.
pmc-13270343:
Laura Langohr and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on two inherited bone marrow failure diseases that can turn into leukemia. Gene activity was mapped in patient skin cells, marrow, and blood across disease stages, at single-cell level. One disease is caused by faults in ERCC6L2, a DNA repair gene.

Red blood cell development showed stress signs, including an iron-linked death signal, before the key TP53 mutation appeared. Mutations arose in stem cells but did not by themselves shift cell cycle or stress programs. Both diseases converged late in red cell formation on the same stress state. The ERCC6L2 disease also showed faulty early red cell priming that shaped its path toward leukemia.
pmc-13270743:
Norio Zimmermann is lead author of a 2026 journal article presenting SCITE-RNA, a new computer method for building family trees of cells from single-cell RNA data. Such data record which genes are active in each cell, plus counts of normal and changed gene copies.

The method searches for the most likely tree by switching between a cell lineage view and a mutation view, a tactic meant to avoid getting stuck on a poor answer. On simulated data it beat existing methods, the authors report. On cancer data, it let them link how tumour cells evolved to the gene activity patterns of those cells.
pmc-13271143:
Atqah AbdulWahab is lead author of a 2026 journal article comparing saliva and blood levels of cortisol, a stress hormone, in children with asthma. Inhaled steroids are the mainstay asthma treatment for children, but they may suppress the body's own cortisol system, a worry that grows when a second drug, montelukast, is added. Blood tests are invasive for children.

The study recruited 150 children, 50 each on inhaled steroids alone, on steroids plus montelukast, and healthy controls. Saliva and blood cortisol levels correlated positively, though modestly, and neither measure differed clearly between the treatment groups. Age, sex, body size, steroid dose, and asthma severity did not affect cortisol. The authors back saliva as a gentler option.
pmc-13271743:
Kathleen S. Metz Reed is lead author of a 2026 journal article on how genome organisation changes as breast cancer progresses. Large-scale shifts in DNA compartments happened mainly in the early stages, while finer changes in domains and loops built up during the later move toward metastasis, the spread stage. Many changed genes were physically linked to distant control elements, and enhancer contact strength tracked gene activity. Strong loop changes were fairly rare, suggesting folding changes help at a subset of genes rather than everywhere.
pmc-13271943: Liam Mitchell is first named author on a 2026 journal article on RNA editing changes in the mouse hippocampus. That is the brain's memory centre. The changes come in response to amyloid beta. That protein builds up in Alzheimer's disease and harms nerve cells. The study identifies site-specific editing of SINE B2 RNAs as an early response. SINE B2 RNAs are short repetitive RNA elements. The response is epitranscriptomic, meaning a change in chemical editing of RNA rather than in the RNA sequence itself. It responds to amyloid beta neurotoxicity.
pmc-13272243:

Low cortisol, the stress hormone made by the adrenal glands, was proposed as a contributor, and the team tracked cortisol and sodium together after surgery to test that idea.

The study reviewed 261 patients operated on for non-functioning pituitary tumours between 2021 and 2024. Delayed low sodium occurred in 54 patients, or 20.7 percent, reaching its lowest point at a median of eight days. Cortisol levels did not differ clearly between patients with and without the complication, and low cortisol during episodes was only somewhat more frequent, not significantly. The title summarises the verdict: hypocortisolism's role looks limited.
pmc-13273443:
Joshua Cuoco leads a 2026 illustrative case treating a pseudoaneurysm in a distal brain artery in a 14-year-old girl with flow diversion. Pseudoaneurysms are dangerous weak spots that lack a true wall and carry high rupture risk. Hers was found on follow-up imaging after surgery for a brain tumor, in the M3 segment of the middle cerebral artery.

Angiography confirmed an 8 millimeter pseudoaneurysm. A Pipeline Vantage flow diverter was placed in the parent vessel, with good wall contact and early slowing of flow inside the lesion. She tolerated the procedure well and was discharged on aspirin and ticagrelor for six months. The authors call flow diversion a safe, feasible option for such rare lesions.
pmc-13273843:
Liu and colleagues report a 2026 cohort study of ustekinumab for Crohn's disease with strictures in China. Strictures are narrowings of the bowel that block flow. The study followed adults who started the drug for symptomatic strictures.

Of 73 patients screened, 54 entered the study. At week 52, 44 patients, or 81.5 percent, met the success target. Success meant staying on the drug without banned add-on treatments. Most patients improved in blockage symptoms and disease activity scores. Scans, scope findings, and blood markers also improved. Non-smoking and C-reactive protein levels predicted success. The prediction model reached 86.4 percent accuracy in telling outcomes apart. One leukemia case and two serious infections were reported.
pmc-13274043:
Henrik Hillerdal and co-authors present a 2026 journal article asking whether Swedish children checked for Lyme disease of the nervous system had other tick-borne infections. Newer tick diseases such as anaplasmosis and babesiosis are reported more often, but rates in children are unclear. Their symptoms can be vague and tests are not always at hand.

The team tested stored samples from 235 children evaluated between 2011 and 2014 for Lyme neuroborreliosis. Lab tests searched blood for four other tick-borne germs, and spinal fluid from some children for one of them. No sign of these infections or co-infections was found. The authors still advise doctors to consider them in children with odd fever or rashes.
pmc-13275543:
Yuanzhao Yang and colleagues present a 2026 journal article forecasting how climate change will shift the ranges of seven Meconopsis poppy species in China. These mountain flowers are prized and climate sensitive. Using an optimized MaxEnt model, software that maps suitable habitat from known locations and climate data, the team projected current and future ranges under several warming scenarios.

All seven species concentrate in southwestern China, with suitable habitat covering just 1.3 to 10.1 percent of the country's land. Day-night temperature stability, seasonal temperature swing, and elevation mattered most. One species, M. lyrata, is expected to lose suitable habitat, while the others show mixed gains and losses. The authors urge botanical institutions to prioritize growing these species outside the wild to safeguard their genes.
pmc-13276143:
Seham El-Sayed Saleh and co-authors present a 2026 survey study from Egypt on mothers, vitamin D, and young children's health. Over eight months in three regions, the team surveyed three hundred mothers of children under five. About two thirds of mothers had satisfactory knowledge about deficiency. More than half, though, scored poorly on actual practices such as giving supplements. Better practices tracked moderately with children's height and weight. Knowledge alone linked more weakly to child health. Mothers' age and education also shaped practice scores. The authors argue that coaching habits matters more than simply sharing facts.
pmc-13276343:
Tsukasa Kato and co-authors report a 2026 pathology study on two kinds of calcium buildup in leg arteries. Scans cannot reliably tell them apart, so their relationship stayed unclear.

The team sliced one hundred twenty-five artery segments from fifty-eight patients into more than thirty-five hundred cross-sections. Medial calcification appeared in over ninety percent of segments and ran heavier below the knee. Intimal calcification showed the opposite pattern. Where one type was extensive, the other was usually minimal: their arcs barely overlapped. Bone even formed inside the wall in about one sixth of segments, marking the most advanced disease. The authors say heavy medial calcification may suppress plaque growth and blunt standard treatments.
pmc-13276743:
Antonia Berz and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a rare blood vessel emergency after a breast biopsy. A pseudoaneurysm, a contained leak from an artery wall, is an exceedingly rare complication.

Their patient was a sixty-four-year-old woman whose biopsy targeted an aggressive pre-cancer beside an invasive cancer. She developed a pseudoaneurysm about two and a half centimeters wide inside the breast. Only about thirty-six such cases after breast biopsy appear in the literature, most handled with surgery. Instead, doctors injected thrombin, a clotting agent, into the leak under ultrasound guidance. The leak sealed without complications. The authors urge early recognition to prevent bleeding, and present the injection as a safe, less invasive alternative to surgery.
pmc-13277643:
Mitsuru Mizuno leads a 2026 study of a system that checks how well workers wipe-clean biosafety cabinets, the enclosed benches used for sterile work. Cleaning with ethanol spray and wiping varies by operator, and quality is hard to verify. The system combines a color camera, a heat camera, and pressure sensors built into the wiping tool.

On steel plates seeded with bacterial spores, only spray plus pressure wiping stopped growth fully, showing that chemical and mechanical action work together. The system mapped sprayed, wiped, and missed areas in real time, with consistent results across speeds and operators. Recordable, measured checks could replace trust-based cleaning routines in drug and cell labs, the authors argue.
pmc-13277743:
Ilias Miltiadis leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of spleen anatomy, combining data from 64 studies. The spleen is a blood-rich immune organ that surgeons find hard to stitch and easy to damage. Knowing its normal size ranges and vessel patterns helps plan operations and preserve the organ after injury.

Pooled averages put spleen length at roughly ten and a half centimeters, with width near seven and volume near two hundred nineteen cubic centimeters. In most people the spleen's artery branches off the celiac trunk and runs above the pancreas before splitting into two or more branches. Variation is wide, so the authors stress careful imaging and planning for each patient.
pmc-13278243:
Sofija Pejkova leads a 2026 study of a nerve-release operation for diabetic foot ulcers. Ten patients with diabetes and chronic foot ulcers, lasting about seventeen months on average, had Dellon decompression, surgery that frees a pinched nerve tunnel at the ankle. The team checked feeling, artery flow, and foot blood supply with a tracer scan before and twelve months after surgery.

Feeling improved clearly, judged by how close together two touch points could be told apart. Flow in the main ankle artery nearly doubled on ultrasound. Tracer scans showed higher uptake in the operated foot at rest and under stress, by roughly a third. All foot ulcers had healed by the twelve-month follow-up.
pmc-13278443:
Andrea Nucita leads a 2026 study of whether AI tools can reliably classify social media posts for sociological research. Human coding is slow, and categories can be ambiguous. The case study covers Facebook posts by two Italian universities from March 2020 to March 2023, sorted into eight types of public communication. Three researchers coded the posts independently as a benchmark.

Human coders themselves disagreed on several categories, showing real interpretive ambiguity. Automated models matched human classifications about as well as humans matched each other. The findings support using AI as an extra coder inside hybrid workflows, the authors say. That pairing could make large-scale, transparent analysis of complex social media data practical for sociology.
pmc-13279943: Remi Sieskind and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to their 2025 Scientific Reports study. That study used a phage virus own DNA polymerase, its DNA copying enzyme, to sequence its hypermodified genome, meaning DNA with heavily altered bases. The error sat in Figure 5B, where the formula in the glycosidic bond, the link that joins a DNA base to its sugar, was drawn wrong. The notice reprints the figure and caption on related phages and their DNA changes. The sequence work and its claims stand.
pmc-13280343:
Katharina Helena Morawitz and colleagues report a 2026 study of biological age after bariatric surgery. The team modelled mortality associated biological age from standard blood markers. Age acceleration is the gap between biological and calendar age. A prospective cohort of five hundred five surgery patients was tracked to two years.

At baseline, age acceleration rose with smoking load and with body mass, most in males. Twelve months after surgery, patients scored on average about five and a half years younger in biological age. The gain held stable to twenty four months. After adjustment for body mass change, the gain shrank to about three and a third years at twelve months. Part of the rejuvenation thus runs apart from weight loss itself, a gain the authors call independent in the title.
pmc-13280543:

The review sums evidence that links pituitary stem cells and tumour stem like cells to tumour start, upkeep and growth. It sets practical criteria for defining tumour stem cells. It weighs work from human tumour function studies, new single cell and spatial gene data sets and mouse lineage tracing models. A curated list of single cell RNA studies flags stem groups across tumour subtypes. Targeting stem like cells is the care hope at the close.
pmc-13280643:
Constance Delaugerre and colleagues reported in 2026 on a French program for people whose HIV no longer responds to most drugs. Forty-two adults got lenacapavir, a drug that blocks the shell of the virus, plus other drugs picked for them. Care ran from 2021 to 2023 under a program for hard cases. Thirty-three patients had HIV type one and nine had type two.

By week twenty-six, about two in three patients with type one had the virus under full control. Results for type two were much weaker, at about one in five. A few patients developed drug resistance, and about a third had sore spots where the shot went in. No severe harm was tied to the drug.
pmc-13282043:
Michele Tizzani and Yelena Mejova present a 2026 study of how viewers engage with vaccine videos on YouTube. Over six months they tracked more than seven thousand vaccine-related videos, posted from November 2024 to May 2025. They classified each video and its comments as for or against vaccination, checking machine labels by hand. They also noted who posted the video and what moderation the platform applied.

Vaccine-hesitant videos drew far more likes and comments than strongly pro-vaccine videos. They also gathered most of their views faster, reaching ninety percent of views in about eighteen days against about thirty-two. Comment threads under hesitant videos tended to agree with the video, forming echo chambers. Pro-vaccine threads drew more open argument. Pro-vaccine content came mostly from news and health bodies, while hesitant content came more often from lone creators. The findings matter for how health groups plan online outreach.
pmc-13285743:
Zhaochen Zhang and co-authors review artificial intelligence for osteoporosis care in a 2026 overview of the field. Weak bones are often found late, since standard scans are scarce and reading them takes expert time. Smart software promises faster screening, sharper risk forecasts, and help in finding new drugs.

Programs now read plain X-rays, CT, MRI, and ultrasound images to flag thin bone and grade fracture risk. Other tools sort risk factors, hunt for gene targets, and predict how patients will fare on treatment. Gains in speed can be large, with some measures done in a fraction of the usual time. Yet studies vary widely in patients, methods, and scoring, and outside checks are often thin, so the authors urge shared standards before wide clinical use.
pmc-13286143:
Tzu-Fei Wang and a large team of colleagues study language and end-of-life care in Ontario in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Most dying cancer patients in the province receive home care, yet care in a language the patient does not share can warp hard choices near death. Records sorted patients by their preferred tongue: English, French, or another language entirely.

The cohort held 33,958 home care patients who died of cancer from 2013 to 2018. Patients in the third group, many of them recent arrivals, died in hospital far more often than English speakers did. They also faced more emergency visits, more admissions, and more aggressive steps in their final thirty days. French speakers too died in hospital more often, a pattern the authors say demands work on root causes and fairer care.
pmc-13287143:
Natalia Muklewicz and colleagues present a 2026 case-based review of granulomatosis with polyangiitis when the illness first affects the bladder, cervix, or urethra rather than airways or kidneys. Their own patient, a woman aged 58, had bladder surgery before the immune cause was recognised.

Searching four databases, the team assembled 40 women in total, including their case. For nearly half, genital or urinary signs came first and often looked like cancer, and many underwent operations that later proved avoidable. Steroids and cyclophosphamide were common treatments. Rituximab controlled disease that kept returning, and the authors urge early rheumatology input.
pmc-13287243:
Xu Bai wrote a letter in 2026 about a study by Utami and others. The study described a life-skills teaching module meant to keep Indonesian teenagers away from drug misuse. The module was built around social cognitive theory. Bai welcomes the move from giving facts alone toward practising real skills such as handling stress and speaking up.

Three concerns follow. The listed skills look much like those in existing programmes, so the local Indonesian shaping needs clearer proof. Activities are not mapped tightly onto theory ideas such as confidence to refuse. Expert approval scoring, reported as 82%, needs plainer handling of disagreement and of weak readability scores for young readers.
pmc-13287543:
Changik Lee, Young-Jin Kim, and Jin-Sung Kim report in 2026 two hard cases of keyhole spine surgery through two small ports, where scar tissue stuck fast to the nerve covering. Working one-handed is a known limit of the method, since the other hand holds the camera.

In one case scarring followed earlier surgery; in the other, a joint cyst caused long-term inflammation. A scope retractor either held sticky tissue steady or served as a dissecting tool, giving an effect much like a second hand. Both cases ended with full freeing of tissue and good nerve relief. The authors recommend the tool for severe sticking in port-based spine work.
pmc-13287843:
Kyungseok Park and co-authors analysed emergency visits in 2026 by 1,445 people aged 24 or younger. All came to a Seoul psychiatric emergency centre after self-harm or a suicide attempt. Records covered January 2015 to December 2022. They searched for traits tied to severe medical harm and to return visits within sixty days.

Most visitors were female, at 75.4%, and most acts were impulsive. Severe medical outcomes hit 8.7% of visits, tied to planned attempts and to high-harm methods. Returns within sixty days hit 7.1%. Living alone, asking for help aloud, prior mental health care, and female sex raised return risk. The authors urge tailored follow-up after discharge.
pmc-13288043:
Sanjida Haque, Rosanna Cavalletto, and Mohammed Ali Alomshani surveyed green dental practice in Saudi Arabia in 2026. They mixed a questionnaire for 200 dentists and clinic directors in Riyadh with six in-depth interviews across the country. Dentistry uses much energy, water, and single-use gear, so the team mapped what clinics already do.

Digital imaging, energy saving, and paper cuts scored high. Reusable tools, water-saving taps, and renewable power lagged, even though awareness ran high. Lack of training was the top barrier, followed by weak motivation and cost worries. The authors call for training, money incentives, and firm clinic policy to close the gap.
pmc-13288143:
Hongyang Zhang and co-authors coated copper oxide films in 2026 with a thin platinum skin to stop sunlight from eating the material away during water-splitting tests aimed at making hydrogen fuel. The porous films were cast from a gel mix, with a mild acid used as a helper for the first time.

Microscope and surface checks showed even platinum coverage over pores tens of nanometres wide. After half an hour under working conditions, coated films kept 57% of their starting current; bare films kept only 2.9%. A layer near twenty nanometres thick worked best. Gas output did not rise, so the gain is durability, not yield.
pmc-13288543:
Farahwahida Mohd Kasim and co-authors study drug prices in Malaysia in 2026. The work deals with public buying of drugs. Records came from 19 ministry sites. Years ran from 2017 to 2021. Eight costly drug groups were covered.

The data held 97 drugs in all. It held 4,702 purchase records and 28 suppliers. East Malaysia had the widest price spread. Small buys spread more and cost more per unit. Imported generics spread most in price. Yet they cost less than brand or local drugs. More rival drugs steadied paid prices. Bid spreads grew at the same time. Rivalry works past headline price, they say.
pmc-13288943:
Joshua Nmezi reports a panic attack during spine numbing in 2026. His case study tells one patient's story. The patient was a 52-year-old woman. She had knee replacement surgery while awake. She had no past mental health history.

About 35 minutes in, panic struck hard. She felt chest tightness and doom. Her heart raced and her blood pressure spiked. Staff thought of stopping the surgery. The lead doctor used calm talk and breath work. Grounding and guided images helped too. Her symptoms cleared in eight minutes. Surgery then finished with no more trouble.
pmc-13289143:
Jeongeun Park and colleagues study mothers who spent childhood in care. Records came from the UK Millennium Cohort Study. It holds 11,252 mothers in all. Of them, 156 had been in out-of-home care. Distress was tracked as children aged 3 to 14.

Mothers with care pasts felt more distress at each age. The gap held across all five checks. Early factors helped explain the later gap. Poor mental health after birth played a part. Low sense of control played a part too. Low income and weak support also counted. The authors urge joined-up help after birth. Such help may break a long chain of hardship.
pmc-13289343:
Hyeon-Kyoung Koo and a multicenter team validated a 2026 short cough questionnaire across many lung diseases. The Rapid Cough Questionnaire has just three items and aims to replace a longer standard tool, the Leicester Cough Questionnaire, in busy clinics. Whether the short form holds up in structural lung disease was still untested before this work.
