Adults with chronic cough, 300 in total, completed five cough scales at respiratory centers. Scores on the short form tracked the long form very tightly and also matched other symptom scales well. Links held across chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, lung scarring, and bronchiectasis groups. Even in lung scarring, where simple scales drifted apart, the short form stayed close to the long form.
pmc-13289443:
Sophie Mårtensson and coauthors share a 2026 think-aloud study checking a questionnaire on virtual patient learning for nursing students. Virtual patients are digital cases for practice, here focused on intimate partner violence, a sensitive topic needing careful teaching tools. Few validated surveys exist for such simulations, so each question needed cognitive testing before wider use.

Eleven undergraduates at one nursing school in western Sweden spoke their thoughts aloud during solo digital interviews. The survey holds eleven background items plus eighteen main items on ease of use and fit within the study module. Students found wording clear and the form easy to follow overall. Some items still needed rewording, and both original and revised forms are shown for future users.
pmc-13289543:
Rachel Hooley led a 2026 report on adapting Pal-Cycles, a palliative care program for advanced cancer, across seven European countries. The program aims to smooth transitions in care near the end of life. Health systems and cultural views on dying differ widely, so a single design cannot simply be copied from country to country without local tuning.

Countries were Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, and the United Kingdom for a stepped trial. Structured group meetings within and across countries reworked five core parts of the program. A total of 36 clinicians, 14 patients or family members, and 16 facilitators took part across five meetings, mostly online. Most countries involved patient and family voices directly.
pmc-13289743:
Morten Hostrup Martinsen and coauthors report a 2026 case of cholesteryl ester storage disease in a girl whose blood tests mimicked inherited high cholesterol. The rare disorder stems from faults in the LIPA gene, which makes an enzyme that breaks down stored fats in cell compartments. Without it, fatty esters pile up in liver cells and scavenger cells, harming organs over time.

Her total cholesterol was 9.3 mmol/L with very high low-density cholesterol and raised liver enzymes as measured. Whole genome sequencing found two different faulty copies of the gene, confirming the storage disease. She had no visible cholesterol deposits and no symptoms of organ damage yet at reporting. Enzyme replacement exists, making early recognition valuable.
pmc-13289843:
Gianfranco Di Gennaro and coauthors compare a 2026 cross-section of websites on health risks of eating meat across the United States, Britain, and Italy. Web quality shapes what shoppers believe and buy, so the top 100 pages per country were graded with a standard benchmark tool. Checks covered professional authorship, intake guidance, substitutes, sustainability, and disease prevention topics across the pages.

High quality was found in 61 percent of American pages and most British pages, but only 22.3 percent of Italian pages in the sample. Stance toward meat also varied: meat-attacking pages and pages by health professionals appeared less often among Italian results than American ones. Pages on environmental and long-term disease risks also appeared less often in Italy.
pmc-13290443:
Women with type 2 diabetes in the West Bank report far heavier gastroparesis symptoms than men, Diya Asad and a large team found in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Gastroparesis slows stomach emptying and brings nausea, fullness, vomiting, early satiety, and bloating.

The survey covered 3,248 patients and scored symptoms with the Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index in its validated Arabic form. Women showed higher rates of obesity and poorer blood sugar control, more of them met the symptom picture of the condition, and their severity scores ran higher for every symptom. In adjusted analysis, female sex was the only independent factor tied to severe symptoms. The authors discuss hormonal and nerve-related explanations and call for work on the mechanisms behind the gap.
pmc-13290543:
Nigerian teenagers meet most of the classic tasks of adolescence, Usani Joseph Ofem and colleagues report in a descriptive study from 2026. Using Havighurst's framework, the team asked how fully secondary-school students manage tasks spanning friendships, body image, independence, careers, and values.

Data came from 2,287 students who completed a validated accomplishment scale. Career aims and social duty were the strongest domains, while gender role identity was the least achieved and several others landed in the middle. Patterns split by gender: boys led on autonomy and career engagement, girls on family- and friend-oriented tasks. Students from monogamous homes and older students aged 17 to 19 also scored higher in several areas. The authors see the framework holding up in this cultural setting.
pmc-13290743:
After a brain injury, the mind's resting networks shift in ways that track specific thinking problems, Madhumathi P C and colleagues synthesize in a 2026 integrative review. They gathered resting-state fMRI studies that link network change with thinking problems after traumatic brain injury.

Across the studies, three networks changed most often: the default mode, frontoparietal, and salience networks. Default mode links tied closely to attention, processing speed, and memory. Frontoparietal changes mirrored executive function deficits, and sensorimotor disruption tracked attentional problems. Networks also kept changing over time, hinting at the brain's plastic repair attempts. The authors propose resting connectivity as a sensitive marker for diagnosis and follow-up care, and they argue treatment should be planned around networks rather than single regions.
pmc-13290843:
Apps and online programs did not ease ICU families' distress in the first three months, Baolin Huang and colleagues conclude in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026. Relatives of intensive care patients often develop anxiety, depression, or post-traumatic stress, a burden named post intensive care syndrome-family, and eHealth tools promise scalable support.

Eleven randomized trials with 1,200 participants were pooled. Overall, eHealth interventions showed no significant benefit for anxiety, depression, or PTSD within three months of follow-up. One subgroup stood out: programs that built in early-stage psychological support did improve depression scores modestly. Huang and colleagues read the pattern as timing mattering more than technology, and call for rigorous trials of early-supported designs before health systems invest broadly.
pmc-13291643:
Blocking one cleanup enzyme may boost a cancer drug class. Glenn Hauk leads a 2026 study of DCTPP1 blockers. The enzyme chews up altered DNA building blocks. That chewing weakens analog drugs used against cancer.

A mass screen hunted compounds that jam the enzyme. New and known classes showed strong submicromolar power. Crystal images showed all blockers in the same pocket. Two key residues grip each blocker in place. Tweaked scaffolds confirmed the grip model. Lead blockers paired with decitabine in prostate cells. Growth blocking grew far stronger in the pair. Gene tests proved the boost needs the enzyme.
pmc-13291743:
Antonia Waldmann and co-authors report a 2026 study of how the uterus heals after birth, comparing tissue samples from humans and mice. They reanalyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from human muscle layer tissue taken from non-pregnant people and from people seven days after delivery. Mouse uteri were also examined with flow cytometry, tissue staining, and gene expression tests.

By day seven, human uterine muscle showed lasting immune activity alongside shrinking muscle components. In mice, the mesometrial triangle, a zone packed with immune cells during pregnancy, was gradually reabsorbed as the muscle layers closed back up. Macrophages, CD8+ T cells, and myofibroblasts gathered near the placental separation site inside a collagen-rich capsule. The authors frame healing as compartment-specific, with each uterine region following its own repair program.
pmc-13292243:
Lorca Alzoubi and co-authors test a 2026 candidate drug, CMPP, in a mouse model where pain and depression arrive together. Reserpine, given for three days, creates that paired state by draining monoamine transmitters. Mice received CMPP at three doses or gabapentin, and the middle dose then fed into brain chemistry analyses.

Reserpine lowered paw withdrawal thresholds, raised immobility in the swim test, and slowed escape in a water maze. CMPP reversed each of those behavioral changes. In brain tissue it restored glutathione, cut oxidative damage markers, partly rebuilt serotonin and norepinephrine, lowered glutamate, and curbed MAO-A activity. Blood inflammation markers TNF-alpha and IL-1beta also fell. The authors back CMPP as a multi-target option for pain-depression overlap.
pmc-13292543:
Mariana de Carvalho Leal, Adilane de Sousa Costa Reis, and Lilian Ferreira Muniz set out a 2026 hearing study. It aims to pin down the binaural interaction component (BIC) in adults whose hearing is normal. Two ears working together let the brain merge sounds, a skill that matters most in noise. The component is computed from auditory brainstem responses by subtracting the summed one-ear responses from the true two-ear response.

The authors frame their goal as establishing normative values for this objective measure in healthy adults. Prior evidence for the method rests mostly on brainstem potentials with particular stimuli, leaving everyday standards thin. Binaural skill itself matures with age and listening experience, which complicates any single cutoff. A solid reference range, they argue, would help clinicians judge binaural processing problems against something firmer than guesswork.
pmc-13293743:
Mohamed Yassine Boujnah and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, lung cancer spread found only in the inner ear canal of a 64-year-old man. Such spread is exceptionally rare, above all with no other brain lesions, and can mimic a benign ear tumor.

The man had stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with an aggressive signet-ring part and developed fast left facial weakness, vertigo, and hearing loss. Brain MRI showed a single enhancing lesion in the left canal, judged a metastasis. Steroids and radiotherapy brought marked gains in vertigo and hearing within three weeks, with partial face recovery. New ear and face signs in cancer patients warrant prompt checks.
pmc-13293843:
Tiffany C. Henderson leads a 2026 prospective study on whether dance classes lift mood for children and teens. Across four studios, 256 students aged 5 to 17 gave mood ratings before and after class over four months in early 2025, using a simple emoji scale. A standard affect survey gave a second check on feelings.

Post-class mood was higher than pre-class mood, and 85.8% of sessions held steady or improved. No class type, visit frequency, skill level, or teacher experience explained extra change. Differences between individual students mattered most. The findings support dance as a low-barrier activity linked to short-term mood gains.
pmc-13294243:
Eline Jasmijn Mertens and colleagues test whether mindset groups beat birthdays for gauging older adult health in a 2026 questionnaire study. Community-dwelling Dutch adults aged 67 and older, totaling 753 people, completed frailty, self-rated health ladder, and vitality scales. Sorting used the Subjective Health Experience model, which groups people by acceptance of their condition and felt control over it.

Frailty, self-rated health, and vitality all differed sharply across the four mindset groups. Frailty ran from 30% in the high acceptance, high control group to 74% in the lowest group in the reported shares. Low acceptance split groups most strongly. Age added little once mindset was known, challenging age-first care decisions.
pmc-13294843:
Rocío Lavigne-Cerván and colleagues test whether a children's intelligence scale shows a clear pattern in ADHD in a 2026 study. Working memory and processing speed are often weaker in the condition, but evidence from the fifth edition of the Wechsler scale for children was still thin. Two presentations of ADHD were compared with controls.

The sample held 188 young people aged 6 to 16, including 57 with combined presentation and 75 with mainly inattentive presentation. Children with ADHD scored lower on working memory, processing speed, and overall ability measures. Those scores also helped sort children into the right groups, supporting the scale as a helpful extra tool in assessment.
pmc-13295343:
Lingling Sun and colleagues link gut microbes and metabolism to anaemia in pregnant sows in a 2026 study. Anaemic sows breed less well, and their gut communities also shift, but the exact signatures were unknown. Blood, litter, gene, and faecal measures were compared between normal and anaemic animals.

Anaemic sows carried lower haemoglobin at three pregnancy stages and slightly smaller, lighter litters. Their blood antioxidant defences ran lower, and a placenta iron gene read higher in healthy sows. Faecal surveys and chemical profiling separated the groups cleanly. Two bacterial species stood out as tied to anaemia status and are offered as leads for feed or breeding work.
pmc-13295743:
Uğur Fidan and colleagues field-test a portable force platform in a 2026 study. Coaches increasingly measure jump and pull strength outside the lab, but pocket platforms must prove they match gold-standard gear. Thirty active male students performed two standard tests on stacked platforms for direct comparison.

Agreement with the laboratory platform ran very high for the mid-thigh pull and for jump take-off measures. Landing force, by contrast, agreed poorly between systems and carried a clear bias. Repeat sessions a day apart were steady across nearly all measures. The authors back the device for pull and take-off work while urging care with landing numbers.
pmc-13295843:
Ruiqi Gao and co-authors describe a 2026 materials study of a sticky patch meant to seal bowel joins without stitches. Leaks after intestinal surgery are dangerous, and ordinary glues often fail on wet tissue or cause unwanted sticking elsewhere.

Their patch has two unlike faces: a slippery, oil-filled top that resists sticking and a lower face that soaks up surface water and grips fast. Tests showed grip far stronger than a licensed sealant, stretch beyond ten times its length, and quick stopping of bleeding. In rats with colon defects the patch sealed the gut and cut later internal adhesions.
pmc-13295943:
In a 2026 review, Noor Hasmee and co-authors examine how intensive care units can run their supply chains better. Shortages, expired stock and hand-kept records still delay care, and the pandemic showed how fragile these systems can be.

Drawing on two decades of literature, the review groups fixes by theme: automatic tracking, computer forecasts of demand, standard buying rules and buffer stock for emergencies. Newer tools such as digital twins and blockchain get a mention for planning and openness. The authors urge hospitals to shift from reactive ordering toward data-led systems, with trained staff and wider supplier links.
pmc-13296043:
Mitra Britton and Peter A. Hosick examine, in 2026, whether activity at work and activity outside work relate differently to tinnitus, the perception of ringing without an outside sound. Using United States survey data from 2015 to 2018, they study 4,301 adults.

About one in six adults reported tinnitus. High levels of non-work activity linked to lower odds of the condition, while high work activity linked to higher odds, and both patterns strengthened step by step. Noise exposure and depressive symptoms also tracked with tinnitus. The authors stress the snapshot design cannot prove cause, but urge separating activity domains.
pmc-13296443:
Aylin Orhaner, Mehmet Cudi Tuncer and İlhan Özdemir combine, in 2026, thymoquinone from black seed with the chemotherapy drug docetaxel against ovarian cancer cells. They test single drugs and the pair in flat cell cultures and in ball-shaped tumour clusters that mimic real growth better.

Together the drugs killed more cells than either alone, pushed cells into programmed death and froze division at a late checkpoint. Stress chemistry inside cells rose sharply, and blunting it partly rescued the cells, implicating that stress in the effect. Immune signal levels also shifted. The authors back the pairing for further study.
pmc-13296943:
The forked fate of senescent cells in cancer is reviewed in 2026 by Xiuhong Chen and co-authors. Cells that permanently stop dividing block tumours early, yet their chemical chatter can later feed inflammation, reshape tissue and help cancers return.

The review covers what triggers the shutdown, how cells stay locked, and how some escape by loosening their identity and gaining stem-like traits. The secreted cocktail's double role gets close attention. Treatment thinking is shifting from simply inducing shutdown toward combined strategies, helped by single-cell tools and machine learning for personalised treatment plans in oncology practice.
pmc-13298443:
Thyroid patterns differ by psychiatric diagnosis, finds a 2026 inpatient study by Georgiana-Adriana Toma and co-authors. They measured thyroid hormones in 88 hospitalized patients, thirty with major depression, thirty with generalized anxiety, and twenty-eight with bipolar disorder, and related them to symptom rating scales.

Depression patients showed the highest TSH and the most hypothyroidism, with subclinical cases at 33.3%, and higher TSH tracked with worse depression and anxiety scores. In bipolar patients, the free hormones FT4 and FT3 ran higher and rose with mania scores. The authors support routine thyroid screening for depressed admissions and hormone-aware monitoring in bipolar care.
pmc-13300443:
Mulberry fruit color owes much to MYB transcription factors, and Xuefei Chen and colleagues catalogued the whole family in Morus atropurpurea for a 2026 study. Genome searches using hidden Markov models and BLAST turned up 145 MYB genes, sorted into 31 subfamilies. Expression was tracked across three stages of fruit development.

One candidate, the DIV-like repressor MaDIV, faded as fruit ripened while pigment built up. When tobacco plants overproduced MaDIV, their flowers held 42 percent less anthocyanin than normal plants. The pigment gene NtDFR was strongly suppressed, while the flavonol gene NtFLS1 rose. The results point to MaDIV as a brake on coloring, useful for breeding and pigment research.
pmc-13302243:
Protecting farm children from pesticides turns on what their parents value, Nuraeni and colleagues find in a 2026 study from Pattapang Village, South Sulawesi, Indonesia. Framed by Social Practice Theory, the survey modeled how competence, materials, norms, and personal traits shape pesticide habits around children. Structural equation modeling with bootstrapping tested the web of influences.

Safer pesticide use patterns lowered the reported toxicity risk to children. Competence proved the strongest driver of those patterns, ahead of materials and short-term goals. Personal values, not social pressure, built personal norms, while self-efficacy and long-term goals showed no real effect. Campaigns should speak to values and skills first, the authors argue.
pmc-13302343:
One in ten siblings of a celiac child has the disease too, most without knowing it, Ahmet Uzger and colleagues report in a 2026 screening study. They tested 250 brothers and sisters of eighty-one children with biopsy-proven celiac disease. Antibody screening followed the 2020 European pediatric guidelines, which allow diagnosis without biopsy when antibody levels run very high.

Twenty-six siblings, 10.4 percent of those tested, received a celiac diagnosis, a rate the authors put at about twenty-two times the national background. Twenty-one of the twenty-six had no symptoms at all. Twelve children qualified for the no-biopsy route. The authors urge screening every sibling of a celiac patient, symptoms or not, to catch the disease early.
pmc-13302543:
Broken femoral heads heal badly more often than not, Christian Prangenberg and colleagues document in a 2026 long-term follow-up from a Level I trauma center. Fifteen men treated for Pipkin femoral head fractures between 2012 and 2021, average age forty-one, were re-examined after a mean of nearly forty-four months. Function was scored with the Harris Hip Score.

Twelve of the fifteen patients suffered complications, an eighty percent rate, led by nerve injuries and posttraumatic arthritis. Average hip function landed in the moderate range, and six patients no longer had their native hip joint at all. The authors stress rapid, stable reduction to limit the damage these rare injuries cause.
pmc-13303743:
Naparat Sukkriang, Suttida Sangpoom, and Sumet Khumphairan examine links between blood sugar and blood fats in type 2 diabetes in a 2026 study from southern Thailand. Fat patterns that raise heart risk often travel with poor sugar control.

A cross-sectional sample of 360 adults with diabetes supplied fasting glucose, long-term sugar marker HbA1c, and lipid measures plus combined ratios. HbA1c tracked harmful lipid patterns more steadily than a single fasting glucose reading. A combined index called TyG best separated patients with poor control from others. Joint checks of sugar and lipid ratios may flag heart risk sooner in clinic care.
pmc-13304443:
Guo-Feng Ren and colleagues refine how grain size spreads predict packing density in widely graded soils and rock fill in a 2026 study. Not every grain size helps a mix pack tightly, so whole-range measures can mislead.

Past data for twenty curved size spreads were rechecked, and twenty-one lab mixes with trimmed ranges were tested for peak dry density. A per-unit contribution score showed each size band's real effect, forming a single-peaked curve whose turning size shifted with mix coarseness. Trimmed measures predicted peak density far better than whole-range ones for both material sources tested.
pmc-13305543:
Zhanar Assirbayeva and colleagues turn petroleum coke into a carbon sensor material for catching a farm pesticide in a 2026 study. Cheap, sensitive field sensors for spraying residues remain in demand.

Coke was baked under nitrogen into porous carbon, then coated with copper oxide nanoparticles spread evenly across the surface. The coating widened the active area and sped electron flow. A glassy carbon electrode bearing the mix detected dichlorvos across a wide low range, with resistance rising as dose climbed. Detection reached very low levels, marking the composite as a low-cost sensing candidate.
pmc-13306143:
Yufeng Hu modelled an electrically tuned light and matter device in a 2026 simulation study. Layers combined a coated gold-silver rod, organic dye aggregates and a single sheet of tungsten disulfide to host three linked energy modes.

Near matched tuning, upper and lower branches split by about 239 meV in the computed spectra. Small gate voltages from 2.0 V to 3.8 V shifted middle and lower branches by roughly 46 meV while the top branch barely moved. A coupled oscillator account explained the selective control, pointing toward compact switches, sensors and programmable light circuits.
pmc-13308043:
Nannan Shen and co-authors probe in 2026 the role of the tetR gene in tetracycline resistance in Aeromonas hydrophila, a germ that hits farmed fish hard. They built a strain with tetR turned down by an antisense method and compared drug response, drug build up, and gene activity with the parent strain.

Turning tetR down made the germ far more resistant to tetracycline drugs in their lab tests. The altered strain also pumped drug out more and held less doxycycline inside its cells over time. Gene reads showed shifts in energy use and in parts of the ribosome, the cell protein factory. TetR may thus act as a brake on resistance in this germ.
pmc-13309743: Computational Intelligence and Neuroscience is the journal named on a 2026 retraction notice for a 2022 article by S. Krishnamoorthy and co-authors on segmenting multiple sclerosis lesions in MRI slices with a VGG-UNet model. The publisher, John Wiley & Sons Ltd, withdrew the article after an inquiry found signs of systematic manipulation of the publication process, such as scope mismatch, incoherent content, and compromised peer review. The notice lists the grounds in full and adds no new research data; it serves only to remove the article from the scholarly record.
pmc-13309943:
Yuxiu Dai writes a 2026 letter on blood-marker guidance for calming the immune storm in septic shock. A recent study found that one marker, sTREM-1, predicted 90-day death and major kidney events about as well as complex computer models. Simple markers appeal for bedside risk sorting, yet disputes follow them into practice.

The letter notes that cutoff values for the marker clash across studies. Older sepsis work used about 400 pg/mL, while the new study puts the death threshold near 1360 pg/mL in its reported figures. Standard test methods, treatment follow-through, and repeat tracking over time all need settling. The author urges harmonized cutoffs before wards rely on the marker.
pmc-13310643:
Akari Hirakawa and co-authors describe function-sparing surgery for a giant genital wart tumor in a 2026 case report. Buschke-Löwenstein tumor is a rare HPV-driven growth that spreads relentlessly, returns in 60 to 70 percent of cases, and can turn cancerous, per figures cited in the report. Its size and site make treatment delicate.

A 69-year-old woman with lymphoma and diabetes histories carried a growth covering the whole vulva and perianal area after creams, freezing, and laser care failed. The mass reached 15 by 9.5 by 2.5 cm in the surgical record. Imaging cleared the urinary and rectal passages, and pre-treatment creams guarded those borders. Surgeons cut wide at the edges and close at sensitive passages to preserve function.
pmc-13311143:
Dylan Siriwardena and colleagues apply a droplet chip to gather fetal cells from neck swabs in a 2026 study. Gold standard prenatal gene tests use invasive sampling with a small loss risk and late results. Cervical mucus holds rare whole fetal cells, but finding them among mother cells is hard.

A digital fluid chip isolates single cells for gene study. Standard marker picks gathered mostly mother cells, so placental gene data were used to define a fresh fetal marker set of 147 genes in shared form. New picks held clear fetal and maternal DNA together. The path may seed safer early diagnosis.
pmc-13311643:
Seema Sahay and co-authors, in 2026, report a demonstration project on HIV prevention pills in India for transgender women and for men who have sex with men. Two delivery settings were compared over twelve months of follow-up.

The project enrolled 650 participants at a community site in Jalandhar and a clinic site in Pune between December 2019 and July 2023. One-year retention reached 63.2 percent overall, far higher at the community site. About 64.8 percent kept to at least 80 percent of doses in this project. Community delivery, more schooling, and living with family each tied to better adherence, guiding wider rollout.
pmc-13312243:
Mariana M Lanata and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, provider report cards built from Medicaid claims as a tool to guide antibiotic use in children's clinics. Most antibiotic prescriptions for children are written in clinics, and up to half may be needless. Yet classic audit programs cannot reach scattered rural practices like those across West Virginia.

Using near real-time claims data, the team sent clinicians report cards every three months that set their prescribing against guidelines. Feedback improved how well prescribing matched guidelines and how well diagnoses were coded, and use of cefdinir, a broad drug often overused in children, fell. The authors present claims-based feedback as a lasting method that a state program could run at scale without visiting each practice in person.
pmc-13312543:
Yao Liu and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, the antioxidant enzyme PRDX4 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, one of the deadliest common cancers. Tumors of this type grow in a harsh, oxygen-poor environment thick with oxidative stress, and the authors asked whether this redox-defense protein helps them thrive and resist treatment.

Patient data linked high PRDX4 levels to aggressive disease features and shorter disease-specific survival. In cell experiments, extra PRDX4 sped growth and migration, strengthened the cells' ability to adapt to oxidative load, and kept reactive oxygen species down, alongside altered signaling through MAPK and PI3K/AKT routes. In animals, tumors with more PRDX4 grew faster, built more blood vessels, and answered gemcitabine chemotherapy more weakly. The authors propose PRDX4 as both a prognostic marker and a redox-linked drug target.
pmc-13312843:
ThanhThanh Vo and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether resilience carries the protective effect of positive childhood experiences into lower distress for health professions students. Good early experiences are thought to buffer later mental health, and these students, drawn from medicine, nursing, physician assistant, and veterinary programs, face heavy training stress.

Wave three of a longitudinal survey supplied 181 respondents who completed measures of childhood experiences, resilience, and well-being. As expected, more positive childhood experiences went with greater resilience, and it went with less distress, and childhood experiences also related to distress directly. That indirect step, however, was not significant. The authors conclude the two factors seem to protect on their own. They urge schools to spot students with thin positive histories and support well-being head-on rather than counting on resilience alone.
pmc-13313243:
Houcong Jin and colleagues describe a lab-made growth hormone mimic in a 2026 paper that aims to stretch dosing well past once a week. Weekly long-acting growth hormone treats hormone shortage in children and adults with more ease than daily shots. But protein drugs fade fast in the body, so no product yet lasts longer than a week.

The team built pH.VHH03, a small antibody-based molecule that switches on the growth hormone receptor and answers to pH. By reshaping its hinge and variable parts, they raised its cell-growth power in lab tests. The tuned molecule then showed effects like long-acting growth hormone in animal tests described by the authors. If later trials hold up, such a drug could mean fewer shots and steadier use by patients who now inject each week.
pmc-13314743:
Stephen Sandelich leads a large panel that reviews drug use screening for teens in emergency care, in work published in 2026. The emergency department is a key contact point, and for many teens it is their main or only source of care, so a missed screen there costs dearly.

Overall teen drug use has leveled or fallen, yet deaths tied to lab-made fentanyl have climbed sharply, the authors note. Health bodies urge screening of every teen with proven tools such as the CRAFFT questionnaire, named in the report. In real departments, though, screening stays spotty due to time pressure, privacy worries, and thin staff training. The review gathers what works so emergency teams can spot use early and step in while help can still change the path.
pmc-13315343:
Yongliang Zhang and colleagues tested a mix of helpful microbes in 2026 on gut and liver harm in young chickens given a bacterial toxin. Twenty-four Lohmann Pink chickens were split into a control group, a toxin-only group, and a group fed the microbe mix plus toxin injections on set days.

Toxin challenge slowed growth, raised body temperature and spleen size, and damaged the lining of the small intestine. Blood markers of gut leakage and liver strain rose, and genes that seal the gut wall fell. Oxidative stress markers also rose. The study design lets the team judge whether the microbe mix, built from two Bacillus species and a yeast, softens that harm.
pmc-13315643:
Lily Foley and co-authors describe in 2026 a core-shell capsule meant to plant chosen gut microbes in place. Live microbe treatments are held back because scientists know little about what single species do inside the gut, and resident microbes resist newcomers, leaving few tools for controlled change.

Their biocapsule works by a kill-and-replace plan. First it briefly clears local native flora at a chosen gut niche, then releases a defined set of helpful microbes to settle the emptied spot. That targeted approach differs from broad antibiotics or mixed stool transfers, which give little fine control over which microbes end up where.
pmc-13316643:
Zhenru He leads a large team reporting 2026 mouse work on how exercise protects bone after the ovaries are removed, a model of postmenopausal thinning. Bone-eating cells drive the loss, and the team traced a surprising shield: lactate, the burn chemical of hard work, tagging gene-reading proteins.

During bone cell growth, lactate levels fell even as bone loss rose. Raising lactate by exercise or by dosing lifted a tag called H3K18 lactylation, which quieted key bone-eating genes and eased bone loss. Two enzymes write and erase the tag, forming a control loop. The findings link workout chemistry to gene control and hint at new drug angles for thinning bones.
pmc-13318043:
Bartlomiej Arendarczyk and colleagues estimate, in a 2026 study, the foreign farmland behind Britain's food and feed imports, now and through 2100. Imports supply nearly half of UK food, yet the land bill abroad had never been projected under future social and climate paths.

A food system model replayed demand, farming, and trade from 2010 to 2020, then ran four scenarios forward. About 11 million hectares abroad currently serve UK plates, against 17 million hectares farmed at home. By 2050 the foreign footprint lands near 10 to 12 million hectares in every scenario, widening to 10 to 16 million by 2100. Judging British diets' true footprint, they argue, must count this hidden acreage.
pmc-13318243:
Christina Tsigalou wrote a 2026 editorial opening a research collection on how gut microbes shape aging, asking whether decline is fixed or partly steered by the trillions living in the intestine. The gathered studies span infection risk, diet, and barrier health in older adults.

One study found gut-type bacteria in the throats of care home residents marking higher infection risk, hinting at system-wide microbial drift. Another tied fiber-rich diets to a tighter gut barrier and fatty diets to a leakier one, measured by a binding protein. The editorial frames the microbiome as both a gauge of healthy aging and a lever, through food and lifestyle, that prevention programs can actually pull.
pmc-13318543:
Mengwei Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 global analysis of liver disease. It covers the years 1990 to 2021. The work builds on Global Burden of Disease 2021 data. Checks used World Health Organization and cancer observatory sources. The framework links all liver disease to hepatitis, cirrhosis, and liver cancer.

In 2021 the total reached 309.72 million new cases worldwide by their accounting. Deaths numbered 1.98 million, and healthy years lost reached 63.53 million across the globe. Age-adjusted rates fell overall. Yet death and disability rates rose in high-income North America and Australasia. Fatty and alcohol-related disease took a growing share. Projections see overall deaths easing while one liver cancer type keeps climbing.
pmc-13318643:
Xiaobo Chen and co-authors review, in 2026, early laboratory work on engineered nanozymes, tiny enzyme-like particles, for periodontitis, a chronic gum disease that destroys tissue and loosens teeth. Standard cleaning and antibiotics often fail against stubborn biofilms and ongoing inflammation.

The review sorts nanozyme types and explains how tailored designs kill bacteria, mop up harmful oxygen species, calm immune responses, and encourage bone and tissue regrowth. Moving versions that push themselves through tissue look especially promising for hard-to-reach pockets. The main barrier to clinic use is long-term safety, above all metal ions building up in the body, so the authors call for better designs and standard safety testing before human trials.
pmc-13318743:
Qiong Gao and colleagues present a 2026 longitudinal qualitative study of women with gestational diabetes in China. They follow how blood sugar management feels and what women need over time. A patient journey map organises the story. Interviews happened at a tertiary hospital in Xinxiang.

Eighteen women were interviewed at three points. Talks came at diagnosis, three months later in pregnancy, and six months after diagnosis. Nineteen themes emerged across the phases. Early on, women felt distress, lacked knowledge, and struggled to adapt daily life. Later, self-management became habit but vigilance and fatigue persisted, and support faded. After birth, burnout and role conflicts threatened long-term control. The authors recommend tiered, nurse-led care with family and online support.
pmc-13319043:
Chiara de Waure leads a large team presenting, in 2026, a European project to build one framework for assessing digital health technologies. Assessment rules across Europe are fragmented and often built for medicines, not apps or wearables. The EU-funded EDiHTA project began in January 2024. It aims to co-create a flexible framework with key stakeholders.

The article lays out the concept design behind the framework. It should cover different technology types and every stage of a product's life. Use across all EU member states is a core goal. The authors review current challenges in judging digital tools, from evidence gaps to stakeholder involvement. They argue a shared approach would help health systems capture the real added value of digital care.
pmc-13319843:
Bertalan Alapfy and co-authors tune water flow at a small hydro plant intake in a 2026 study of the At-Bashy site in Kyrgyzstan. Shaft type plants tucked into old weirs offer compact low head power, but tight shapes and shifting flow can hurt both output and fish safety. A three dimensional flow model was used to test intake shapes before any build work.

Nine intake layouts varied rack length and water depth above the rack while flow to the turbine stayed fixed. Deeper water above the rack cut sharp downward jets near the rack and smoothed the flow field. Longer racks mainly eased the average downward bend. A mid length rack with mid to deep cover gave the best balance of fish safety and cost.
pmc-13320243:
Youngju Song and co-authors test a hormone marker for early ovary failure after pelvic beam care in a 2026 records study. Beam care to the pelvis often shuts down the ovaries early in younger women. The marker falls as egg stores fade, so its path was weighed against a second hormone rule for naming failure.

Records covered 23 women age 45 or younger who had pelvic beam care. Failure showed in nine women by the marker rule and eight by the second rule, with most women classed the same way by both. Marker levels plunged after care and in some women rose again months later, ahead of the second marker settling. Higher least dose to the ovary and added inner beam care tracked with failure.
pmc-13320443:
Anne Shirley Hoselton and co-authors present a case report from 2026 on cancer spread to a keyhole port site after robot bladder removal. Spread to a port wound is a rare snag of keyhole and robot cancer surgery. A newer single port robot uses just one cut, which in theory should lower that risk further. No such case after single port bladder removal had been reported before.

A 74 year old woman with high grade bladder cancer had her bladder removed by the single port robot path. Later a fresh lump grew at her port cut that proved to be spread of the same cancer. The case shows the risk is low but not zero, and urges care in how tumor tissue is bagged and drawn out.
pmc-13320543:
Christophe Gautrelet and colleagues share a 2026 vibration test data set for engineers who shake parts in three directions at once. A triaxial shaker rig held a magnesium cube fitted with many motion sensors. Such tests help judge whether parts will survive real shaking in use.

Eleven sweep and random tests ran across 5 to 2000 Hz under four closed loop control plans. The release holds raw readings, response curves, power spectra, and coherence tables from the control system. Fixture echoes and sensor place strongly shaped results, above all past 1500 Hz. Other teams can use the data to compare control plans, study spread across space, and check computer models of shaking.
pmc-13321043:
Izza Shahid, Bashir Hanif, and Khurram Nasir argue for fuller heart artery checks in South Asian adults in a 2026 article. South Asians carry a high burden of early artery disease, shaped by early metabolic illness and body fat patterns that standard risk scores miss. Guidelines already treat South Asian ancestry as a risk raising factor when judging cholesterol treatment.

Calcium scoring of heart arteries is cheap and steady, and a score of zero signals low short term risk. Yet calcium scans cannot see soft, non-calcified plaque or flag high risk plaque traits that may matter most in younger patients. The authors press for plaque based imaging plus markers such as Lp(a) and apoB to sharpen personal prevention.
pmc-13322843:
Bo Huang and a large team review how the muscle signal protein Metrnl shapes immune cells in skeletal muscle, in a 2026 article. Macrophages in muscle can shift form and thereby affect repair, metabolism and the local immune setting.

Metrnl, a protein released by muscle, acts through a linked set of signals to steer that shift, with effects on sugar control and age-related muscle loss seen in human and rodent studies. Its action runs both ways and depends heavily on tissue and disease, so results in one setting may not transfer to another. Open questions include where its receptor sits and how it affects each macrophage type, with gene-wide and imaging tools proposed for next steps.
pmc-13322943:
Cuiping Hao and co-authors relate a simple blood ratio to short-term death in sepsis, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study from a large hospital in China. Their set held 1,103 critically ill patients with sepsis, and the death rate within 28 days reached 29.9 percent in that group.

The ratio joins creatinine with cystatin C and is thought to reflect muscle mass. Patients with higher ratios died less often within 28 days, with the top quarter showing far lower risk than the bottom quarter after adjustment. Survival curves and flexible modelling pointed the same way, and extra checks held up. The authors suggest this cheap ratio could aid early risk judgement in sepsis care.
pmc-13324843:
Zheng Sun and co-authors follow child weight paths after cesarean birth in the VDAART birth cohort in a 2026 study. Whether cesarean delivery feeds childhood obesity stays contested, and gut microbes may carry part of any effect.

Body mass index percentiles covered 683 children aged 2 to 8 years, with 1,672 stool samples from 3 months to age 5. Only cesareans done during labor, not planned ones, linked to a higher weight path, a gap of 31.8 percent in percentile terms. The pattern appeared in girls alone. Early gut profiles predicted later overweight best in girls born by in-labor cesarean, and 24 microbe types may mediate the risk. Timing and sex seem to matter.
pmc-13325343:
Alcino Trindade Rosa-Machado, Bruna Coelho Lopes, and César Mota Filho review evidence on the resistant fungus Candidozyma auris in wastewater in a 2026 article. The germ, once called Candida auris, resists many drugs and is hard to identify in the lab.

Findings of the fungus in sewage raise questions about spread through treated water and sludge spread on land. The review weighs how studies collect, grow, and name the fungus, and finds reporting too uneven for firm risk calls. No rules target pathogenic fungi in treatment plant byproducts today. The authors propose a shared workflow for sampling and reporting under a One Health frame that links clinics, farms, and the environment.
pmc-13326043:
Patricia Maass and colleagues pair venetoclax with drugs that lower methylation against B-cell leukemia in a 2026 study. The duo already works in myeloid leukemia. Its value in acute lymphoblastic leukemia was untested.

Four cell lines got venetoclax, azacytidine, or decitabine alone and in pairs. The pairs cut cell activity far more than single drugs. Single-cell scans of a treated patient-derived model showed venetoclax jamming both energy routes. Cells lost both oxygen-based burning and glycolysis. Adding a partner drug deepened the energy crash. Decitabine helped most, with lower breathing and ATP output. No joint effect showed on methylation itself. The synergy runs through cell energy.
pmc-13326743:
Anna Richert and co-authors set out tuned lab protocols for electron microscopy of cultured cells in a 2026 methods paper. Pinpointing proteins inside cells at nanometer scale guides work on gene activity, signaling, and cell traffic.

Their post-embedding immunogold routine labels one or more proteins in cells grown on plastic coverslips, whether the cells stick or float. Resin embedding is arranged so thin slices cut cleanly and collect well. The routine balances keeping cell structure crisp against keeping target sites readable by antibodies. A companion procedure covers plain ultrastructure study when labeling fails. Protein traits and cell compartment still sway the best settings.
pmc-13326943:
Xuanjun Gong and colleagues study how curiosity steers the books people pick in a 2026 paper. Choosing what to read pits safe favorites against fresh finds, much like animals balancing feeding spots.

A large real-world reading dataset plus a controlled experiment traced step-by-step choices. Readers leaned on past taste spread across a meaning map of books, yet also probed uncertain titles on purpose. More curious people explored more and enjoyed the exploring itself. The twin habits of reward generalization and directed exploration, known from physical foraging, carried over to knowledge hunting. Curiosity thus tunes the explore-exploit balance in daily media life.
pmc-13327543:
Misato Shimoyama, Kumiko Nakada-Tsukui, and Tomoyoshi Nozaki pin down a movement switch in the amoeba that causes dysentery in a 2026 study. Entamoeba histolytica carries many small GTPase switches and many activators for them, most still unstudied. One switch, EhRacM, curbs fluid gulping yet promotes directed movement, and its activator was unknown.

Binding tests and lab assays showed a protein named EhGEFM switches EhRacM on directly. Silencing the activator left fluid gulping untouched but weakened directed movement, partly copying loss of the switch itself. Imaging placed both proteins at the cell edge, while only the switch moved onto maturing gulp vesicles. Movement and feeding thus run through separate control paths in this parasite.
pmc-13328043:
Polly Lama and co-authors link disc matrix fragments to inflammation in painful back disease in a 2026 study. Worn spinal discs drive much long-lasting low back pain, and broken pieces of their matrix may act as danger signals. Disc tissue came from 20 healthy cadaver donors and 35 patients with painful degeneration.

Fragments of aggrecan and small leucine-rich proteoglycans, sized 22 to 45 kDa in their blots, clustered in the most worn discs, and the alarm receptor TLR-2 ran higher in patient disc cells. Patient discs leaned inflammatory, with IL-6 up 1.37 times in the reported profile, while healthy discs favored growth factors. Blocking TLR-2 calmed the response in cell tests.
pmc-13330543:
Stefan Andrei and colleagues study skin blood flow signs after heart surgery in a 2026 article. Capillary refill time, checked by pressing the skin, is now advised as a resuscitation target in shock care. Big-picture measures such as arterial pressure can look restored while tiny vessels still underperform, so a bedside sign tied to tissue flow matters.

The work links refill time changes to the vascular waterfall idea, a frame for the pressure gradients that drive capillary flow. Candidate drivers include vessel muscle tone, nerve-driven tightening, vessel recruitment, lining function, and local heat control. Sorting which drivers matter most could sharpen fluid and drug choices after cardiac surgery. The study sits in intensive care practice.
pmc-13331143:
Sandeepa Arora and colleagues compare health and social care outcomes by household size for children in Northwest London in a 2026 study. Linked records from 2005 to 2024 covered 477,602 children aged up to 18 years. Small homes held one or two children, while larger homes held three or more.

Raw rates showed larger-home children had more tooth removals, breathing admissions, and child-in-need status, but fewer emergency visits and antidepressant scripts. Adjusted models kept higher odds for tooth removal and child-in-need status per added child, with lower odds for scripts and visits. Household size marks clear inequality patterns that policy should weigh, the authors conclude.
pmc-13331443:
Sai Sanikommu and a large team review suction pump systems for stroke clot removal in a 2026 article. Mechanical removal now stands beside clot drugs for large vessel stroke, with stent retrievers and suction as its two main forms. The first suction case in 2002 used a hand syringe to pull a clot.

Since then pumps have grown far stronger and more refined, led by Penumbra systems and newer rivals named in the review. The authors detail each system's build, trial proof, and device contrasts, plus access tricks for hard vessel paths and large clots. Some patients still fare poorly despite full reopening, which keeps recovery research open.
pmc-13332443:
Conor J R Scott and co-authors introduce metaLoc, a 2026 software workflow that predicts where proteins end up inside or outside the cell. Knowing a protein's destination helps researchers filter the huge datasets that modern sequencing produces, but the best prediction tools are scattered, each with its own setup and output format.

MetaLoc bundles existing tools for signal peptides, localization, and membrane helices into one Nextflow pipeline that runs with a single command and accepts either protein or DNA sequences. Each tool sits in its own Conda environment, keeping results reproducible, which suits screening of proteomic and metagenomic data. The workflow is free on GitHub, and an archived release sits permanently at Zenodo. The authors aim it at researchers with limited bioinformatics experience who need quick, combined answers.
pmc-13333743:
Yiju Tang, Junjie Wei, and Haoyang Ren authored a 2026 mini review on acceptable risk as a psychological judgment. People rarely accept a risk from probability figures alone, so the authors gather research on perception, trust, and fairness to explain how such judgments form.

Their framework separates three situations: risks people take on themselves, risks controlled by others, and risks governed collectively or imposed by mandate. Each arrangement changes how much weight falls on felt threat, on the credibility of those in charge, and on whether exposure seems legitimate. That lens explains why nearly identical hazards can be tolerated in one setting and fought in another. The review closes with directions for research on risk communication and public legitimacy.
pmc-13334143:
Joon Hyuk Lee and Tae Gon Kim reported reconstructing an irradiated, necrotic scalp with two free flaps in a 2026 case report. The patient, a 62-year-old woman, had multifocal scalp angiosarcoma, a rare and aggressive cancer.

After wide excision and skin grafting, she received adjuvant radiotherapy. Seven months later, radiation necrosis with exposed bone appeared in frontal and occipital areas, while biopsies showed no cancer return. Eleven months after radiotherapy, the team rebuilt the defects using a radial forearm flap and an adipofascial thigh flap joined in a piggyback arrangement on one vessel pair. Early venous congestion was rescued with a vein graft, and both flaps survived fully. More than 2.5 years after radiotherapy she remained disease-free with stable coverage.
pmc-13334443:
Chiyu Zhou and co-authors traced how school climate reaches teacher innovation in a 2026 survey analysis from China. Climate and innovation correlate, but the steps between them were unclear in Chinese schools.

Data came from TALIS 2018 responses of 3,976 Shanghai secondary school teachers, analyzed with a path model. School climate showed a strong positive effect on teacher innovation. The path ran through two middle steps: a positive climate raised teacher autonomy, autonomy strengthened self-efficacy, and self-efficacy fueled inventive behavior. Framed by empowerment theory, the chain suggests leaders who want inventive teaching should hand teachers real freedom, since confidence and creativity follow from it.
pmc-13336443:
Young Hyun Son and co-authors built a stretchable OLED platform designed to survive on the body for light therapy in a 2026 device study. Wearable light treatment needs displays that are soft, bright, and sealed against the environment, a trio that usually trades off against itself.

Their multilayer design stacks emissive pixel islands and deformable wiring on separate planes, decoupling light output from stretching. Analysis and testing showed strain redirected into soft elastomer layers, yielding about 54 percent system stretchability while electroluminescence stayed stable under repeated loading and 50 percent uniaxial strain in their trials. A hybrid seal, atomic-layer nanolaminate reflector films plus parylene-C, guards against moisture for outdoor and long-term use. The architecture aims at durable phototherapy patches rather than laboratory demos.
pmc-13336943:
Zhiang Bai, Wai Lean Koay, Xin Yi Oh, and Vinh Xuan Truong make a color-changing gel from natural solvents in a 2026 study. Their eutectogel mixes a soft polymer with a deep eutectic solvent of betaine and lactic acid, crosslinked by viologen units. The gel is clear, stretchy, heat-stable, and sticky on many surfaces.

Its hydrogen-bond web resists freezing, keeping optics steady at −20°C in cold tests. Electricity, ultraviolet light, and heat each trigger reversible color shifts, enabling rewritable photo patterns and layered encryption. Stretched, the gel senses motions from big joint bends down to heartbeat signals. Its electric output can even tap out Morse code, merging security tags with body sensing in one soft material.
pmc-13337443:
Huachen Wang and co-authors read sugar tags on antibodies to tell sepsis types apart in a 2026 nested case-control study. Sepsis kills many patients, and choosing antibiotics fast depends on whether Gram-negative or Gram-positive bacteria are to blame. The study enrolled 180 septic patients, 100 Gram-negative and 80 Gram-positive, plus 100 healthy controls.

Antibody glycan patterns differed sharply between the two infection types, with many peaks rising or falling in Gram-negative cases. A model mixing glycan peaks with routine clinical markers separated the groups with an AUC of 0.931 in training and 0.917 in validation cohorts in the study evaluation. The tags also carried prognostic signal for 90-day survival, offering a possible blood test for quicker, better-aimed treatment.
pmc-13337643:
Yi Chen and colleagues feed water fleas Bt maize to test crop safety in a 2026 chronic study. Engineered maize expressing three insect-killing Cry proteins is debated, partly because effects blamed on the trait may really come from the plant's genetic background. Daphnia magna, a standard aquatic test animal, ate four maize materials for 21 days.

Protein levels varied widely across pollen, leaves, flour, and straw leachate and between maize lines. Yet survival, reproduction, and growth tracked plant background far more than the presence of Bt proteins. Nearly every response under Bt maize fell inside the natural range set by eight conventional varieties. The authors argue that natural variation baselines should anchor future environmental risk assessment of engineered crops.
pmc-13337843:
Anna C. Ciao and co-authors test a body image program built with middle schoolers in a 2026 study. The Body Justice program has eight short lessons mixing media literacy and challenges to appearance ideals. Students and staff in the Pacific Northwest helped create the content.

Seventh graders received the program over three years, with 333 students in total. Near-peer college leaders and student co-leaders delivered the lessons. Satisfaction was moderate overall and higher among students of color and gender-diverse students in the reported ratings. Unhealthy weight control acts fell by two-month follow-up for most groups, though gains were smaller for students of color.
pmc-13337943:
Jea Chul Ha and colleagues link low mood to several signs of brain aging in older adults in a 2026 cohort study. Late-life depressive symptoms often travel with brain changes and weaker thinking, but markers are usually studied one at a time. Here they are examined together.

Baseline data from 2,746 community-dwelling older adults with brain scans and thinking tests were analyzed. Depression scores came from a standard epidemiologic scale. Higher symptom burden tracked with more white matter damage, smaller hippocampus volume, and poorer overall cognition in the reported models. Links held after accounting for heart and lifestyle factors, supporting joint screening of mood and brain health.
pmc-13339143:
Fuping Pan and colleagues show how support curvature flips oxygen reaction paths in a 2026 catalysis study. Iron phthalocyanine usually drives full oxygen reduction, rarely the two-electron route to peroxide. Placing the molecule on curved carbon pores changed that choice.

Molecules in concave pores favored peroxide with selectivity above 80 percent in the reported tests. Molecules on convex supports favored the full four-electron route instead. Infrared readings during operation and theory traced the split to shifted orbital overlap at the iron site. Curvature thus acts as a dial for steering electrochemistry without changing the catalyst itself.
pmc-13341443:
Combined body and mind fatigue changes how football players land, in a 2026 study by Zilong Wang and colleagues. Twelve male collegiate American football players completed baseline, physical fatigue, and mixed fatigue sessions in randomized order, with the mixed state induced by cycling plus a Stroop task.

Motion capture and force plates recorded a landing task. Mixed fatigue specifically cut ankle dorsiflexion and raised inversion at peak landing force, and peak inversion stayed higher through the landing. Hip and knee patterns, coordination measures, and impact loads did not change significantly. A rolled-in ankle posture under combined fatigue could raise sprain risk, the authors suggest.
pmc-13342643:
Mohamed Shaker S Adam and co-authors present a 2026 green chemistry study making a new family of fused ring compounds in a single pot. Three starting materials react together to form pyrazolo-tetrazolo-pyrimidine products, and the team confirmed each structure with infrared, NMR, and mass tools before testing biological effects.

One product, labeled 4c, killed breast and colon cancer cells at low doses, close to the reference drug vinblastine, and several products fought bacteria and fungi well. A hydroxyl-bearing product, 4f, quenched free radicals most strongly in antioxidant tests. Computer docking work then probed how the leading compounds might bind their targets, guiding future drug design.
pmc-13343343:
Lenka Slavickova and co-authors study the TET gene family in multiple myeloma in 2026, asking how DNA methylation marks on the genes' own promoters shape their activity. Myeloma grows from clonal plasma cells in bone marrow, and chemical marks that silence or free genes are gaining attention as drivers of the disease.

Working with sorted cells taken from patients at diagnosis and at relapse, plus five myeloma cell lines, the team measured methylation with several sequencing and digestion methods. New patients showed high TET1 activity with low promoter methylation, while TET3 sat more heavily methylated. Demethylating drugs selectively raised TET2 in one cell line, and the protein Sp3 latched onto it more. TET1 may drive tumors, while restoring TET2 could suppress them.
pmc-13345743:
Aurelia-Alexandra Colceriu and co-authors review artificial intelligence in facial cosmetic surgery in 2026. Millions of aesthetic operations a year push surgeons toward smarter planning and judgment tools. The team searched two databases under PRISMA 2020 rules for studies using AI anywhere along the care path.

Of 1,832 records, 29 studies qualified, mostly from Asia and the United States and mostly testing or building tools rather than running interventions. Convolutional neural networks dominated, usually commercial ones, with strongest use in facelifts, nose surgery, and eyelid work for planning and outcome grading. The authors call for standard reporting, refreshed regulation, and training that lets surgeons co-design the models they will use.
pmc-13345843:
Yuhan Lu and Jianrong Ye review matrine, the chief active compound of the herb Sophora flavescens, as a regulator of ferroptosis in 2026. Ferroptosis kills cells through iron build-up and fat peroxidation, and matrine seems to steer that process across heart and vessel disease, brain disorders, pancreatitis-driven lung injury, and cervical cancer.

Gathering scattered preclinical work, the review weighs how one natural molecule protects organs in some settings and attacks tumors in others through the same death pathway. The catch is dose-linked tissue toxicity. The authors call for derivative tuning, targeted delivery, and dose markers, plus rigorous multi-center trials, before matrine can move from bench promise toward precision clinical use.
pmc-13346043:
C. Helan Princey and A. David Maxim Gururaj model magnetic nanoparticles riding the spinal fluid in 2026. Delivering drugs through cerebrospinal fluid could target brain and cord disorders precisely. Iron-gold core-shell particles can be steered and heated by outside magnets. Their flow physics inside porous channels stayed underworked.

Using a Brinkman-Darcy flow frame with Kelvin magnetic forces and heat terms, the authors solved the system in dimensionless form by perturbation methods. Stronger permeability, flow speed, and magnetic pull sped the fluid, while more particles thickened it and slowed travel. Magnetic heating raised temperatures notably, and better conduction spread that heat away. The model offers design rules for magnet-guided brain drug delivery.
pmc-13348043:
Mst. Shamima Akter and a large team sequence the full genome of a fowlpox vaccine virus from Bangladesh, in an announcement from 2026. The live weakened strain, called Buddett, was made by the Livestock Research Institute yet had never been sequenced, even as fowlpox still cuts growth, egg output. Bird survival on farms despite vaccine use.

Virus grown in ten-day chick eggs gave DNA for shotgun sequencing with a modified library method, and the complete read now sits ready for open comparison. Matching the vaccine genome against field strains should show where protection may slip and guide better seed choices for national poultry programs.
pmc-13348843:
Animesh Acharjee and Daniela Santos argue for self-running artificial intelligence in bowel disease care, in a review published in 2026. Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis shift over time, yet clinic, blood, scan. Molecular data arrive in fragments at spaced visits, pushing doctors toward reacting late rather than acting early when change first stirs.

Agentic systems that keep merging fresh streams into a living disease picture could close that loop, linking watch, reading, and action for timely tweaks in the model proposed. Data quality, clear reasoning, and smooth fit into clinic routines are named as gates that must be passed before such agents can safely steer long-term bowel care.
pmc-13350043:
Hao Ji and colleagues examined digital government services and mental health in China in a 2026 analysis linking province-level data to a national social survey. Online public services have become a core part of governance, yet their effects on residents' wellbeing were little studied.

Provincial digital development scores from 2020 and 2022 were matched to survey answers a year later for thousands of residents. Higher digital development consistently tracked with better mental health, possibly through fewer activity limits from health problems and greater life happiness. The link held more steadily for rural residents. Extra statistical checks were used to guard against reversed cause and effect.
pmc-13350243:
Sarah M. Ostrowski and colleagues developed a nose-delivered nanoparticle vaccine against respiratory syncytial virus in a 2026 mouse study. RSV is the top cause of serious chest infections in children under five, and current antibody protection fades quickly, leaving a gap for a childhood vaccine.

Their particle carries the virus's prefusion protein and can be loaded flexibly with antigen and boosters. In mice previously exposed to RSV, nose dosing raised helpful immune cells in the lung, including resident memory T cells, and gave complete protection for up to eight weeks with less mucus. Needle-free delivery to the airway where infection starts is an appealing route for young children.
pmc-13350343:
Fan Ruoxi and co-authors analysed in 2026 whether China's diagnosis-intervention packet payment system fits traditional Chinese medicine's personal style of care. The payment reform pays set amounts per case group, while Chinese medicine tailors treatment by syndrome pattern.

Using 48,398 inpatient records from one hospital between 2018 and 2021, they compared wards using much Chinese medicine against those using little. After the payment change, high-use services saw significant rises in both total hospital costs and patients' own payments. The evidence is meant to guide fairer payment adjustments so a standardised funding model does not quietly penalise traditional practice.
pmc-13351943:
Shiyu Zhang and co-authors test ultrasound signs of pleural invasion by lung cancer in a 2026 rabbit study. Invasion worsens outlook but is hard to judge during staging. Thirty rabbits carried a lung cancer model next to the chest lining, and ultrasound measured the contact surface and tumour widths.

A ratio of arch distance to upright tumour width separated deeper invasion levels, with a cut-off of 1.55. That cut-off gave sensitivity of 100.0 percent and accuracy of 92.9 percent in the model. Breaks in the inner pleural layer were also scored against tissue checks with special stains. Combining the ratio and the break sign improved judgement of invasion depth.
pmc-13358843:
Rakesh M Suri and Shaan A Asif wrote a 2026 commentary on robotic heart valve repair in hard cases. Calcium buildup around the mitral valve, called annular calcification, stiffens the ring the surgeon must sew to and narrows the margin for error. A team led by Pickering repaired such a valve in a 59-year-old woman using a fully robotic, camera-guided approach.

Her recovery was smooth and the repair held at four years. Suri and Asif argue the case shows how careful imaging and planning can widen what repair can do, while judgment still decides when repair is wise at all. The piece speaks to surgeons weighing bold technique against patient safety.
pmc-13359543:
Wolfgang Jungraithmayr and co-authors describe a silent lung defect in a 2026 case report. An adult with no symptoms had a patch of overinflated lung in the right lower lobe, found on CT scans. The cause was bronchial atresia: one small airway branch had never opened, likely from a mishap before birth. Mucus pooled past the block while the tissue beyond it swelled with trapped air.

A three-dimensional rebuild of the airway tree confirmed the single break, with all else normal. Because the patient feels well, the authors advise no treatment, only repeat scans to confirm the area stays stable. The case shows how imaging can name a rare defect without surgery.
pmc-13359943:
Julia K. Bar and co-authors test stem cells for cartilage repair in a 2026 study. Cartilage heals poorly, so engineers grow replacement tissue from stem cells on a scaffold. The team compared two human cell sources, fat tissue and dental pulp, grown on a biodegradable scaffold called PLCL. Primary cartilage cells on the same scaffold served as the benchmark.

Both stem cell types stuck to the scaffold, grew, kept their identity markers, and switched on cartilage-making proteins at levels close to the real cartilage cells. The pulp cells are a notable find, since they come from tissue often discarded. Both pairings look fit for bioimplants in future cartilage engineering.
pmc-13361843:
Ana Maria Bică and co-authors reviewed childhood acute myeloid leukemia cases in a 2026 study. This fast blood cancer varies widely in its biology, and gene profiling now guides risk sorting and care. The team looked back at 38 children newly diagnosed and treated between 2020 and 2025 at one center. Gene faults were mapped with classic chromosome tests, targeted probes, and modern sequencing.

Two-thirds of the children reached full remission after the first round of chemotherapy. The team linked remission to genomic risk, transplant decisions, and survival. They are frank that 38 cases make the study exploratory. Even so, single-center series show how gene-guided care plays out in real clinics, and where children with the hardest risks still fall through.
pmc-13362043:
Michał Pomorski and co-authors review pelvic organ prolapse with a focus on the central compartment in a 2026 paper. In apical prolapse, the uterus or the top of the vagina sinks because the highest level of pelvic support fails. It often drags the front and back walls with it, causing bulge, pressure, bladder and bowel trouble, and lost quality of life. The team searched four databases for studies through February 2026.

The review moves from gene risk factors and new biomarkers to today's surgery. Sacrocolpopexy, which anchors the vagina to the sacrum, gets close attention as the leading fix. Robotic assistance is the rising innovation in that operation. The authors aim to give surgeons a single map from molecular causes to the newest operating-room tools.
pmc-13363543:
Rabeea Razaq and a large team wrote a 2026 review on plasmonic nanomaterials for disease testing with SERS, a light method that reads molecular fingerprints. Tiny metal structures amplify the faint scatter signal of molecules near them by huge factors, letting tests catch cancer markers and stray tumor DNA at very low levels. The review covers material designs, early test results, and the pairing of these sensors with artificial intelligence.

AI sorting of the complex light signals promises faster, sharper answers at the bedside. Practical hurdles persist: surfaces foul with use, signals fade, and materials must prove safe against body tissue. The authors map where the field must harden before these sensitive tests reach routine clinics, while judging the outlook bright.
pmc-13364143:
Aoxiang Pan and colleagues present a 2026 study on labeling spacecraft parts directly from radar echoes, skipping the usual step of forming a radar image first. In the classic pipeline, making the image discards echo phase and scatter detail that could guide the labeling, and hand-marking pixels is costly. Their One-Stop Segmentation design works in the complex signal domain and adds an automatic labeling module that builds masks from the echoes' own scattering traits.

A matching network then learns from those labels to segment new echoes end to end. The authors report lower application cost through the shorter chain and machine-made labels, with spacecraft structure priors steering focus to bodies and edges. The frame targets on-orbit inspection and servicing.
pmc-13364743:
Dohwi Yun leads a team that maps in 2026 the world toll of liver cancer from 1990 to 2021, with a look to 2050. They draw on a huge world health data bank, split by age, sex, place, wealth, and cause. Death rates per head held near flat across the span.

Liver B germ stays the top cause, then liver C germ and strong drink. Risk marks shift by sex: drink and smoke lead for men, drug use and drink for women. On trend, the toll stays high to 2050, but cuts to drink and body risks could bend it down.
pmc-13367543:
Prakash Mishra and co-workers sum up in 2026 swift room care for blood cough, a sign that can run from mild to a flood that chokes breath. The first job is to sort true lung bleed from nose or gut blood, then guard the air way and find the source.

Scan with dye finds most bleed sites, while a scope can both find and treat. A clot drug mist shows worth as a fast add. A wide team, from lung and ray pros to chest knife pros, gives the best odds. Gaps stay in when to stack each step.
pmc-13367643:
Anthony Izzotti and co-workers find in 2026 a no metal route to build bridged ring goods from flat chain starts with a ring tip. A spark, by a plant made base or a Lewis acid, starts a join then ring crack run. The run builds a bridge ring frame in one pass.

Math maps point to an odd bent charge shape that lets the small ring grow in a rare way. The fresh frame end can catch a loose acid or fold to an inner ring to make a four ring good. Such frames feed drug and nat goods work.
pmc-13371743:
Artemisa R Dores and a large team surveyed body image strain across nine lands in a 2026 study. A total of 3,514 people filled in a web survey on worry about looks, web habits, gym habits, and drug use to shape the body. Social feeds push hard, thin, or built ideals each day.

Worry about looks showed in about one in eight people, with the top shares in Mexico, Japan, and Italy. Hard gym habits were less common, at under four in a hundred. The team links web strain, hard training, and body drugs as one chain of risk. Their counts can guide fair warnings and help plans in each land.
pmc-13374143:
Grand-Guillaume-Perrenoud and colleagues follow health students' views toward working in interprofessional teams, in 2026 health training research from Switzerland. Three undergraduate cohorts training as dieticians, midwives, nurses, or physiotherapists, who began between 2018 and 2021, answered a scale several times. Of 879 students who started, 234 gave data at least twice and entered the final analysis. The team modeled two attitude axes over time: teamwork, roles and duties, and community-centeredness, a focus on patients' community context.

No cross-lagged effects appeared between the two, meaning neither drove later change in the other. Both instead showed fair to strong stability across time, moving little once formed. Semester of study was positively associated with community-centeredness, while male sex was negatively associated with it, and program mattered too. pmc-13375643:
Filip Ventorp and co-authors tried a joy-loss drug in sad mood care in a 2026 trial. Joy loss, a flat feel where fun things stir no lift, is a core sign of mood ills and has few cures. The drug lifts a brain joy path and is used in nerve care.

A total of 85 adults with mood ills and high joy-loss scores joined the blind trial at one center. Half got the drug as an add-on for nine weeks, and half got a sham. The main score was change in joy-loss marks. The trial also checks if brain scans show the drug hit its mark, a link past trials lacked.
pmc-13377143:
Miscia Fortna and co-authors give long news on proton care in young men with prostate cancer in a 2026 study. The group held 85 men aged 50 or less, cared for from 2006 to 2017. Protons place their dose with a sharp stop, which may spare near parts.

Watch ran a mean of more than 12 years. At ten years, cancer-free rates by blood marks sat at nine in ten or full in each risk set. Just three men saw the cancer come back. Harm scores from doctors and tales from patients were both logged. Long, clean runs in young men count, since they live long with late harms.
pmc-13377343:
Esposto and colleagues link brain structure to metabolic markers in adults with autism spectrum disorder, in 2026 neuroimaging research. The study scanned 145 adults, 74 with autism and 71 controls, using 3-Tesla MRI to measure cortical thickness and brain volumes, plus magnetic resonance spectroscopy for brain lactate, a fuel-use signal. Blood markers of mitochondrial and energy metabolism, including acylcarnitine molecules, were measured alongside symptom scales for autism and ADHD traits in both groups.
